Self-tests check the operation of control systems.
Navigation systems, including GPS where available, supply position information.
The processor uses sensor and navigation data to determine control actions.
Actuators adjust components such as throttle, wing flaps and rudder.
Reliable handling of abnormal conditions is essential.

Automatic control could reduce some errors caused by pilot fatigue or mistakes.
Continuous sensor-based adjustments could improve passenger comfort.
Reduced flight-crew requirements could lower some staffing costs.
A design without a conventional cockpit could allow changes to the aircraft's shape.
Automated monitoring could identify developing problems quickly.
These are potential design benefits rather than guarantees of safe operation.

Unusual emergencies may be difficult for the control software to handle.
No on-board pilot may make some security or passenger emergencies harder to manage.
Hacking could compromise control or communication.
Software defects can produce unsafe behaviour.
Failure of sensors or navigation inputs can affect decisions.
Some passengers may be unwilling to fly without a pilot.
Strong testing, redundancy and emergency arrangements would be required.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Prolonged IT use can be associated with eyestrain, headaches, RSI and back or neck discomfort.
The risk depends on activities, posture, equipment position and working conditions.
Repeated typing and clicking are associated with RSI.
Poor sitting position or monitor height can contribute to back and neck strain.
Screen glare and unsuitable lighting can contribute to eyestrain.
Prevention strategies should address the specific cause.
Health problems are different from physical safety hazards such as trailing cables.
Keep health conditions separate from physical safety hazards and match each condition to its cause.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Sitting at a computer for long periods can contribute to back and neck strain.
Poor posture while using the computer puts strain on the body.
An unsuitable chair may fail to support the back.
A screen at the wrong height or angle can cause awkward neck positioning.
A cramped workspace can encourage poor posture.
Remaining in one position without movement can increase discomfort.
Explain poor posture or unsuitable positioning while using the computer.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Use an adjustable ergonomic chair that supports the back.
Sit upright with the back supported.
Use a footrest where needed for a supported position.
Position the screen so its top is at or just below eye level.
Adjust the screen angle to avoid bending the neck awkwardly.
Arrange enough space to work comfortably.
Take opportunities to stretch or exercise the back rather than simply stopping work.
If suggesting a break, specify stretching or exercise. Use distinct measures such as an adjustable chair and footrest.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

RSI stands for Repetitive Strain Injury.
Repeated movements during computer work can affect fingers, wrists or other parts of the upper limbs.
Continuous keyboard typing is a common exam example.
Repeated clicking of a mouse button is another example.
Holding the mouse tightly or incorrectly can add strain.
Poor arm or wrist position and a cramped workspace can contribute.
A cause describes the activity or condition, rather than naming RSI again.
Give causes such as repeated typing or clicking, not the name of the condition again.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Use an ergonomic keyboard or mouse.
Arrange the workspace so the user is not cramped.
Maintain a comfortable arm and wrist position.
Use an appropriate wrist support.
Regularly rest and exercise the fingers and hands.
Voice input can reduce repeated keyboard or mouse activity.
Use distinct strategies rather than repeating the same break or ergonomic-equipment point.
For breaks, specify resting or exercising the hands. Give distinct strategies rather than repeating ergonomic equipment.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Staring at a computer screen for a long time can cause eyestrain.
Sitting too close to the screen can contribute.
Glare and reflections make the display harder to view.
Screen brightness that does not match the room lighting can be uncomfortable.
Flicker and dirt on the screen can make viewing more difficult.
Unsuitable screen position can contribute to discomfort.
Causes should be kept separate from prevention measures.
Keep causes separate from prevention measures.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Adjust screen brightness to match the room lighting.
Reduce glare using blinds, suitable screen positioning or an anti-glare screen.
Use a clear, flicker-free display.
Keep the screen free of dust and dirt.
Look away from the screen regularly to rest the eyes.
Sit at a suitable viewing distance rather than too close.
Have eyes tested regularly and use appropriate correction where advised.
Specify matching screen brightness to room lighting. Take breaks or lower brightness alone is insufficient.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Prolonged screen viewing can be associated with headaches.
Unsuitable room lighting can make viewing uncomfortable.
Glare or reflected light can cause squinting and discomfort.
A flickering display can contribute to discomfort.
Screen brightness that does not match surrounding lighting can be a factor.
A cause should identify the working condition rather than merely repeat the symptom.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Reduce reflections with blinds, an anti-glare screen or suitable screen positioning.
Match screen brightness to the room lighting.
Use a clear, flicker-free display.
Look away from the screen regularly and vary screen work.
Have eyes tested where appropriate.
Use suitable workstation positioning to reduce associated strain.
Make glare, screen positioning and lighting measures specific to the health risk.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Some laser printing equipment can emit ozone during operation.
Accumulation in a poorly ventilated area can irritate the respiratory system.
The textbook also identifies dry skin as a possible irritation symptom.
This is a health issue associated with emissions, rather than a mechanical printer hazard.
The amount of exposure depends on the equipment and ventilation.
Not every printer produces the same emissions.
Explain the printer-emission health effect accurately rather than confusing it with a physical safety hazard.
Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment

Provide suitable ventilation in areas containing printing equipment.
A designated printer room can separate high-use equipment from regularly occupied work areas.
Position and maintain equipment according to its operating guidance.
Consider a suitable alternative printing technology where appropriate.
The aim is to reduce exposure to accumulated emissions.
Ventilation and equipment choice address the source of the risk.

Open a suitable word-processing or publishing application.
Obtain photographs from a camera, scanner, existing files or permitted online sources.
Transfer and save images, then import them into the document.
Crop, resize and position images without distorting them.
Enter or import text and apply suitable formatting and text wrapping.
Proofread the content, check the layout, save and print or export the document.
A PDF can preserve the intended layout when sharing with suitable viewing software.
Use images and other material with the required permission or licence.

A spell checker compares words with a dictionary.
Correct proper nouns or scientific terms may be flagged because they are missing from the dictionary.
A different language or language variant can produce inappropriate suggestions.
A correctly spelled word used in the wrong context may not be identified.
Check flagged words before changing them.
Add a verified word to the dictionary or ignore it where appropriate.
Manual proofreading remains necessary.
A correctly spelled name or scientific term may be absent from the dictionary. Check it before adding it or ignoring the flag.

Choose content, language and presentation for the intended audience.
Use clear readable fonts and an appropriate text size.
Create a clear distinction between headings and body text.
Balance text, suitable images and white space rather than overcrowding pages.
Columns can organise longer articles and photographs.
Use consistent formatting and contrasting colours.
Choose printed or electronic delivery according to audience access.
An electronic newsletter may add links, multimedia and interactive features.
Make language, layout and images suitable for the actual audience; a newsletter is not automatically interactive software.

An event poster should state the event, date, time and location.
Include relevant admission charges, contact details and accessibility information.
A film poster can include an appropriate image, release date and principal cast.
Use a clear visual hierarchy and text readable at the intended viewing distance.
Place posters where the intended audience is likely to see them.
Large printed posters can be eye-catching, but display space may be costly.
Outdoor posters can be damaged by weather and become outdated.
Digital distribution avoids some printing costs but needs a suitable display or device.

An organisation can create its own website or pay for space on another site.
A site can be built with web-authoring tools or a content management system.
Content includes suitable text, images and other permitted media.
Hosting places the website files on a server so users can access them.
Development may require design skills, software and technical support.
Hosting, maintenance, content updates and security have continuing costs.
Test pages, links and presentation before making the site available.

Websites can combine text, images, audio, video and animation.
Links, navigation and search help users find detailed information.
Content can be updated without reprinting and redistributing copies.
Websites can reach users over a wide geographical area.
Usage data can help an organisation assess how people use the site.
Users need a suitable device and connection; a printed item can be read without these.
A website requires maintenance and security, and users still need to find it.
Printed advertising can target a particular local audience through distribution or placement.
Explain how the website’s features communicate the required information in context, rather than giving generic advantages.

A multimedia presentation combines text with images, sound, video or animation.
Hyperlinks and interactive controls can let users choose a path through the material.
Transitions and animation can support an explanation when used appropriately.
Content and language can be tailored to the audience.
Consistent layout, clear headings and balanced white space improve readability.
Charts can present statistics and suitable images can explain ideas visually.
Presentations can be edited and reused.
Obtain the required rights or permission for included material.
Match design choices to the stated audience and explain their purpose; do not substitute a different audience.

Creating and presenting multimedia requires suitable hardware and software.
Equipment failure can interrupt the presentation.
Online content may depend on a reliable connection.
Excessive animation, sound or transitions can distract from the message.
Overcrowded slides can be difficult to read.
Incompatible formats or missing media can prevent correct playback.
Preparation and testing take time.

Streaming delivers live or recorded media over a network for playback as data arrives.
The user need not retain a complete downloaded copy before playback begins.
Downloading saves a file locally so it can be used later, subject to access restrictions.
Streaming uses less persistent local storage but normally needs a suitable connection during playback.
Insufficient bandwidth can cause pauses, lag or sound and picture synchronisation problems.
A downloaded file uses local storage but may be usable without a continuing connection.
Subscriptions, availability and ownership depend on the service; streaming is not necessarily free.
Define streaming as playback of delivered media, use generic terms and develop both benefits and drawbacks in the stated context.

A buffer is temporary storage used between receiving media data and playing it.
Incoming packets are collected in the buffer.
The player takes data from the buffer at the rate needed for playback.
Stored data helps absorb short variations in packet arrival time.
If the buffer empties, playback may pause while more data arrives.
A consistently inadequate connection cannot be fixed by buffering alone.
Some initial delay may be needed to collect enough data to start smoothly.
Link poor bandwidth to buffering during playback; show understanding of streaming rather than relying only on personal experience.

E-publications are electronic versions of material such as books, magazines, journals and catalogues.
They can be read on suitable computers, mobile devices or e-readers.
Search, navigation and hyperlinks help readers find information.
Some formats support enlarged text, text-to-speech, multimedia and interactivity.
Updated versions can be distributed without printing a new edition.
Many publications can be carried on one device.
They reduce printing and distribution needs but require compatible equipment and power.
An e-publication is not necessarily social media or dependent on a continuous internet connection.
Describe electronic features such as hyperlinks, multimedia and interactivity. An e-publication is not necessarily social media or continuously online.

A cellular network divides an area into coverage cells served by base stations.
A mobile device communicates by radio with a nearby base station.
Overlapping coverage helps maintain communication as the user moves.
As signal conditions change, the network can hand the connection to another cell.
This transfer is called handover.
Coverage depends on the availability of suitable base stations and radio conditions.
Remote areas may have limited cellular coverage.
Cellular phones rely on land-based towers; satellite communication is a different service, not satellite navigation.

A SIM identifies a mobile subscription to the cellular network.
It contains information used in subscriber authentication.
A physical SIM or eSIM supports access to the subscribed cellular service.
A mobile device can also use Wi-Fi to join a local network.
Wi-Fi internet access depends on the access point's external connection.
Cellular and Wi-Fi are different routes for connecting the device.
Connection availability and charges depend on the service used.

SMS stands for Short Message Service.
It allows short text messages to be sent through a mobile network.
Sender and recipient do not have to take part at the same moment.
A message can wait for delivery when the recipient is temporarily unavailable.
It is useful when a voice call would be inconvenient.
Predictive text can speed entry but may introduce unintended words.
Charges and delivery depend on the mobile service.

A mobile phone allows voice communication while away from a fixed telephone.
Its battery supports portable operation.
It can be used for emergency contact and business communication.
Calls require suitable network coverage and service availability.
Moving between coverage areas can require handover.
Poor signal conditions can reduce quality or disconnect a call.
Battery exhaustion prevents ordinary use until power is restored.
Link coverage to the communication service: cellular phones need suitable land-based base stations.

VoIP stands for Voice over Internet Protocol.
Speech is captured and encoded into digital data.
The data is sent in packets over an IP network, commonly the internet.
The receiving device reconstructs and plays the sound.
A microphone and speaker or headset provide audio input and output.
Existing computers or smartphones can avoid the need for a separate telephone.
VoIP can reduce call costs and support features such as group calls or video, depending on the service.
Expand VoIP correctly and describe communication over an IP network. Develop benefits for the stated company or user.

VoIP quality depends on sufficient bandwidth and a stable network connection.
Delays or lost packets can cause distorted speech, dropouts or lag.
Speaker sound picked up by a microphone can produce echo.
Internet failure can interrupt internet-based calling.
Unauthorised access can expose account details or communications.
Scam calls and malicious links or downloads can put users at risk.
Appropriate authentication, encryption and updated software help protect the service.
Explain VoIP-specific drawbacks such as internet dependence and call quality, rather than generic mobile-phone claims.
Video calling and cloud meeting services

Video calling lets users in different locations see and hear each other in real time.
A camera captures images, a microphone captures sound, and a display and speakers provide output.
Meeting services can support group calls, shared screens, documents and recordings.
Built-in smartphone hardware supports portable participation.
Remote meetings can save travel time, travel costs and accommodation costs.
A small screen can make people or shared details harder to see.
A stable connection is needed to avoid lag, frozen images or disconnection.
Audio-only conferencing uses less bandwidth but cannot convey visual information or body language.
Use generic equipment names and explain their roles. For smartphone evaluation, develop effects such as screen size and connection reliability.

A mobile device can access internet services through cellular data or Wi-Fi.
A responsive or mobile-optimised page adapts content to the screen size.
Readable text and appropriately sized controls reduce unnecessary zooming.
Layouts should avoid difficult horizontal scrolling.
Large media files can increase loading time and data use.
Connection speed, charges and battery use vary with the device, service and activity.
A mobile page should preserve the information and functions needed by its audience.

A computer model is a software representation of a real system.
It uses data, mathematical relationships and programmed rules.
The user supplies inputs or changes variables.
The model processes these to predict outcomes or simulate behaviour.
Different what-if scenarios can be tested.
Results are compared and interpreted before decisions are made.
A computer model is different from a physical scale model.
A computer model is a software representation using formulas to predict outcomes, not a physical model of a computer.

Models can test dangerous situations without exposing people to the real hazard.
Alternative designs can be compared before expensive construction.
Variables can be changed repeatedly to explore what-if scenarios.
Time can be sped up or slowed down to study changes.
Computers can perform complex calculations quickly.
Models can reveal problems before a real system is built or changed.
The usefulness of a benefit depends on the situation being modelled.
Develop the benefit and its reason in the actual modelling context; construction-material savings do not fit weather forecasting.

An incorrect formula, program or input can produce incorrect results.
A model may omit important variables or unexpected events.
Simplifying assumptions can make simulated behaviour differ from reality.
Specialist hardware, software and skilled staff can be expensive.
Development, testing and interpretation take time.
Users need to understand how to use the model and assess its results.
Overreliance can lead to decisions based on predictions that are not sufficiently realistic.
Explain how inaccurate inputs, omitted variables or programming errors make the particular model’s results unreliable.

A spreadsheet can model income, expenditure, sales or a budget.
Inputs can include prices, quantities, wages and other costs.
Formulae calculate values such as revenue, total cost and profit.
Changing an input recalculates the dependent results.
What-if scenarios show the possible effect of price or spending changes.
Charts can help compare outcomes.
Incorrect formulae or omitted expenses can make predictions misleading.
The user must distinguish predicted figures from actual financial results.
Evaluate the budget model itself: calculations and what-if tests versus incorrect formulas or omitted expenses.

A design model represents a bridge or building before construction.
Inputs can include dimensions, materials, loads and environmental conditions.
Tests can simulate wind, vibration, earthquakes, water pressure or fire conditions as relevant.
The model predicts stress, movement or possible failure.
Designers modify the design and rerun tests.
This reduces the cost and danger of discovering faults after construction.
Results still depend on realistic assumptions and accurate data.
Physical scale tests can supplement computer-model validation.
Discuss the computer simulation rather than a physical model, and explain why the safety and cost effects matter.

A design can be displayed from several viewpoints.
Rotation helps inspect parts hidden in a single view.
Zooming allows examination of fine details.
Different designs or materials can be compared.
Simulation results can show where a design may fail under particular conditions.
Visualisation supports changes before construction starts.
A convincing display does not by itself prove that the model's calculations are correct.

A flood model predicts water levels, flows and possible flood extent or depth.
Inputs can include river cross-sections and surrounding terrain.
Bridge, weir and sluice dimensions affect predicted flow.
Tides, winds, upstream flow and downstream levels provide boundary conditions.
The simulation covers a specified time period.
Past observations can be used to calibrate or test the model.
Different scenarios help identify areas at risk.

Flood models can compare barriers and other protective measures before construction.
Sensors can continuously monitor water level, wave height and other relevant conditions.
Automated measurements reduce the need to expose people to hazardous locations.
New readings can reveal deteriorating conditions quickly.
Warnings can be issued earlier when thresholds or predictions indicate danger.
Observed data can be compared with predictions to refine the model.
Defences may be modified as new evidence is collected.

A motorway simulation models how lane closures affect traffic flow.
Inputs can include traffic density, time of day and vehicle speed.
Different lane arrangements and speed restrictions can be tested.
A breakdown or incident can be simulated.
Outputs can show queues, delays and throughput.
Designers compare scenarios to choose an arrangement allowing work and traffic movement.
Simulation is safer and cheaper than repeatedly experimenting on the real motorway.
Results depend on realistic traffic data.

Collect vehicle counts for each direction at the junction.
Record the time of day and day type, including weekends or holidays.
Measure queue lengths and time needed to clear the junction.
Record turning movements and pedestrian-crossing demand.
Include slow vehicles and other factors affecting clearance time.
Induction-loop sensors can collect repeated vehicle data.
The data should represent the real range of traffic conditions before the model is trusted.
Explain data used by the model and its effect on simulated flow; do not switch to describing only live traffic control.

Enter measured traffic data and run the model.
Compare its initial results with observed traffic flow.
Vary the traffic-light timings.
Increase or decrease traffic and turning movements.
Test pedestrian demand and emergency-vehicle scenarios.
Compare resulting queues, delays and potentially unsafe conditions.
Use the results to improve the proposed junction design.
A simulation tests scenarios; it is not the same as controlling the live traffic lights.
Describe running the model and varying scenarios. A live controller changing actual lights is a different process.

Road sensors detect vehicles and send data to the control system.
Analogue readings need conversion where the processing system requires digital data.
The processor compares current data with stored rules or parameters.
It decides whether the signal timings need to change.
Control signals are sent to the lights.
The lights change according to the permitted sequence.
The system repeats its monitoring and decision cycle as conditions change.

Weather stations measure temperature, pressure, humidity, rainfall and wind conditions.
Observations are entered into a mathematical model of the atmosphere.
A three-dimensional grid represents locations and conditions.
The computer calculates how conditions may change over time.
Results support forecasts and early warnings of severe weather.
Computers handle many variables and complex calculations faster than manual methods.
Predictions are compared with actual weather so the model can be assessed and improved.
Missing variables, inaccurate data and high computing costs remain limitations.
Explain how modelling predicts weather using complex calculations; listing sensors alone does not explain its purpose.

Industrial robots carry out programmed tasks under computer control.
Uses include welding, paint spraying, component assembly and moving goods.
An embedded controller or linked computer issues instructions.
Sensors provide information about position, objects and operating conditions.
Actuators move the robot or operate its tools.
Robots are useful for repeated tasks and work hazardous to humans.
They need suitable programming, setup and maintenance.

A robot can be programmed with a sequence of instructions.
A worker can guide the robot arm through the required movements.
The controller records positions or coordinates for later repetition.
Wearable sensors can capture a demonstrator's movements in suitable systems.
An interface can also let an operator guide movements and save the sequence.
The stored sequence is tested and adjusted before regular operation.
Teaching by demonstration is an alternative to typing all movement instructions.
Describe how demonstrated movements are recorded and stored. Merely naming AI or rewording typed code is insufficient.

Sensors provide feedback about the robot's surroundings or state.
They can detect an object, its position or the availability of material.
The controller uses the readings to decide the next action.
An end effector is the tool or attachment at the working end of the robot.
Examples include a gripper, welding tool or spray nozzle.
The attachment must suit the task.
Feedback helps the robot perform repeated actions in the correct position.

Robots can work continuously without ordinary rest breaks.
They can perform hazardous tasks without exposing workers to the same risk.
Repeated movements can improve consistency and productivity.
Accurate control can reduce waste or defects.
Purchase, setup and maintenance can be expensive.
Reprogramming or new equipment may be needed for different tasks.
Automation can displace workers or reduce some skills.
Unexpected situations outside the programmed task can cause difficulty.

Production lines divide manufacture into repeated stages.
Controllers coordinate stations such as filling, sealing and labelling.
Sensors check product position and measurements.
Actuators move products or operate tools.
Automatic checks can identify and reject defective items.
Consistent processing can improve output quality and productivity.
Reduced staffing needs can lower some operating costs.
Initial equipment costs and breakdowns can be significant.

A sensor detects a bottle in the filling position.
The controller receives the signal and commands an actuator to open the filling valve.
A level sensor repeatedly measures the liquid level.
The controller compares the reading with the required level.
When the bottle is full, an actuator closes the valve.
The controller activates the conveyor motor to move the filled bottle and position the next one.
The cycle repeats until stopped or a fault requires intervention.

Each student's magnetic card stores identifying information or an ID linked to a record.
The student swipes the card through a reader on arrival or departure.
The system identifies the student in the database.
It records the date and entry or exit time.
Records can be searched to produce attendance summaries.
Reports can be shared with authorised teachers or parents.
A missed swipe or use of another person's card can make the record inaccurate.

An additional PIN can reduce use of another student's attendance card.
Access permissions protect attendance records from unauthorised viewing.
Lost cards can be disabled and replaced.
Entry and exit records show recorded events, not necessarily a person's exact current location.
Location tracking requires a suitable separate tracking system.
A passive RFID identity tag alone does not provide continuous GPS location.
Tracking raises privacy concerns because it can reveal people's movements.

The school enrols each student and stores a biometric template linked to their identity.
On arrival or departure, a scanner captures the selected biometric.
Software compares it with the authorised stored templates.
A matching record identifies the student.
The system records the date and time of the attendance event.
Unmatched or unreadable captures require an appropriate exception process.
Biometric records need protection from unauthorised access.

A biometric cannot be forgotten or misplaced in the same way as a card.
It makes it harder for another student to register using a borrowed card.
Magnetic cards can be lost, copied or damaged.
Biometric enrolment and specialist equipment can be costly and time-consuming.
Dirty readers or injured fingers can cause recognition failures.
Biometric data creates privacy and security concerns.
The comparison must use the actual method specified, such as handprints rather than fingerprints.
Keep the specified biometric consistent: handprints and fingerprints are different examples. Develop both benefits and drawbacks.

Inputs include student identities, assessment marks, attendance, punctuality and behaviour records.
The system stores and organises the records.
Processing can calculate individual or class averages.
Actual grades can be compared with forecast or target grades.
Sorting, filtering and charts help identify patterns and students needing support.
Outputs include progress reports, grade lists and statistical summaries.
Each output should be linked to the data and processing that produce it.
Link the student data to processing and a specific output, such as marks being averaged to produce a progress report.

Computer-aided learning uses specially designed software to help someone learn a subject.
It can let learners work at their own pace and revisit material.
Interactive tasks, multimedia and simulations can support explanation.
Tests can produce immediate scores and feedback.
The system can record progress and adapt material to previous performance.
Learners may access material at convenient times.
CAL supports a learning approach rather than simply meaning any use of a computer.
Define CAL as specially designed software assisting learning a subject; listing features alone does not give the definition.

CAL needs suitable devices, software and sometimes network access.
Purchase, integration and staff training can have costs.
Technical faults can interrupt learning.
Learners may become distracted or isolated.
Software may not answer unusual questions as a teacher can.
Simulations do not replace every form of practical equipment experience.
Teachers still need to select suitable activities and support learners.

An online booking system displays current availability.
A selected seat or time slot can be held temporarily during checkout.
The system checks availability again when confirming the transaction.
A successful booking updates the shared records immediately.
Other users should no longer be offered the same exclusive seat or slot.
Timed holds can be released if checkout is abandoned.
Coordinated updates prevent double-booking when several users book at once.
Describe general booking characteristics such as immediate confirmation and prevention of double-booking, rather than narrating one transaction.

Customers can book from different locations at any time the service is available.
Availability and confirmation can be shown immediately.
Users may choose seats or time slots from the available options.
Electronic tickets reduce printing and delivery needs.
An organisation can monitor capacity and manage bookings centrally.
Users need access to suitable equipment and a connection.
Service failure, incorrect details or payment problems can prevent completion.
Personal-data security and reduced face-to-face assistance are potential drawbacks.
Apply benefits and drawbacks to the customer and the stated booking situation; do not substitute retail shopping or system-development points.

Enter departure point, destination, travel dates and passenger details.
Search for available flights and compare suitable options.
Select the required flight and check the fare and conditions.
Enter passenger information accurately.
Provide the required payment information and confirm the booking.
The system records the booking and updates availability.
A confirmation and electronic ticket or booking reference are issued.
Check the confirmation before travelling.

Select the event, performance date and time.
View availability, often through an interactive seating plan.
Choose the required seats and ticket types.
The system holds the selection while the user completes the booking.
Enter the required details and complete payment.
Confirmed seats are marked as booked in the shared records.
The user receives a confirmation and ticket or booking reference.

An electronic ticket is delivered digitally, for example through email or an application.
It contains booking details and an identifying reference or code.
A QR code can represent ticket-identification data.
A scanner reads the code at entry.
The system checks the code against booking records and admission rules.
A valid ticket permits the appropriate entry and can be marked as used.
Electronic delivery can reduce printing costs and queues, but users still need access to their ticket.
Explain the benefit of electronic delivery in context, such as reduced ticket printing and quicker entry.

Select the sporting event, day and number of tickets.
Choose a preferred seating area or block where applicable.
The system searches for available places.
Select the required tickets and check details and charges.
Enter customer and payment information and confirm.
The system updates availability and sends confirmation or tickets.
Some events use general admission instead of individual reserved seats.
Travel or accommodation can be separate optional booking services.

ATM stands for Automated Teller Machine.
Services can include cash withdrawal and balance enquiries.
Some machines provide mini statements or transaction information.
Suitable ATMs may accept cash or cheque deposits.
Other supported services may include transfers or bill payments.
The customer provides authentication and selects the required service.
The available functions depend on the machine and banking network.
Answer the particular ATM service and requested stage; mini-statement processing is different from cash withdrawal.
ATM cash withdrawal: user and system stages

The ATM reads the inserted card and accepts the customer's PIN and withdrawal request.
The system communicates with the bank to check the card, account and authentication.
It checks whether the card is valid and whether restrictions apply.
It checks available funds and the permitted withdrawal limit.
If authorised, the transaction is recorded and the account balance is updated.
The ATM returns the card and dispenses the cash in the system's required order.
A receipt may be printed if selected.
Entering data is input; validation and balance checks are processing; dispensing cash is output.
Entering a PIN is input; checking it, account funds and withdrawal limits is processing. Keep these stages distinct.

Authenticate and choose the cheque-deposit service at a suitable ATM.
Insert the cheque as instructed.
The machine captures the cheque image.
Recognition software reads the relevant printed or written details.
The user checks the displayed amount and confirms or corrects it as allowed.
The system records the deposit and may issue a receipt.
Funds may remain pending until the cheque has been checked and cleared.
The exact procedure depends on the bank and machine.

ATMs provide access to supported services outside branch opening hours.
Convenient locations can reduce the need to visit a staffed branch.
Routine transactions can be completed without a teller.
A damaged card or faulty machine can prevent access.
Daily withdrawal limits or fees may apply.
Shoulder surfing, card copying and theft create security risks.
Machines can run out of cash or lose their connection.
Customers receive less personal assistance than at a staffed counter.

Electronic Funds Transfer moves money between accounts through electronic instructions.
The payer supplies the destination account and payment details.
The banking system checks and processes the instruction.
Account records are updated to debit the payer and credit the recipient as appropriate.
Payroll payments and card payments are examples.
Electronic processing avoids physically moving cash or a paper cheque for each payment.
Authentication and accurate recipient details are important.

EFT can be faster and more convenient than handling cash or paper cheques.
It can reduce manual processing and cash-handling costs.
Electronic records provide an audit trail.
Payments can be initiated remotely or scheduled where supported.
Incorrect recipient details can send money to the wrong account.
Fraud or compromised credentials can cause unauthorised transfers.
Access depends on the payment system and communication facilities.
Fees, timing and reversal rights vary with the service and banking rules.

The terminal reads the payment card's chip and transaction details.
The customer enters the required PIN.
The system checks the authentication and card validity.
The payment request is sent securely through the payment network.
The issuer checks the account or available credit and relevant limits.
An authorisation or rejection is returned.
For an approved transaction, the payment is recorded and funds are transferred through the banking process.
A receipt can be issued; a PIN adds protection if the card is stolen.

A debit-card payment is normally charged against funds in the linked bank account.
A credit-card payment uses credit provided by the issuer, subject to a limit.
Credit-card spending must be repaid under the account terms.
Interest or fees may apply if credit is not repaid as required.
Both can be used for electronic payments where accepted.
Both need protection of card and authentication details.
Charges, limits and consumer protections depend on the issuer and applicable rules.

A cheque gives written instructions for a bank payment.
It provides a record of the intended payee and amount.
It avoids carrying the equivalent amount in cash.
Processing and clearing can take time.
A cheque can be rejected if it is invalid or funds are insufficient.
Forgery, alteration or theft can create fraud risks.
Acceptance, charges and any stop-payment arrangements depend on banking rules.
Electronic payments can be more convenient where available.

The cheque is scanned to create a digital image.
Recognition software reads details such as bank information, account information and the amount.
Relevant image and data files are sent electronically through the clearing system.
The paying bank checks the account, cheque validity and payment conditions.
It sends an approval or rejection response.
Approved payments lead to the appropriate account updates.
Image transfer reduces the need to transport the original paper cheque through every stage.
Recognition errors and uncertain details require checking.

A patient database links records to a unique patient identifier.
Records can include personal details, medical history, allergies, diagnoses and treatment.
Scans and other investigation results can be linked to the record.
Authorised staff can search for relevant information quickly.
Shared records support communication between healthcare providers.
Pharmacy records and electronic prescriptions support medication management.
Current records can help staff identify known allergies or possible medicine interactions.
Confidential information needs controlled access and accurate updating.

CT or MRI data can be used to construct a three-dimensional digital model.
A 3D printer builds a physical representation in layers.
Anatomical models can show organs, blood vessels, tumours or damaged bones.
Clinicians can use the model to explain a condition or planned procedure.
Surgeons can plan and practise aspects of a procedure before operating.
A bone model can help test the position of plates or screws.
The printed aid represents anatomy; it is different from printing living tissue or a prosthetic limb.
Give the specific medical use, such as an anatomical model for surgical planning, rather than repeating an example already supplied.

A prosthetic is an artificial replacement for a missing body part.
A digital design can be customised to the individual.
A 3D printer builds the designed shape layer by layer.
The design can be saved, modified and reused.
Customised production can reduce some manufacturing time or cost compared with particular manual methods.
The printer and suitable materials can be expensive.
Printing can take time, and a defective print may need replacement.
The finished prosthetic must meet its required fit and performance needs.
Qualify comparisons: a customised prosthetic, expensive equipment to buy, or time taken to print. Faster or expensive alone is too vague.

Tissue engineering uses cells, suitable materials and supporting structures to develop biological tissue.
Bioprinting places biological materials in controlled layers.
A digital design guides the position of the deposited material.
Supporting structures help the printed tissue retain its form.
Applications studied include skin, bone and vascular tissue models.
Living tissue must remain viable and develop the required structure and function.
Research towards replacement organs is different from routine printing of non-living anatomical models.

Biomimetics means designing structures or systems that imitate features found in nature.
Bio-inks can contain living cells within a supporting material such as a hydrogel.
A printer places the material according to a digital pattern.
Layering can create tissue-like shapes or channels.
Artificial vessel research aims to reproduce useful features of natural blood vessels.
The cells and supporting material must be compatible with the intended biological use.
Producing a vessel-like structure does not by itself establish suitability for implantation.

Customised printed tablets are sometimes called printlets.
A digital design specifies the required shape, structure and composition.
The printing material contains the medicine and suitable supporting ingredients.
The printer deposits or binds material in repeated layers until the tablet is formed.
Shape and internal structure can affect the release of the medicine.
A design can combine specified medicines or doses where clinically appropriate.
The textbook also describes vapour deposition, in which evaporated medicine forms thin films on a cooled surface.
Printing methods differ; not every printed tablet uses vapour deposition.
Explain repeated layers using medicine-containing material; describing plastic or metal printing misses the tablet context.

Customised manufacture can tailor a medicine's form or dose to an individual prescription.
A designed structure can help control the release profile.
A combined tablet may simplify a prescribed multi-medicine regimen.
More suitable dosing could reduce waste or unwanted exposure in some applications.
Potential benefits depend on accurate design, materials, production and clinical validation.
A digital blueprint could support local production using suitable authorised equipment.
These are potential applications, not a guarantee that any printed formulation is safe or available.

An expert system uses stored specialist knowledge and rules to help solve problems in a particular field.
A user interface gathers facts or responses from the user.
An inference engine applies rules to knowledge and supplied facts.
The system produces a conclusion, recommendation or possible solution.
An explanation system can show how the conclusion was reached.
Applications include medical diagnosis, prospecting, identification, financial advice and route scheduling.
Its expertise is limited to the domain and knowledge represented in the system.
Apply expert-system components to the stated specialist task rather than describing an unrelated application.

Expert systems can provide consistent answers to the same facts and rules.
Stored expertise can be available when a human specialist is unavailable.
They can process relevant facts quickly and explain their reasoning.
Knowledge can be retained and shared.
Building and maintaining the system requires expertise, time and money.
Incorrect user input or inaccurate stored knowledge can cause incorrect conclusions.
New situations absent from the knowledge base may not be handled well.
Users can become overdependent on an impersonal system with limited judgement.
Link an incorrect result to its cause, such as wrong responses, incorrect knowledge or a new condition absent from the system.

The user interface allows communication between the user and the expert system.
It displays questions and accepts responses.
Responses may include yes/no answers or entered facts.
Later questions can depend on earlier answers.
It displays conclusions, probabilities or recommendations.
It can show the explanation of the result.
Authorised experts may use an interface to enter or correct knowledge.
Its role is more specific than simply being a GUI or command-line interface.
Explain questions displayed, responses accepted and results shown. Simply saying it allows interaction is incomplete.

The explanation system tells the user how a conclusion was reached.
It can identify the facts and rules used.
It can describe the decision process step by step.
This helps the user understand or assess a recommendation.
Some systems also present a confidence or likelihood value.
Explaining the reasoning is different from merely displaying the final answer.
Explain how the reasoning is shown step by step, rather than repeating explanation system.

The inference engine is the reasoning component of an expert system.
It receives the facts or responses supplied through the user interface.
It searches relevant knowledge and applies rules from the rules base.
It compares conditions with known facts.
Rules can derive new facts or suggest further questions.
The process continues towards a conclusion or possible solutions.
Results are passed for display, with reasoning available to the explanation system.
Explain the inference engine applying rules to knowledge and user facts; naming the components alone is insufficient.

The knowledge base stores specialist knowledge about the system's domain.
It is populated from experts and other reliable domain resources.
It contains facts, descriptions and relationships relevant to the problems being solved.
Rules may be held within the wider knowledge base or described separately as a rules base.
The inference engine uses this knowledge with user-supplied facts.
Missing, outdated or incorrect information can produce unreliable conclusions.
It is more specific than an unspecified collection of data.
Describe specialist facts and information supplied by experts, not merely a collection of data.

The rules base contains logical rules used to reason about the problem.
Rules often take an IF condition THEN conclusion or action form.
Conditions are tested against user-supplied and stored facts.
The inference engine applies matching rules.
A rule may derive another fact, select a further question or support a conclusion.
Rules encode specialist reasoning for the particular domain.
The rules base supplies the criteria; the inference engine applies them.
Explain the criteria and rules applied to the inputs, and how they support searching and reasoning.
Setting up and testing an expert system

Define the specialist problem and the scope of the system.
Gather facts and reasoning from suitable experts and other reliable sources.
Organise the knowledge base.
Create logical rules representing how conclusions should be drawn.
Provide an inference engine and a suitable user interface.
Provide explanations where required.
Test known cases and compare the results with expert conclusions.
Correct errors and update the knowledge and rules as the domain changes.
Distinguish setting up expert knowledge from a user answering questions; label the required inputs and outputs precisely.

The interface asks questions about symptoms and other relevant patient information.
The user supplies responses, sometimes through yes/no questions.
Responses can determine which questions are asked next.
The inference engine searches the knowledge base using the rules base.
The system produces possible diagnoses or likelihoods.
The explanation system shows how the results were reached.
Incorrect responses, incorrect stored facts or an unrepresented new condition can produce an incorrect result.
The system supports specialist decision-making within its defined scope.
Explain questions, responses and the inference engine searching knowledge using rules. Produces a diagnosis alone is incomplete.

The user enters geological information for a possible prospecting location.
The interface asks further questions based on the information supplied.
The inference engine applies rules to relevant stored geological knowledge.
The system compares the inputs with known indicators of deposits.
Outputs can suggest likely locations, depth or probability of finding a resource.
Maps or other displays can present the findings.
An explanation identifies the reasoning supporting the recommendation.
Results remain dependent on the quality and completeness of the evidence.

The user enters start and end points, delivery locations and relevant constraints.
Inputs can include distances, road links, vehicle capacity and deadlines.
The interface may ask additional questions based on earlier responses.
The inference engine searches relevant knowledge using the rules base.
Possible routes and schedules are generated.
The system can suggest vehicle or staffing requirements.
The explanation system shows why a proposed schedule was selected.
This is expert-system reasoning, distinct from explaining GPS position calculation.
Describe the expert system scheduling routes, not customers ordering deliveries or GPS calculating a position.

A point-of-sale terminal records and processes sales.
A barcode scanner reads an item's identifying code.
The code is used to locate the product record in a database.
The barcode normally identifies the item rather than directly storing its current selling price.
A check digit helps detect some errors in the captured code.
Retrieved data supports pricing, receipts and stock updates.
Scanning avoids manually typing the item code or price for every product.
Explain the POS functions and their effects; a personal description of paying at a checkout is insufficient.

The scanner reads the product code at the checkout.
The system searches the stock database for the matching record.
The description and current price are retrieved.
The quantity sold is recorded.
The stock quantity is reduced by the number sold.
The transaction contributes to the sale total.
An itemised receipt can show the products and prices.
Sales records can support reports on buying patterns.
Develop how product lookup and sale records support the business, rather than describing only payment.

The system reduces the stock quantity when items are sold.
It compares the remaining quantity with the preset reorder level.
When stock reaches the reorder condition, an order can be generated for the supplier.
A pending-order flag helps prevent duplicate orders.
Order details specify the required product and quantity.
When goods arrive, the received quantity is added to stock.
The pending order is updated or cleared.
Sales trends can help adjust future ordering levels.
Link sales tracking to when and how much stock is reordered, so goods do not run out or remain unsold.

The POS system adds item prices and quantities to calculate the bill.
It applies valid discounts or offers according to stored rules.
The completed sale updates the daily takings records.
A linked loyalty account can receive points according to the purchase.
Receipts provide an itemised transaction record.
Self-checkout lets customers scan items and complete supported payment steps.
Comparable product lookup and stock-update processing still takes place.
Self-checkout can reduce some checkout staffing needs but still requires support and controls.
Explain features such as itemised bills or self-checkout and their linked benefit.

EFTPOS links point-of-sale transactions with electronic payment processing.
A chip-and-PIN terminal reads the card and receives the entered PIN.
Card details, authentication and the requested amount are checked through the payment system.
The issuer authorises or rejects the transaction.
Approved payment is recorded and settled through the banking system.
A PIN makes a stolen card harder to use than a card requiring no additional authentication.
PIN entry can be observed through shoulder surfing.
Faults, connection loss or unsupported cards can prevent payment.
When comparing readers, give both similarities and differences and explain why the PIN changes security.

NFC stands for Near Field Communication.
The customer brings a compatible phone close to a payment terminal.
The device and terminal exchange payment information over a short-range radio link.
The wallet can require device authentication, such as a PIN or biometric check.
The payment request is checked and authorised through the payment system.
Payment systems can use encrypted communication and transaction-specific security data.
The terminal displays approval or rejection.
Short range alone does not replace authentication or other security measures.

A mobile wallet is set up with an eligible payment card through a secure registration process.
Tokenisation replaces the actual card account number with an alternative payment identifier.
The device presents the token in a supported payment transaction.
The payment system links the token to the account for processing.
The retailer need not retain the actual card number for that transaction.
Transaction-specific security information can further reduce reuse of intercepted details.
Tokenisation reduces exposure of card details but does not remove every fraud risk.
Internet banking and online shopping: services

Internet banking provides account access through an authorised website or application.
Supported services include balances, statements, transfers and bill payments.
Online shopping lets users browse a catalogue and choose products or services.
Items and quantities are added to a virtual basket.
The customer checks out, enters required delivery and payment details and confirms.
The system records the order and sends confirmation.
Authentication protects account functions, and users should check transaction details.

Customers can access services from home or another suitable location.
Many routine online services are available outside physical opening hours.
Reduced travel can save time and transport costs.
Online stores can offer a wide choice of products.
Prices, specifications and reviews can be compared.
Home delivery helps customers who find travel difficult.
Online banking avoids some branch queues for supported transactions.
Benefits depend on access to suitable devices and a connection.
If asked for characteristics, describe what online shopping offers; do not assume a benefits-and-drawbacks answer is requested.
Online shopping/banking: disadvantages and social effects

Users need suitable equipment, skills and internet access.
Fraud, phishing or unauthorised access can expose data or money.
Products cannot always be physically inspected before purchase.
Delivery delays, charges and returns can cause inconvenience.
Incorrect payment or transfer details can be difficult to correct.
Reduced visits can limit face-to-face interaction and physical activity.
Growth in online services can affect high-street shops and branch employment.
Deliveries and packaging also have environmental and traffic impacts.

An online organisation can reach customers beyond a local shop's area.
Orders can be accepted outside ordinary shop opening hours.
Fewer premises or counter staff can reduce some costs.
A wider customer base can increase sales.
Website development, maintenance, security and customer support add costs.
Retailers still need storage, packing, dispatch and delivery arrangements.
Staff may need retraining or different skills.
Competition, customer trust and technology dependence affect success.
Evaluate effects on the organisation separately from customers' travel savings.
Evaluate effects on the organisation, such as staffing, premises and distribution; customer travel savings are a different perspective.

An OMR attendance register uses marked positions to record attendance.
Each mark position corresponds to a student and attendance value.
The completed sheet is read by an optical mark reader.
The system interprets the marked positions and links them to student records.
Attendance data is stored in the central database.
Staff can search, sort and produce attendance reports.
Marks must be in the specified positions for reliable reading.
State the specific OMR use, such as reading marked attendance registers, rather than a vague location or activity.

OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition.
A form provides fixed positions for the permitted answers.
Registration or timing marks help align the sheet with its template.
The reader detects which answer areas are marked.
The detected choices are compared with a stored answer key.
The system calculates scores and records or exports the results.
Multiple or unclear marks can be flagged for checking.
OMR detects mark positions rather than reading the written meaning of characters.
Specify reading multiple-choice answer forms rather than merely marking exams.

OMR can input many completed forms quickly with little manual typing.
Standard forms support consistent automated processing.
It is useful for multiple-choice responses, surveys and attendance marks.
Forms need accurate design and alignment.
Users must mark the correct areas and follow the completion instructions.
Stray marks, damaged sheets or ambiguous answers can cause errors.
Responses are limited to the choices or positions provided.
Unlike OCR, OMR does not convert written words into editable text.
Explain that OMR detects marks in fixed positions while OCR recognises characters; examples alone do not explain the difference.

A barcode represents an identifying code read optically.
A QR code is a two-dimensional code that can hold information such as a reference or web address.
OCR recognises characters from an image and converts them into machine-readable text.
OCR is used in cheque processing and number-plate recognition.
OCR reduces manual typing but unclear characters can be misread and need checking.
OMR detects marks in predefined positions rather than recognising characters.
RFID uses radio communication and does not require the same optical line of sight as barcode reading.
OCR converts an image of text into editable characters. Do not confuse it with image scanning or OMR, and explain why checking is needed.

A camera captures an image of the vehicle.
Software locates the number-plate region.
Brightness and contrast can be adjusted to improve readability.
The characters are separated and recognised using OCR.
The result is converted into machine-readable registration text.
The registration can be stored with the capture time and location.
It can then be compared with relevant database records.
The camera captures the image; software and the database perform the recognition and checking stages.
Include software recognition and database comparison; the camera alone does not perform the whole ANPR process.
ANPR car-park entry, payment and exit

The system reads the registration as the vehicle enters.
It records the entry time and booking or ticket information as required.
When payment is requested, the system calculates the charge from the relevant record.
Payment is recorded against the registration or parking session.
At exit, another capture identifies the vehicle.
The system checks payment, authorisation or other exit conditions.
A control signal raises the barrier when the conditions are met.
Unrecognised plates or incomplete payment need an exception process.
Keep the car-park access process in context rather than switching to speeding or stolen-vehicle detection.

ANPR automates identification of vehicle registrations.
A car park can admit only registrations in its authorised database.
Automatic checking can reduce manual work and staff costs.
Entry and exit records support parking charges and traffic analysis.
Time-stamped observations can support average-speed calculations over a known distance.
Registrations can be checked for congestion charging or vehicles of interest.
The benefit depends on the particular system and its database.
Security and privacy need to be considered alongside convenience.
Explain benefits for the stated ANPR use; school parking and road-speed monitoring are different contexts.

Dirt or damage can make plate characters difficult to recognise.
Another vehicle or person can obstruct the camera's view.
Poor lighting, weather or camera position can reduce image quality.
Unusual fonts or character spacing can cause misreading.
A valid plate absent from the database may be rejected.
Cloned plates can cause the wrong vehicle to appear authorised.
Records of movements raise privacy and access-control concerns.
Database maintenance and correction of recognition errors are necessary.
Link the condition to its effect on recognition, such as dirt obscuring characters, rather than naming a bare problem.

RFID uses radio waves to identify tags.
A tag can be read without direct optical line of sight.
Suitable systems can read several tags in one operation.
Tags can remain readable when the visible surface is defaced, if the electronics are intact.
Some tags hold more data and support rewriting.
Automation can speed identification and tracking.
Tags and readers can cost more than printed barcodes.
Interference, collisions or deliberate jamming can affect reading.
Data may be intercepted if the system lacks appropriate protection.
RFID still requires reading. Explain radio-based identification without line of sight rather than claiming no scanning is needed.

An RFID tag contains a chip and an antenna.
The chip stores identifying data or other information.
A reader transmits radio signals and receives the tag's response.
A passive tag obtains the energy needed for its response from the reader's field.
An active tag has its own power source, usually a battery.
Read distance and capabilities depend on the tag and system.
The returned identifier can be used to find further details in a database.
Name the RFID reader and explain reader activation followed by the tag’s returned data. RFID alone names the technology.

An animal's RFID identifier can link to ownership or veterinary records.
A reader sends radio waves that activate a compatible passive implanted chip.
The chip returns its stored identifier for the reader to capture.
An implanted chip is harder to lose than a collar tag.
Stock tags can identify goods at receipt, storage, checkout or dispatch.
Readers at suitable points help update movement or stock records.
A passive pet-identification chip is not itself a GPS tracker.
Specify the use and processing rather than saying only tracking.
For an implanted chip, link benefits to being harder to lose or damage. Bulk-reading or distance claims do not explain that benefit.

An electronic passport can contain a contactless RFID chip and antenna.
The chip stores relevant identity and biometric information.
A compatible reader communicates with the chip at a checkpoint.
The information can be compared with the passport document and holder.
Access controls and cryptographic checks help protect the stored information and authenticity.
The system supports automated identity checks.
Read range depends on the passport and reader; it is not a general long-range tracking system.
Give the precise use, such as electronic-passport identification, rather than just naming a place.

An RFID tag can identify a vehicle to a compatible reader.
A parking system compares the identifier with authorised records.
If access is permitted, the controller can raise a barrier.
A toll system can link the identifier to a payment account.
Weigh-station records can be associated with the identified vehicle.
Assembly-line tags can record progress through manufacturing stages.
Readers capture identity at designated locations rather than inherently providing continuous position.

A contactless card contains a chip and antenna.
A compatible reader creates a radio field.
A passive card obtains energy from this field and exchanges payment information.
The card is held close to the terminal rather than inserted into contacts.
The payment system checks and processes the transaction.
A PIN or other check may be required according to the transaction rules.
Contactless communication is the input method; authorisation still takes place through the payment process.
State a specific RFID application such as contactless card payment, not merely in a supermarket.

NFC is a short-range contactless technology related to RFID.
It operates over close proximity, typically a few centimetres.
General RFID systems can have different operating frequencies and ranges.
NFC devices can act as readers or emulate compatible cards.
A connection can be initiated by bringing compatible devices close together.
Ordinary NFC exchanges do not require Bluetooth-style pairing.
Close proximity is useful for deliberate tap interactions but does not by itself guarantee security.

In reader/writer mode, an NFC device reads data from or writes data to a compatible tag.
A phone can read a tag containing a link or other information.
In card-emulation mode, a device behaves like a contactless card.
Card emulation can support payment, access or transport-ticket interactions.
In peer-to-peer mode, two compatible NFC devices exchange information.
The roles and supported functions depend on the devices and application.
Reader/writer mode is not limited to a passive tablet receiving one-way advertisements.

Biometric recognition identifies or authenticates people using measurable characteristics.
Physical examples include fingerprints, hand geometry, face, iris and retina patterns.
Voice characteristics and some behavioural patterns can also be used.
Captured features are compared with enrolled templates.
Biometrics are difficult to forget or lend in the same way as a card or password.
Enrolment, equipment, recognition errors and privacy are possible limitations.
Name the biometric method rather than only its capture device.
Keep the selected method consistent with the scenario.
Name biometric methods, keep the specified method consistent, and distinguish each factor category from its example.

Retina recognition uses the pattern of blood vessels at the back of the eye.
Specialised equipment captures the pattern, commonly using infrared light.
Features are compared with an enrolled template.
The user needs to position the eye carefully for capture.
The process can be less convenient than less intrusive recognition methods.
Specialist equipment can be expensive.
It is associated with specialised high-security identification.
The retina is different from the coloured iris surrounding the pupil.
Name the recognition method rather than only the device that captures it.

The iris is the coloured region surrounding the pupil.
A camera captures a detailed image, often using near-infrared illumination.
Software locates the iris and extracts identifying pattern features.
The features are compared with a stored template.
A match supports the identity or access decision.
It can support rapid identity checks such as border-control authentication.
Image quality and capture conditions affect recognition.
Iris recognition is different from scanning the blood vessels in the retina.
Name the recognition method rather than only the device that captures it.

GNSS means Global Navigation Satellite System; GPS is one such system.
Satellites broadcast signals containing precise timing and orbital-position information.
A receiver measures signal travel times to estimate its distance from satellites.
Using several satellites, the receiver calculates its position.
A normal three-dimensional fix also needs correction of the receiver's clock, usually using at least four satellites.
The GPS receiver receives broadcast signals; it need not send a request to the satellites.
GPS supplies position and time, while route planning requires additional maps and software.
Satellites broadcast position and timing signals; the receiver calculates its location without sending a request back to them.

A satellite-navigation device receives satellite signals and calculates its position.
The position is placed on a stored digital map.
The user enters a destination and relevant route preferences.
An algorithm calculates a route using the map and permitted roads.
The device displays directions and can provide spoken instructions.
Its position is updated as the user moves.
A route can be recalculated if the user leaves it or new traffic information is available.
Traffic updates require an additional information source; GPS signals do not contain every road condition.
Distinguish GPS positioning, satnav routing and GIS analysis. Do not claim that the vehicle sends a navigation request to a satellite.

Satnav can find a suitable route and estimate distance or arrival time.
Spoken directions reduce the need to memorise routes or repeatedly consult a paper map.
Updated map and traffic information can support rerouting.
Digital navigation avoids carrying several paper maps.
Outdated maps can omit new roads, closures or restrictions.
Buildings, terrain or other obstructions can weaken satellite reception.
Incorrect destinations or unsuitable route choices can lead users astray.
Power or device failure can interrupt navigation.
Users need to apply judgement and avoid unsafe interaction while travelling.
Apply navigation benefits and failures to the specified user, such as a walker or taxi driver, and explain each consequence.

GIS stands for Geographic Information System.
It links geographic locations with data about those locations.
Information is organised into layers such as roads, boundaries, population or land use.
Layers can be overlaid to explore relationships.
Queries select features meeting conditions.
Spatial analysis can compare distance, position or areas.
Results can be shown as maps, tables or graphics.
GIS analyses location-linked information; GPS primarily supplies positioning information.

Emergency services can use GIS to locate incidents and plan dispatch routes.
Conservation teams can map habitats and environmental change.
Crime analysis can compare incident locations with other area data.
Agriculture can map soil, crops or irrigation needs.
Public-health work can examine geographic patterns in disease or access to services.
Wildfire analysis can combine vegetation, terrain and risk information.
Teaching can use layers to investigate relationships between places.
The useful result depends on the geographic data included.

GIS integrates large datasets linked to locations.
Layer overlays can reveal relationships that are difficult to see in separate tables.
Maps and queries support planning and decision-making.
Data and displays can be updated as conditions change.
Software, data collection and skilled staff can be costly.
Training is needed to use and interpret the system.
Inaccurate, outdated or incompatible data can produce misleading results.
Complex interfaces and large datasets can affect ease of use and performance.

A communication satellite has antennas and transponders to receive and retransmit signals.
An Earth station sends an uplink signal to the satellite.
The transponder receives the signal and processes or amplifies it.
It commonly changes the frequency before retransmission.
The downlink carries the signal towards a receiving Earth station.
Solar panels supply electrical power and control systems maintain the required orientation and orbit.
The complete path links ground equipment through the satellite.
This relay function differs from GPS broadcasting position and timing information.
Satellite media communication: uses and benefits

Communication satellites support television broadcasting, telephone services and data links.
A footprint can provide coverage across a large region.
Remote locations can be connected where terrestrial infrastructure is limited.
A broadcast can reach many suitably equipped receivers.
Links can cross oceans or difficult terrain without laying a continuous ground cable.
Capacity and quality depend on the satellite system and service.
A satellite phone uses a communication service, not merely a GPS receiver.
A satellite phone provides communication in suitable remote areas; it is different from GPS or satnav.

The long signal path can cause noticeable delay, especially with high-altitude satellites.
Rain or other atmospheric conditions can weaken some signals.
Buildings, trees and terrain can obstruct a terminal's view of the satellite.
Antennas may need suitable positioning and alignment.
Space weather can interfere with satellite operation or signals.
Satellites need monitoring, control and maintenance arrangements.
Equipment, launch and service costs can be high.
Available bandwidth and reliability vary with the system; satellite communication is not automatically secure.
Compare satellite-phone coverage and limitations in context, including signal obstruction and available data rates.

Existing hardware may become obsolete, unreliable or difficult to repair.
New equipment can offer improved speed, efficiency or reliability.
Business expansion can exceed the current system's capacity.
Changes in working practices can require new functions.
Changes in legislation or taxation can require software changes.
User feedback can reveal limitations that justify an upgrade.
The expected benefits should be considered alongside cost and disruption.

A systems analyst investigates the current system and the problem to be solved.
The analyst identifies current inputs, processing, outputs, storage and data flows.
Research reveals weaknesses and user requirements.
Suitable improvements and hardware or software are proposed and justified.
Costs and benefits are reported to management.
The analyst communicates between users, managers and developers.
The role includes helping specify and oversee the new solution.
Describe information about the current system, including its data inputs, processes, outputs and problems; devices alone are not that information.
Systems life cycle: stages and iteration

Analysis investigates the current system and establishes requirements.
Design specifies the new solution's structures, interfaces and processes.
Development and testing build the solution, identify errors and check expected behaviour.
Implementation introduces the new system into use.
Documentation supports users and technical staff.
Evaluation compares the result with the requirements and identifies improvements.
The process is iterative: testing or evaluation can lead back to redesign and further development.

The analyst watches staff carry out tasks using the current system.
This reveals actual inputs, processing, outputs and working practices.
It can provide an overall view and expose delays or errors.
The analyst does not need to rely only on users' descriptions.
Workers may change their behaviour because they know they are being watched: the Hawthorne effect.
Non-standard practices may be concealed during observation.
The observation period must cover the activities being investigated.
Explain an analyst watching staff use the current system; repeating observation means observing is insufficient.

An interview is a one-to-one question-and-answer conversation between the analyst and a user or other stakeholder.
The analyst can ask follow-up questions and explore a particular issue in depth.
Questions can be clarified or adapted during the conversation.
Body language and expressions can provide additional feedback.
Interviews take time and can be expensive for many participants.
Participants are not anonymous and may give biased or incomplete answers.
Arranging a suitable time can be difficult.
Describe a two-way, one-to-one question-and-answer conversation, not merely asking questions.

A questionnaire presents a prepared set of questions to users or other stakeholders.
Many people can respond, often in their own time.
It is relatively cheap because each response does not need an interviewer.
Structured responses can be analysed quickly.
Anonymous responses can encourage openness.
Response rates may be low and some answers may be careless or exaggerated.
Fixed questions make follow-up and clarification difficult.
The analyst cannot observe respondents' body language as in an interview.
Compare both sides with interviews: scale, cost and flexible completion versus limited follow-up and no visible body language.

The analyst examines existing forms, files, reports, instructions and manuals.
Documents show what data is collected and what outputs are produced.
File contents and volumes help estimate storage and processing needs.
Operating and training instructions show intended procedures.
Accounts and records can reveal the scale of the organisation's activities.
Documents provide detailed evidence not always obtained through questions or observation.
Examining a large volume of material can be time-consuming and costly.
Documented procedures may need checking against actual practice.
