Use the recognised research-method name examining existing documents or document analysis.

Observation is useful for seeing how tasks are actually performed.
Interviews provide detailed explanations and allow follow-up questions.
Questionnaires collect views from many people at relatively low cost.
Existing documents reveal data, formats, volumes and recorded procedures.
Choose methods according to the information required, available time, budget and access.
Combining methods can check findings and reduce dependence on one source.
Use recognised method names and justify their suitability for the investigation.
Use recognised method names and develop reasons for the comparison; questionnaires and interviews offer different depth and scale.

Identify the data entered into the current system and its sources.
Identify the processing applied to the data, such as searching, calculating or updating records.
Identify the outputs and their recipients.
Identify what is stored, where it is stored and how it is retrieved.
Trace how information moves between tasks or departments.
For booking, inputs can include journey and customer details; processing checks availability and creates the reservation.
Outputs can include a confirmation or ticket, while the database stores booking records.
Specify the current system’s inputs, processes and outputs. Naming only input and output devices is insufficient.
Data flow diagrams: interpretation and scope

A data flow diagram represents how data moves through a system.
It shows relationships between external sources or recipients, processes and data stores.
Inputs enter processes and outputs leave them.
Processes transform or use data rather than merely storing it.
Data stores hold information needed by the system.
Following the flows helps an analyst identify missing information, duplication or bottlenecks.
Interpreting a supplied diagram can support analysis of the current system.

A bottleneck is a stage that limits the flow or speed of work.
Repeated manual entry can cause delay and copying errors.
Missing, duplicated or inaccurate data can reduce reliability.
Inadequate capacity can prevent the system meeting demand.
Unsuitable outputs may fail to provide information when needed.
The analyst identifies where each problem occurs and its effect on the organisation.
Findings support requirements for the proposed replacement.
Identify current-system problems and distinguish them from proposed new-system features.

User requirements describe what users need the new system to do.
They are written in clear language that customers and managers can understand.
They identify required tasks, outputs and practical constraints.
Accessibility needs should be included.
Users review the requirements to confirm that the proposed solution matches their needs.
Agreed requirements guide later design and provide criteria for evaluation.
Requirements for the new system are distinct from descriptions of the current system.
State the user requirements for the new system and distinguish them from information about the current system.

Information requirements identify the data or information needed to support the organisation.
They specify what information is needed and when it is needed.
They identify who supplies it and who needs to receive it.
Required accuracy, detail and format affect the proposed outputs.
Customers, suppliers and employees may have different information needs.
These requirements help determine the system's data collection, processing, storage and reporting.

A specification states what the proposed system must do.
It records agreed functions, capabilities and relevant requirements.
It can include performance, security, hardware and software requirements.
It translates user and information needs into requirements developers can implement.
Relevant constraints and timescales guide development and implementation.
It provides a shared understanding between the client and developer.
It is a specification for the solution, rather than instructions teaching an end user how to operate it.
Define what the specification states about the system’s functions and requirements; it is not a user guide or simply a life-cycle position.

Choose input devices according to the data and task, such as barcode readers for product codes.
Choose output devices according to the required output, such as a monitor for screen information or a printer for hard copy.
Justify choices through accuracy, speed, accessibility and suitability.
Consider capacity, compatibility and reliability.
Purchase, maintenance and operating costs affect the choice.
Required assistive equipment should support users' accessibility needs.
Naming hardware without linking it to a task does not establish its suitability.
Identify and justify suitable hardware for the required tasks rather than making a vague reference to the system.

Identify an operating system compatible with the required hardware and applications.
Select application software that supports the organisation's tasks.
Consider required functions, file compatibility and integration with existing systems.
Consider usability, accessibility and staff training.
Security, support, licensing and updates affect suitability and cost.
The specification should explain what the selected software needs to do.
Selection is based on requirements rather than a product name alone.
Explain suitable software and what it must do; the specification guides development.

Off-the-shelf software is already developed for a wider market.
It is usually available sooner and development costs are spread across many customers.
Established support, training material and a user community may be available.
It may contain unnecessary features or require compromises in working practices.
Bespoke software is developed for a particular customer's requirements.
It can provide a closer fit and specialised functions.
Bespoke development normally requires more time, cost and testing.
Support and future changes may depend strongly on the developer.

Estimate the volume of data that must be stored now and as the system grows.
Consider file sizes, numbers of records and backup needs.
Choose media or services with suitable capacity and access speed.
Direct access suits retrieving individual records quickly.
Serial access can suit sequential archival or backup tasks.
Consider reliability, durability, compatibility and replacement needs.
Cost includes the devices or services, maintenance and protection of stored data.

Design file and data structures.
Specify fields, names, data types, lengths and keys.
Design data-capture forms and input formats.
Design screen layouts, printed outputs and report formats.
Specify validation routines and processing algorithms.
Plan a testing approach and suitable tests.
Design decisions should satisfy the requirements established during analysis.
Name items actually designed, such as structures, input formats, output layouts and validation routines.
Files, records, fields and primary keys

A field stores one attribute, such as a name or price.
A record groups the fields describing one entity.
A file or table contains a collection of related records.
A primary key uniquely identifies each record and must contain a value.
A table has one primary key, which may be defined using one or more fields.
A foreign key references an appropriate key in another table to support a relationship.
Relationships link tables within a database rather than requiring separate databases.
A primary key uniquely identifies a record and must contain a value. Describe relationships between tables, not separate databases.

Give each field a clear name describing its contents.
Choose a data type appropriate to the values and their use.
Set a maximum field length where the type requires it.
Allow enough space for the longest permitted entry.
Avoid unnecessary allocation while allowing realistic future values.
Specify any codes, validation rules and key fields.
Input controls and display areas should accommodate the intended field content.
Name specific structure elements such as field name, field length, data type and keys.

Coding represents categories or values with shorter agreed symbols.
Each code must have a clear, unambiguous meaning.
For example, distinct product models can use distinct one-letter codes.
Short codes require less typing than full descriptions.
They can reduce storage requirements and make searching or identification quicker.
A defined code list supports validation and can reduce entry errors.
Users need to understand the code meanings; ambiguous codes can cause mistakes.
Use distinct codes and explain their effects, such as fewer characters to type or store; do not give one code for every category.

Text or string data can contain letters, digits and symbols.
Alphanumeric is a generic term for data containing letters and numbers.
A character field holds a single character where that is the intended requirement.
Names and descriptions normally use text.
Identifiers such as telephone numbers can use text because arithmetic is not performed on them.
Text can preserve leading zeros and symbols in identifiers.
An ISBN containing a letter cannot be stored as an integer without changing the data.
Choose the type from the actual content: an ISBN containing X needs text rather than integer.

Boolean data represents one of two logical states.
Examples include true or false and yes or no.
A field such as whether an item is scented can use Boolean values.
A checkbox can provide a suitable input control.
The logical value is distinct from the label displayed to the user.
Boolean is the data type; Y/N describes possible representations rather than naming the type.
Name Boolean as the generic data type; Y/N is a representation rather than the type name.
Numeric types: integer, real and currency

An integer stores whole numbers.
A real or decimal type stores values that can have a fractional part.
Currency is a numeric type or format suited to monetary amounts.
Counts often use integers, while measured heights or weights may need decimals.
Prices should use an appropriate monetary representation.
A field containing digits is not necessarily numeric if it is an identifier rather than a quantity.
The chosen type must support the permitted values and operations.
Specify the numeric subtype where required, such as currency for prices or decimal for measured height.

Date and time types represent calendar dates or times rather than arbitrary text.
They support operations such as chronological sorting or calculating intervals.
The display format specifies how a stored value is shown.
A date can be displayed as day, month and year in a specified order.
The input pattern and permitted dates must be defined.
A correctly formatted entry is not automatically a valid calendar date or the intended date.
Copy supplied field names accurately when identifying a field.

Validation is an automatic check that input meets specified acceptance criteria.
It tests whether data is sensible, reasonable or in the required form.
Examples include range, type, length, format, presence and check-digit checks.
Invalid data can be rejected or produce an error message.
A value can pass validation while still being factually wrong.
Verification checks accurate copying from the source rather than acceptability.
Using both reduces errors, but neither guarantees that the source information is true.
Validation checks acceptance criteria; verification checks accurate copying. Neither proves the original source is correct, and verification here is not identity checking.

A range check tests whether a value is within permitted limits.
The lower and upper limits must match the field's requirements.
Limits can be inclusive or exclusive.
For an allowed price from 10 to 100 inclusive, values below 10 or above 100 are rejected.
A date field may be restricted to an appropriate date interval.
A value within the range can still be the wrong value.
A range check tests value limits, not the number of characters.
Name the range check and state the actual permitted limits; field contents alone do not justify the check.

A type check tests whether input is compatible with the required data type.
A numeric field should reject alphabetic text that cannot represent an allowed number.
An integer field should reject fractional values where only whole numbers are permitted.
A character check can restrict entries to a permitted class of characters.
For an all-digit identifier, the check can require numeric characters.
Type checking does not prove that the value is within its allowed range.
The permitted characters and type must suit the actual field.
Explain which types or characters are permitted. Do not substitute a range or format check for the required type check.

A length check tests the number of characters entered.
It can require an exact length, minimum length or maximum length.
An identifier specified as six digits must contain exactly six characters as well as satisfy its digit rules.
A password rule may require at least a specified number of characters.
Count separators if they form part of the stored input.
An entry with the correct length can still contain incorrect characters or values.
Exactly a specified length is different from up to that length.
Distinguish exactly a specified length from up to that length, and count all required characters.

A format check tests whether input follows a specified pattern.
The pattern can define letters, digits, separators and their positions.
For example, LLNNN requires two letters followed by three digits.
A date pattern can specify DD/MM/YYYY.
The required separators and year length must be included.
Correct format does not prove the value is factually correct.
Additional checks may be needed to confirm a real calendar date or permitted value.
Give the recognised check name and the full required pattern, including separators and year length.

A presence check tests that a required field has not been left empty.
It rejects a null or missing entry where a value is mandatory.
A primary-key field must contain a value.
Optional fields should not automatically be given a presence requirement.
For example, a sale date may legitimately be empty before an item is sold.
Presence does not prove that an entered value is correct, well formed or within range.
Check whether the field is mandatory. A field that can legitimately be empty does not need a presence check.

A check digit is an additional digit calculated from the other digits in an identifier.
The calculation follows a defined algorithm.
On entry or reading, the system repeats the calculation and checks the result.
A mismatch indicates that the code may have been entered or read incorrectly.
Depending on the algorithm, it can detect substitutions, transpositions or missing or extra digits.
It detects some errors but does not itself correct the original data.
Not every possible error is detected by every check-digit method.
Explain the calculated extra digit in the context of the identifier rather than giving only a generic validation label.

Use a clear title and labels showing what data is required.
Give understandable completion instructions.
Provide enough space for the longest expected answers.
Use separate character boxes where a fixed structure is helpful.
Provide tick boxes or other appropriate selections for fixed choices.
Use readable font sizes and sufficient contrast.
Arrange fields and white space in a logical order.
The design should help accurate completion rather than merely list field names.
Describe design features and how they aid completion; do not substitute the form’s contents.

Electronic forms use labelled fields suited to the required data.
Text boxes support free entry; drop-down lists restrict choices to permitted options.
Radio buttons allow one choice within a group; checkboxes can allow independent selections.
Calendar controls help enter dates.
Validation and clear error messages guide correction.
Help, navigation, save, clear and exit controls should have understandable functions.
Readable fonts, suitable contrast and enough entry space improve usability.
Accessibility can include larger controls, voice input or text-to-speech where appropriate.
Explain how controls and layout help users complete the form accurately, rather than only listing fields or control names.

Double-entry verification requires the same source data to be entered independently twice.
The two entries can be made by one person on separate attempts or by different people.
The computer compares the entries.
A mismatch is flagged for checking against the source.
Visual verification instead involves a person comparing entered data directly with the original.
Both aim to detect copying errors.
Matching entries do not prove that the original source is correct.
Data verification here is different from authenticating a person's identity.
Include independent second entry and computer comparison. Visual verification compares with the source; neither proves the source itself is correct.

Choose a text box for values that need free entry.
Use a drop-down list for a controlled set of permitted categories.
Use grouped radio buttons when exactly one of a small set of options is allowed.
Use checkboxes for independent yes/no selections.
Use a date control for dates and suitable numeric fields for quantities or prices.
Match field widths and character boxes to expected content.
Justify each control through reduced errors, faster entry or clearer selection.
The reason for choosing a control is different from the reason for collecting that field.
Justify why the particular control suits the field, rather than describing the field’s purpose or only how to use the control.

Use clear labels and descriptions so users understand each displayed value.
Allow enough space to show full field contents.
Choose readable font sizes and styles.
Use sufficient contrast between text and background.
Arrange related information logically.
Balance content with useful white space.
Design the display for the intended users and their accessibility needs.
Test that important values are not hidden or truncated.

Give reports clear headings and subheadings related to their content.
Use readable fonts, suitable text sizes and contrasting colours.
Display the relevant results in an organised layout.
Ensure field contents and labels are fully visible.
Use headers, footers and page numbering where useful.
Fit information sensibly across pages and avoid unnecessary blank space.
Check that printed output remains understandable and complete.
Report layout is different from selecting data-entry controls.
Describe report layout, readability and visible data; data-entry controls and database field lists are different matters.

Development creates the files, processing routines and interfaces specified in the design.
Validation and verification procedures are implemented where required.
Testing checks that the system meets user requirements.
It checks storage, retrieval, input and output behaviour.
Tests identify errors that must be corrected.
The system should produce the expected results without crashing under the tested conditions.
Corrections must be retested before implementation.
Explain testing against user requirements and expected outputs, with errors corrected; checks it works alone is insufficient.
Test designs: structures, inputs and outputs

A test strategy describes the overall approach to testing.
It states how modules, functions and the complete system will be tested.
File and data structures are checked for correct storage, retrieval and compatibility.
Input formats are tested to ensure users can enter data as intended.
Output formats are tested for complete, clear and readable results.
Validation routines are tested to ensure they handle acceptable and unacceptable data correctly.
The detailed test plan records individual test cases and outcomes.
When asked why, explain the testing purpose. When asked for strategy, explain how modules or the full system will be tested.

Testing validation checks whether acceptance rules are implemented correctly.
Use valid data that should be accepted.
Use data at permitted endpoints to test the limits.
Use invalid values, wrong types or incorrect formats that should be rejected.
Check that appropriate error messages appear.
Compare the actual behaviour with the expected result.
Correct faulty rules and rerun the relevant tests.
Testing a validation routine does not establish that all accepted real-world data is true.
Explain that validation testing checks rejection of unreasonable data and required formats; do not replace purpose with procedure.

The system can be divided into smaller modules or functions.
Each module is developed and tested separately.
Tests check the module's required inputs, processing and outputs.
Errors are corrected before the module is accepted.
The module is retested after changes.
Modules are then combined and tested together.
Separate successful tests do not prove that the combined system will work correctly.
Describe the approach to testing modules or functions, not merely a list of test-data categories.

Integration testing checks whether combined modules communicate and work together.
Whole-system testing checks complete workflows against requirements.
Tests can reveal incompatible data formats, conflicting actions or resource problems.
Actual results are compared with expected outcomes.
Faults may require changes to code, structures or the original design.
Changes are followed by repeated tests, including affected related functions.
Development and testing can therefore lead back to redesign.
Explain how the complete system is tested and how that fits the testing approach.

A test plan identifies the test or feature being checked.
It states the reason or objective of the test.
It records the input data and relevant test-data category.
It states the expected result before the test is run.
The actual result is recorded after execution.
Actual and expected results are compared to determine success or failure.
Faults, corrective action and retest results can be recorded.
A plan describes specific tests; a strategy defines the broader testing approach.
Give genuine plan elements such as input data, test reason and actual result; unexpected results is not the opposite of expected results.

Normal test data is valid data within the permitted limits or rules.
The system is expected to accept it and process it correctly.
Use representative permitted values to check ordinary behaviour.
For whole numbers from 1 to 10 inclusive, 5 is a normal example.
A permitted boundary is also valid, but an interior value clearly distinguishes a normal example from an extreme one.
A requested example should be an actual value rather than only a definition.
If asked for a test-data type, name normal; if asked for an example, give one actual accepted value.

Extreme test data lies at the valid limits of acceptability.
It tests whether the boundary comparisons are correct.
For whole numbers from 1 to 10 inclusive, the extreme values are 1 and 10.
For month numbers, valid endpoints are 1 and 12.
The endpoint must be included in the permitted range to be a valid extreme value.
Values just outside the permitted limits are abnormal, not valid extreme values.
Use the actual endpoints for the specified field or formula.
Extreme values are valid endpoints, not values far outside the range. Give the actual requested boundary value.

Abnormal test data does not meet the acceptance rules.
It can be outside an allowed range.
It can have the wrong type, length or format.
For whole numbers from 1 to 10 inclusive, 11, 0 or alphabetic text are abnormal examples.
A fractional value is abnormal when only integers are allowed.
The system should reject the entry or produce the expected error response.
Testing confirms that invalid data is trapped rather than processed as valid.
Give an actual invalid value for the stated rules when an example is requested; a definition alone earns no example mark.

Live test data is real data from the existing or operational system.
Its known results can be used to check the new system.
Run the data through the new solution.
Compare outputs with the established correct results and investigate differences.
It helps test realistic values and workloads.
Live data is not another name for real-time processing.
Personal or confidential data requires appropriate permission and protection during testing.
Live data means real existing data or data with known outcomes, not real-time processing. Consider permission when it contains personal data.
Selecting test inputs and analysing results

Identify the field's type, permitted values and exact boundary conditions.
Select a normal value, valid endpoints and relevant invalid values.
State what the system should do for each test.
Enter the test data and run the relevant function or formula.
Record the actual output and compare it with the expected result.
Investigate differences and correct the program or rule.
Repeat the tests after correction.
Examples alone do not describe the complete testing process.
Describe entering data, running the test, comparing actual with expected results, correcting and retesting. Examples alone are incomplete.

Prepare the new hardware, software and access arrangements.
Train staff before or during rollout as the chosen method permits.
Transfer existing data through entry, scanning or suitable file import.
Check that transferred data is complete and accurately copied.
Decide how and when operational work will move to the new system.
Prepare support, recovery and contingency arrangements.
The changeover method must suit continuity needs, resources and risk.
Explain how training and operational changeover work for the selected method, including when the old system is removed.

Direct changeover stops use of the old system and introduces the whole new system at once.
The new system can be used immediately after changeover.
Only one operational system needs to be maintained after the switch.
Data does not have to be entered routinely into both old and new systems.
This can reduce staffing and duplicated operating costs.
Staff need to be ready to use the new system at changeover.
If it fails, the old operational system is no longer available to fall back on.
Thorough preparation and testing reduce risk but do not guarantee no failure.
Explain why costs or training differ. Direct changeover leaves no old operational system to fall back on; do not equate that with having no data backup.

Parallel running operates the old and new systems together for a transition period.
Required operational data is entered into both systems.
The old system remains available if the new one has problems during the transition.
Staff can become familiar with the new system gradually.
Running two systems increases staffing, equipment and maintenance costs.
Duplicated entry takes time and can produce inconsistent records.
Once the new system is accepted, the old system is removed.
Parallel running does not mean keeping both systems indefinitely or simply choosing either one.
Both systems run during transition and the old one is eventually removed. They are not permanent alternatives users simply choose between.

Pilot implementation introduces the new system at one selected branch, site or user group first.
That pilot location uses the new system while other locations continue with the old arrangements.
Its performance and problems are assessed before wider rollout.
A failure initially affects a limited part of the organisation.
Training and support can be concentrated at the pilot site.
Experience from the pilot can improve later implementation.
The pilot must be sufficiently representative for its results to be useful.
Pilot concerns a limited location or group, rather than introducing functions one at a time.
A trial at one branch or site is pilot implementation; introducing functions one at a time is phased.

Phased implementation introduces parts or functions of the new system in stages.
One part is introduced and checked before the next stage proceeds.
Other functions continue under the previous arrangements until replaced.
Problems can be identified within a smaller part of the change.
Training can be spread across stages.
The full benefits take longer to obtain than with immediate replacement.
Old and new components may need to work together during transition.
Phased describes staged functions; pilot describes an initial site or user group.
Introducing one process or function at a time is phased implementation, not pilot.

Choose according to the consequences of failure and the need to keep services operating.
Direct changeover is quick and avoids duplicated operation but removes the old operational fallback.
Parallel running retains the old system temporarily but duplicates work and costs.
Pilot limits the initial rollout to one location or group.
Phased introduces functions gradually and delays complete replacement.
Training time, staffing, budget and technical compatibility affect the decision.
Comparisons should link the method's feature to its effect in the organisation.
All selected methods require preparation and an eventual move to the new system.
Develop the effects of each method in the scenario, including eventual replacement of the old system.

Technical documentation is intended for programmers, analysts and other technical staff.
It explains how the system is structured and operates.
It supports maintenance, fault diagnosis and repairs.
It helps developers make improvements or updates.
It preserves information needed by people who did not build the original system.
Its technical detail differs from everyday operating instructions for end users.
State both the technical audience and purpose: programmers or analysts use it to maintain, repair or improve the system.
Technical documentation: program and structure details

Program listings and the programming language describe the implemented code.
Algorithms and program or system flowcharts describe processing and control flow.
Lists of variables explain the data used by the program.
File structures describe how stored data is organised.
Validation rules record the acceptance checks.
Hardware, software and memory requirements describe the operating environment.
Sample or test runs record inputs and results.
Known limitations, errors and relevant technical details support maintenance.
Use precise component names such as program listing, algorithms and file structures; vague labels like code or input alone may be insufficient.

Both user and technical documentation can state the system's purpose and limitations.
Both can give hardware and software requirements.
Input and output formats can appear in both.
Sample runs can illustrate expected behaviour.
The meanings of relevant error messages can be useful to both audiences.
Shared content does not make the two document types identical.
Detailed program listings and internal algorithms primarily serve technical staff.
Use recognised documentation-component terms and respect any list or examples excluded by the question.

User documentation helps users learn how to operate the software or system.
It can explain installation, loading and starting the program.
It describes logging in and out.
It explains entering data and adding, editing or deleting records.
It can show how to search and sort records.
It explains saving files and printing results.
Screenshots or sample runs can illustrate the steps.
Instructions should use language appropriate to the intended users.
Explain help with operating the program or troubleshooting, and name specific user instructions when components are requested.

Tutorials guide users through common tasks.
A troubleshooting guide links symptoms or errors to corrective steps.
Frequently asked questions address common difficulties.
A glossary explains unfamiliar terms.
Help facilities or support contact details show where assistance is available.
Error-message explanations help users understand what to do next.
The material supports operating the system rather than changing its internal program logic.
Name specific support components such as FAQs, glossary and troubleshooting guide, avoiding examples already supplied.

User documentation teaches end users how to operate the system.
Technical documentation helps programmers and analysts maintain or modify it.
User material includes task instructions, tutorials and troubleshooting help.
Technical material includes program listings, algorithms, variables and file structures.
Both may include purpose, limitations, requirements, sample runs and error meanings.
The level and wording of detail should suit the audience.
The distinction depends on purpose and content, not simply whether the document is printed or electronic.

Compare the completed solution with the original user and task requirements.
Check whether the required functions and outputs are provided.
Assess whether the solution is appropriate for the intended task.
Assess efficiency and ease of use.
Identify limitations and necessary improvements.
Consider users' experiences of the new system.
Evaluation can lead to maintenance or redesign.
Evaluation assesses the solution; testing checks specific behaviour and identifies faults.
Describe evaluation against the original task, limitations and feedback. Do not confuse evaluation with testing.

Run comparable tasks on the old and new systems.
Compare outputs using known data and investigate important differences.
Measure the time taken to complete the same tasks.
Observe users' accuracy, effort and difficulties.
Compare performance with the stated improvement targets.
Use evidence to judge whether the new system is more efficient or suitable.
A new system should be judged against requirements as well as against its predecessor.
Explain the comparison or measurement being made rather than only naming an evaluation task.

Interview users about their experience of the new system.
Questionnaires can gather feedback from a wider group.
Observe users carrying out set tasks.
Ask about usability, missing features, errors and suitability.
Compare reported difficulties with observed performance or task timings.
Analyse feedback and identify priorities for improvement.
Collecting feedback is part of evaluation rather than a substitute for technical tests.
Explain how users’ responses are assessed and used to identify improvements.

Evaluation may identify faults, limitations or unmet requirements.
Maintenance can correct errors and improve operation.
Substantial changes may require redesign, development and repeated testing.
User feedback can justify new or improved hardware.
New devices can offer capabilities the organisation now needs.
Business growth or changes in structure can require additional or replacement equipment.
Updates should be assessed against the organisation's requirements and constraints.

User feedback can reveal functions that need changing or improving.
Changes in business structure can require altered workflows or access arrangements.
New services or working practices can require additional software capabilities.
Changes in legislation or taxation can require modifications.
Discovered faults need correction and retesting.
The updated solution should be checked against the revised requirements.
Documentation and training may also need updating after a software change.

Physical safety concerns hazards that can cause accidental injury, such as electric shock, fire, trips or falling equipment.
Health risks include effects of prolonged computer use, such as RSI, eyestrain and back strain.
A hazard is a source of possible harm; a precaution reduces the chance or severity of that harm.
The effect on a person is distinct from damage to the equipment.
Safety measures should address the particular hazard present.
Give physical hazards and harm to people rather than prolonged-use health conditions or equipment damage.

Liquids spilling onto electrical equipment can create a risk of electric shock.
Exposed conductors, damaged insulation and unsafe plugs or sockets can also cause injury.
Keep drinks and other liquids away from computer equipment.
Inspect accessible cables and stop using equipment with visible damage.
Qualified personnel should carry out appropriate electrical checks and repairs.
Suitable residual-current protection can reduce the risk of serious electric shock.
Do not handle exposed live wiring or attempt electrical repairs as an ordinary user.
Link the precaution to the equipment: keep liquids away from electrical devices. The risk to the person is electric shock, not just a broken computer.

Overloaded sockets or extension blocks can overheat.
Blocked cooling vents and accumulated dust can cause equipment to overheat.
Damaged wiring can cause a short circuit and fire.
Avoid overloading power outlets and use an appropriate electrical installation.
Keep ventilation openings unobstructed.
Arrange suitable inspection, cleaning and maintenance of equipment.
Provide appropriate workplace fire precautions and follow the relevant emergency procedures.
The safety risk is fire and injury, rather than simply a computer malfunction.
Name fire as the safety risk rather than assuming equipment will explode.

Trailing cables can cause users to trip and fall.
Damaged flooring or loose objects can also obstruct walking routes.
Use cable ducts, trays or other suitable cable management.
Route cables away from walkways and secure them appropriately.
Keep access routes clear and repair damaged flooring.
Wireless connections can reduce some trailing data cables.
Measures should reduce the physical trip hazard rather than address online security.
Trailing leads are a physical trip hazard. Explain cable management or another measure that removes the walking obstruction.

Heavy equipment can fall if it is unstable or close to an edge.
A weak or unsuitable desk can collapse under the equipment's weight.
Use surfaces strong enough for the intended load.
Provide sufficient space so equipment is securely positioned away from edges.
Secure equipment where its mounting requires it.
Keep the workspace arranged to reduce accidental knocks.
The concern is equipment falling and injuring people, not merely the device breaking.
Explain heavy equipment falling and injuring someone, not merely the equipment breaking.
Data protection acts: purpose and scope

Data-protection legislation regulates how personal data is handled.
Its purpose includes protecting the rights of the people described by the data.
It sets requirements for appropriate collection, processing, storage and disclosure.
It helps prevent misuse and inaccurate records.
The textbook model covers both computerised and relevant paper records.
Principles include lawful use, stated purposes, relevant data, accuracy, limited retention and security.
The precise legal rules depend on the jurisdiction; the chapter presents general principles.
Explain protection of individuals’ rights and appropriate use of personal data. Listing principles alone does not explain why legislation is needed.

Personal data should be processed fairly and lawfully.
The purpose of collecting and using it should be specified.
Processing should be transparent to the people concerned.
Data should be used for the stated legitimate purpose.
Collecting data for one activity does not automatically justify unrelated use.
These principles help prevent undisclosed or inappropriate processing.
State the data-protection principle accurately, including lawful, fair and transparent processing or a specified purpose.

Data collected should be adequate for its stated purpose.
It should be relevant to that purpose.
Organisations should avoid collecting excessive or unnecessary information.
Records should be accurate and kept appropriately up to date.
Incorrect information should be investigated and corrected.
Inaccurate or irrelevant records can lead to unfair or mistaken decisions.
Explain adequate, relevant and non-excessive collection or accurate, current records rather than a vague protects data claim.

Personal data should not be kept longer than needed for its purpose.
Retention decisions should consider the reason for holding the data.
Data no longer required should be disposed of appropriately.
Processing should respect the data subject's applicable rights.
The data subject is the person the personal information concerns.
Protecting individual rights is different from simply maintaining a computer file.
State limited retention and protection of the individual’s rights clearly.

Personal data should be protected against unauthorised access, disclosure, alteration or loss.
Controls can include access permissions, secure storage and protected communication.
Staff handling data need appropriate procedures and responsibilities.
The textbook's transfer principle requires adequate protection when data is sent to another country.
A transfer does not remove the need to protect the data.
The applicable transfer conditions depend on the relevant legal framework.
Explain secure processing as a data-protection principle rather than merely naming security.

Keep sensitive papers away from unattended desks.
Store paper records in locked cabinets with controlled access.
Lock the screen or log out when leaving an unattended computer.
Protect passwords and allow access only to authorised users.
Check recipients and the sensitivity of information before sending it.
Use suitable protection for portable storage and backups.
Physical security and controlled working practices complement software security.
Explain why separate account passwords matter: compromise of a reused password can expose other accounts too.

Personal data relates to an identifiable living individual.
A person may be identified directly or by combining the data with other information.
Examples include name, address, date of birth and contact details.
Account numbers, identity-document numbers and photographs can also identify a person.
Device or online identifiers can become personal data when linked to an individual.
Disclosing an address can reveal where someone lives; a phone number can enable unwanted contact.
Combined information can support impersonation, scams or identity theft.
Use precise personal-data examples such as date of birth. If explaining disclosure, link the specific item to its possible misuse.

Sensitive personal data needs particular care because disclosure can cause serious harm or discrimination.
Textbook examples include medical history and criminal records.
Other examples include racial or ethnic origin, political opinions and religious beliefs.
Trade-union membership and sexual orientation are also examples.
Genetic and biometric information can be highly sensitive.
Sensitive data is a category of personal information, rather than its opposite.
Ordinary identifying details and sensitive categories should be distinguished when examples are requested.
Give sensitive-data examples, such as medical history or political opinions, rather than substituting ordinary contact information.

Confidentiality means information is available only to those authorised to receive it.
Disclosure can be deliberate or accidental.
Sending to the wrong address, exposing a screen or losing storage can reveal private data.
Access controls restrict who can retrieve information.
Encryption protects the meaning of data if an unauthorised person obtains the encrypted copy.
A recipient needs the appropriate decryption capability to recover the original information.
Cloud storage introduces third-party access and management considerations.
Confidentiality controls do not by themselves prevent every deletion, loss or alteration.
Explain the encryption key and the recipient’s decryption capability, not just that information becomes unreadable.

E-safety is the safe and responsible use of digital technology.
It includes behaviour when browsing, emailing, gaming and using social media.
Risks include fraud, abuse, inappropriate content and disclosure of personal information.
Users need to protect their own privacy and respect others' confidentiality.
Reporting problems and using appropriate privacy settings support safer participation.
Monitoring activity is different from restricting access.
Technical security is one part of e-safety rather than the whole subject.
Monitoring observes activity or history; controlling access uses restrictions such as time limits or blocked sites.

Use trusted sources and check the address of the service being visited.
Be cautious with downloads and use legitimate software sources.
Keep the operating system and anti-malware protection updated.
Scan files and removable storage before opening or running their contents.
Safe-search settings and appropriate content controls can reduce unwanted material.
Log out of accounts when finished, especially on shared devices.
HTTPS protects the connection but does not prove that all content or requests on a site are trustworthy.
Supervision, browsing-history checks and access controls have different purposes.
Match the measure to the risk. Virus protection needs up-to-date scanning and trusted downloads rather than an unrelated firewall statement.

Check the sender's actual address and the destination of links rather than relying on a display name.
Do not follow suspicious links or supply personal details in response to an unverified request.
Email filters can reduce unwanted or suspicious messages.
Check unexpected requests independently through a known contact route.
Scan attachments with up-to-date protection before opening their contents.
Delete or report a suspicious message rather than replying to it.
A familiar sender name does not guarantee that an attachment or request is genuine.
An unsubscribe link in a fraudulent message may itself be unsafe.
Give specific phishing precautions and check links or addresses. Naming a firewall or spam filter alone did not meet this question’s requirement.

Avoid unnecessary disclosure of identifying or sensitive information in email.
Check the exact recipient address before sending.
Check that the intended attachment is selected.
Remove personal data that the recipient does not need.
Use suitable encryption or protection when confidential material must be sent.
Bcc prevents ordinary recipients from seeing the other Bcc addresses.
Protect the email account's credentials and log out on shared devices.
An identifying photograph can reveal details such as a person's school or location.
Check the exact recipient email address and attachment, remove unnecessary personal information and protect confidential content.

Limit who can view a social-media profile and posts.
Do not publicly share home addresses, telephone numbers or other unnecessary identifying details.
Avoid location information and images that reveal where a person can be found.
Review contact requests and accept only appropriately trusted contacts.
Use private-profile settings and control who can contact the account.
Personal information shared within a group may be forwarded outside it.
Cyberbullying, misinformation and excessive use can harm users or distract them.
Privacy settings reduce exposure but do not guarantee that information will stay private.
Specify practical social-media actions, such as private profiles and limiting identifying images; do not rely on do not talk to strangers alone.

Block and report abusive, suspicious or unwanted accounts.
Use respectful language and do not distribute inappropriate images.
Respect other people's personal information and confidentiality.
Do not give private information to an unverified online contact.
Do not arrange to meet an unknown contact alone; children should involve a trusted adult.
Be cautious if someone pressures a user into private communication or secrecy.
Moderators can remove inappropriate posts and reduce abuse in a group.
Report concerning behaviour through the platform and suitable support channels.
Link safeguards to the social-media situation: privacy, reporting abuse and protecting others’ confidential information.

Protect personal and location information when interacting with other players.
Use suitable account privacy settings and strong, unique credentials.
Do not follow unknown links or accept suspicious downloads or trades.
Block and report abuse, bullying or fraudulent requests.
Use age-appropriate games and communication settings.
Agree sensible time limits and balance gaming with other activities.
Parents or carers can supervise and use appropriate controls for children.
Precautions should address the player's actual gaming risks rather than unrelated system-development issues.
Explain gaming precautions from the player’s perspective and link each action to a risk; avoid repeated or developer-focused points.

Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or data.
Access occurs without the owner's permission or consent.
An intruder may copy confidential information or misuse personal details.
Data may be altered, deleted or corrupted.
Access can support impersonation or identity theft.
Copying data does not necessarily remove the original from the system.
The definition concerns unauthorised access, not merely a computer running slowly.
Define unauthorised access and develop its consequences. Data may be copied without the original being removed.

Use strong authentication and appropriate access permissions.
Keep software updated to reduce known vulnerabilities.
A firewall can restrict unauthorised network traffic.
Monitor relevant activity and investigate suspicious access.
Anti-malware can help detect malicious programs involved in an attack.
Encryption can prevent an intruder understanding protected data without the key.
Encryption does not itself prevent entry to the system or deletion of encrypted files.
Different controls address different parts of the risk.
Develop how the chosen authentication practice maintains privacy rather than saying only more secure.

Phishing uses deceptive messages that appear to come from a trusted source.
The attacker tries to make the recipient disclose confidential information or take another unsafe action.
An email may contain a link to a fake website imitating a genuine service.
The user follows the link or replies and supplies information.
The copied details can be used for fraud or identity theft.
Check addresses and links, do not respond to suspicious requests, and verify independently.
Appropriate email filtering and reporting can reduce exposure.
Phishing relies on deception through a message; pharming uses underlying redirection.
Explain the deceptive legitimate-looking message, fake destination and requested information. Do not confuse email phishing with pharming or SMS smishing.

Smishing is phishing carried out through SMS or text messages.
The message may impersonate a bank, delivery service or other trusted organisation.
It may contain a fake link or contact number.
Urgency or a claimed problem pressures the recipient to act.
The attacker seeks personal information, credentials or payment details.
Avoid using unverified links or contact information in the message.
Check the request using a known official route and block or report suspicious messages.
Anti-virus alone does not prevent someone voluntarily disclosing data in reply.
State that smishing uses SMS or text messages. Link precautions to that message-based deception rather than substituting anti-virus.

Vishing uses phone calls or voice messages to deceive people.
The caller pretends to represent a trusted organisation.
The caller pressures or persuades the person to reveal private information.
The disclosed details can enable fraud or unauthorised account access.
Do not disclose credentials or other sensitive information to an unverified caller.
End the call and check through a known contact route.
Block or report suspicious numbers where appropriate.
The voice-call mechanism distinguishes vishing from email or SMS phishing.
Include the phone-call or voice-message mechanism and the attempt to obtain personal information.

Pharming redirects a user to a fraudulent website without requiring a deceptive message link to be clicked.
Malicious changes on a device or in name-resolution infrastructure can cause the redirection.
A user may type the intended genuine address but reach the fake service.
The fake page imitates the legitimate site to collect confidential details.
The user may not realise the destination has changed.
Use up-to-date anti-malware and check the actual site and certificate information.
Avoid entering personal information if the destination or connection is suspicious.
Pharming is different from merely receiving an unsolicited email.
Explain the malicious redirection to a fake site even after the intended URL is typed. Mentioning a virus alone does not explain pharming.

Both phishing and pharming can lead to fake sites seeking confidential information.
Both can impersonate legitimate organisations and enable identity theft or financial fraud.
Phishing commonly uses a convincing message and a link or request for a reply.
Pharming changes the underlying route or lookup so a user can be redirected after typing a genuine address.
Phishing involves interaction with the deceptive message; pharming need not.
The original data may remain after it has been copied or disclosed.
Prevention should match the mechanism rather than treating all safeguards as interchangeable.
Develop both similarities and differences: a phishing message induces action, while pharming redirects through malicious changes.

Malware is software designed to carry out harmful or unwanted activity.
A virus is a type of malware that replicates by attaching to a host file or program.
Running an infected host can activate the virus and spread infection.
Possible effects include corrupted or deleted data and disrupted operation.
Infection can arrive through infected files, attachments, downloads or removable storage.
Anti-virus tools can use known signatures and other detection methods.
Not all malware is a virus, and not all threats are detected by one product.
Define a virus through malware replication and effects. Physical damage or how a download arrives does not define it.

Use up-to-date anti-virus or anti-malware protection appropriate to the threats.
Scan files, attachments and removable media before use.
Avoid running software from untrusted sources.
Keep systems updated and run appropriate scans.
Detected threats can be blocked, quarantined or removed.
A backup does not prevent infection.
Backing up infected files can copy the malware into the backup.
Restoring that infected copy can reinfect the system.
Clean, recoverable backups support recovery but need separate protection.
Explain both stages: infected files copied into a backup can reinfect the system when restored. Backups do not prevent viruses.

A worm is malware that can replicate and spread between systems without attaching itself to a host file.
It often spreads across networks using vulnerabilities or other automated routes.
A virus replicates through an infected host file or program.
Both can consume resources and disrupt operation.
Rapid worm spread can overload systems or network links.
Updates, restricted network access and suitable malware protection reduce exposure.
The distinction concerns replication and spread rather than whether either can be harmful.

A Trojan is malicious software disguised as useful or legitimate software.
The user is persuaded to install or run it.
It can open unauthorised access, copy information or install other malware.
The disguise helps the attacker gain the user's trust.
A Trojan does not need to self-replicate to perform its harmful role.
Use trustworthy software sources and suitable malware protection.
The term describes deception and hidden behaviour rather than a particular visual appearance.

Spyware secretly monitors activity and can disclose information to another party.
A keylogger records keyboard input.
Keylogging can be performed by software or a hardware device.
Captured data can include passwords, card details and other confidential entries.
The recorded information can be sent to an attacker.
Anti-spyware or suitable anti-malware can detect and remove supported threats.
System updates and checking devices before confidential entry can reduce risk.
A strong password does not protect it if the actual keystrokes are captured.
Explain recording and disclosing actual keystrokes; rearranging the word keylogging is not an explanation.

A keyboard logger captures typed input, so software countermeasures must address that capture.
Anti-keylogging or anti-malware tools can detect or block supported threats.
The textbook describes partial-password prompts and on-screen selection as ways of reducing exposure to some keyboard capture.
Those methods do not prevent every form of monitoring.
Screen-recording malware can capture visible selections or displayed information.
A hardware logger may require physical inspection or control of access.
Keeping the system updated and avoiding compromised devices are relevant precautions.
Covering the keyboard addresses observation, not malicious software recording keystrokes.
Address malware interception with anti-keylogging, anti-spyware or suitable anti-malware. Covering the keyboard and strong passwords do not stop software capture.

Adware displays unwanted advertisements, pop-ups or promotional content.
Some adware changes browser settings or redirects searches.
It may be bundled with software the user installs.
Unwanted background activity can reduce performance or usability.
Some advertising software also tracks activity, creating privacy concerns.
Check installation choices and use trusted software sources.
Suitable removal or anti-malware tools can help with intrusive adware.
Advertising alone does not make every program malicious; behaviour and consent matter.

Ransomware prevents access to a system or data and demands payment.
It commonly encrypts files so the user cannot open them normally.
It can arrive through deceptive downloads, malicious attachments or exploited vulnerabilities.
The disruption can stop an organisation carrying out its work.
Updates, cautious handling of files and suitable malware protection reduce risk.
Protected backups can support recovery if clean and available.
Paying does not guarantee restoration of data.
A backup that is accessible to the malware may also be damaged or encrypted.

A virus replicates through an infected host file or program.
A worm can spread independently between systems without attaching to a host file.
A Trojan disguises harmful behaviour as legitimate software.
Spyware monitors and discloses activity or confidential information.
A keylogger specifically records keystrokes.
Adware produces unwanted advertising or related browser behaviour.
Ransomware restricts access or encrypts data to demand payment.
A single malicious program can combine more than one behaviour.

Shoulder surfing obtains private information by watching someone enter or display it.
An observer or camera may capture a PIN or password.
Overhearing confidential spoken information can create a related disclosure risk.
Shield the keypad and avoid entering secrets where they can be observed.
Turn off visible password display when others are nearby.
Do not disclose card credentials to unverified people.
Suitable additional authentication reduces dependence on exposed details.
The threat is observation or eavesdropping, rather than software keylogging.
Explain watching someone enter a password or PIN and remembering the observed information.

Card skimming captures information from a card using an unauthorised reader.
A concealed device can copy magnetic-stripe data.
The copied information may be used to create a fraudulent duplicate card.
A separately obtained PIN can enable further misuse.
Inspect readers for signs of tampering and keep the card in sight.
Use appropriate payment alternatives and account alerts where available.
Check transactions and report unexplained activity through the bank's official process.
Copying magnetic-stripe information is not the same as duplicating a secure chip's secret keys.
Describe copying card information and creating an unauthorised duplicate rather than merely naming card theft.

A shim is a concealed device associated with a compromised chip-card reader.
It attempts to capture information exchanged during a card transaction.
Captured data does not by itself duplicate the genuine chip's secret authentication capability.
Protection also depends on correct terminal and issuer security checks.
Look for signs of terminal tampering and avoid suspicious equipment.
Account alerts and transaction checks help identify unexplained spending.
Report unusual transactions promptly through an official banking channel.
Reader checks and account monitoring complement the card's technical protections.
Give relevant additional safeguards, such as keeping a card in sight and checking the reader, without repeating an example excluded by the question.

A keylogger on a compromised device can record card information as it is entered.
Captured information may include card numbers, expiry details or security codes.
PINs or passwords can be exposed if entered on that device.
An attacker can use the captured details for fraudulent activity.
Use trusted devices and keep suitable malware protection updated.
Avoid entering confidential payment information on a suspected compromised system.
Masking the display or choosing a longer secret does not stop a keylogger capturing input.

Biometric authentication checks identity using physical or behavioural characteristics.
Examples include fingerprints, face, iris, retina and voice recognition.
A captured sample is compared with an enrolled template.
A match supports an authentication decision.
Biometrics are harder to forget or lend than a card or password.
Recognition errors, capture conditions, cost and privacy remain considerations.
Name the method rather than only the device used to capture it.
Name biometric methods rather than capture devices, and keep the specified method consistent.

A fingerprint sensor captures features of a finger's ridge and valley pattern.
The system extracts identifying features and compares them with a stored template.
A sufficient match supports the user's identity or access decision.
Uses include phone unlocking and building access.
The user must enrol a suitable reference sample first.
Dirt, damage or poor positioning can reduce capture quality.
The matching process is performed by the system, not simply by the existence of a scanner.
Name fingerprint recognition as the method rather than giving only a scanner device.

A user does not have to remember a password or carry a separate identity card.
A finger is not misplaced in the same way as a card.
Fingerprints provide distinguishing features for identification.
Enrolment and suitable capture equipment have costs.
Dirty, wet or injured fingers can cause failed recognition.
Stored biometric information raises privacy and security concerns.
The system needs a suitable way to handle a genuine user who cannot be recognised.
Benefits and drawbacks should be linked to fingerprint authentication specifically.

Face recognition captures an image of the person's face.
Software identifies facial features or measurements.
The extracted representation is compared with enrolled data.
A sufficient match supports identification or authentication.
It can avoid typing a password or presenting a card.
Lighting, pose, obstruction or changed appearance can affect some systems.
Recognition accuracy and resistance to impersonation depend on the implementation.
Facial-image processing also creates privacy concerns.
Give facial recognition as a biometric method rather than the camera used to capture it.

Signature recognition compares a captured signature with an enrolled pattern.
Dynamic systems can use features such as movement, timing or pressure as well as shape.
It is familiar to many users and can be relatively non-intrusive.
Suitable capture and comparison can be quick.
A genuine person's signature may vary between attempts.
Variation can cause false rejection, while imitation creates a false-acceptance risk.
The equipment, enrolment and comparison method affect reliability.

Retina recognition uses blood-vessel patterns at the back of the eye.
Iris recognition uses patterns in the coloured area around the pupil.
Both compare captured features with enrolled biometric information.
Retina capture generally requires specialised close positioning.
Iris capture uses a detailed image and can be less intrusive.
Equipment cost, capture speed and accuracy depend on the system.
Both involve highly personal data that needs secure handling.
The iris and retina are different parts of the eye and should not be confused.
Distinguish the biometric methods and avoid repeating an example already supplied in the question.

Voice recognition authenticates using features of a person's voice.
The system compares a captured voice sample with an enrolled profile.
It can provide fast, hands-free access without typing.
An existing microphone can reduce the need for additional capture equipment.
Background noise can affect recognition.
Illness or other changes in the voice can prevent a genuine match.
Recordings or imitation can create impersonation risks if the system lacks effective checks.
The user may need time to enrol or train the system.
Develop both impacts of voice login, including convenience and recognition problems when the voice changes or the environment is noisy.

Biometric systems store or process highly personal identifying information.
Users may have concerns about monitoring or reuse beyond the intended purpose.
A compromised biometric cannot be replaced as easily as an ordinary password.
False acceptance permits the wrong person; false rejection blocks a genuine user.
Capture conditions affect convenience and reliability.
Equipment, enrolment, training and support have costs.
Compare the actual method's accuracy, intrusiveness and usability.
No biometric method provides a universal guarantee of correct recognition.
Link the trade-off to the actual biometric method and develop both advantages and disadvantages.

A digital certificate binds identity information, such as a website's domain, to a public key.
It is digitally signed by an issuer such as a certificate authority.
It contains the subject's identifying details and public key.
Other contents include issuer information, serial number and validity dates.
The browser checks the certificate and its chain against trusted issuers.
It checks that the certificate is valid for the intended site.
The certificate contains a public key, not the holder's private key.
A valid connection certificate does not guarantee that every request or item of website content is trustworthy.
Specify certificate contents precisely, such as the subject or owner’s name and public key. Relate its purpose to the website’s identity.

Asymmetric cryptography uses a related public-key and private-key pair.
The public key can be shared; the private key must remain secret.
For public-key encryption, data encrypted to a recipient's public key is decrypted with the corresponding private key.
For digital signatures, the private key signs and the public key verifies.
A certificate helps establish which identity controls a public key.
The private key should not be sent alongside the encrypted message as ordinary unprotected data.
Encryption and signature verification are different cryptographic operations.
Explain the public key’s identity link through the certificate; do not claim it is used to read the certificate itself.

The textbook term SSL refers to protection of communication between a client and server.
Modern HTTPS uses TLS, the successor to SSL.
The connection encrypts data in transit between the browser and server.
Integrity protection helps detect modification during transmission.
A server certificate supports authentication of the server's identity.
HTTPS in the address indicates use of the protected HTTP connection.
Browser security indicators can vary; a padlock is not proof that the site's content is honest.
Transport protection does not itself secure every stored copy of the data.
Explain an encrypted browser-to-server connection; expanding SSL or saying extra security alone is incomplete.

The browser begins a secure-connection handshake with the server.
The server provides its certificate and the required authentication information.
The browser checks the certificate's validity, trusted issuer chain and match to the requested site.
The parties agree supported security settings and establish session keys.
The server proves control of the private key associated with its certificate.
The session keys protect subsequent data exchange.
The private key is not transmitted as a public part of the certificate.
A failed certificate check can indicate that the connection cannot be trusted as requested.

HTTPS protects web traffic for services such as online banking and shopping.
Protected connections can also secure cloud, intranet and extranet access.
Suitable encrypted protocols protect email transport and file transfer.
Secure calls or messaging can protect communication content depending on the service.
Encryption reduces the usefulness of intercepted data to an unauthorised reader.
The protocol must be appropriate to the particular service.
Using the internet or cloud alone does not guarantee that a transfer is encrypted.
Name encrypted transfer methods or protocols rather than devices or general security procedures.

Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and an encryption key.
The ciphertext is difficult to understand without the appropriate decryption capability.
Decryption recovers the original information using the required key or keys.
Encryption can protect data in transit or at rest.
The recipient must have secure access to the correct decryption capability.
Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret key; asymmetric encryption uses related public and private keys.
Encryption protects confidentiality but does not itself prevent unauthorised access, copying or deletion.
Key protection is essential to maintaining confidentiality.
Explain plaintext-to-ciphertext conversion using an algorithm and key, with appropriate decryption; naming ciphertext or a key alone is insufficient.
