Stored-data encryption protects information on devices such as HDDs or SSDs.
An unauthorised person obtaining the device should not be able to read the protected plaintext without the required key.
Files can also be encrypted before upload to cloud storage.
Key access determines who can decrypt the information.
Encryption does not stop a provider or attacker deleting the encrypted file.
Losing the decryption key can make the data inaccessible to its legitimate owner.
Backups and access controls address risks that encryption alone does not solve.

A protected connection can encrypt traffic between the user and email provider.
Message-level encryption protects the message content beyond a single transport connection.
Stored or archived email can be encrypted separately.
The sender encrypts using the appropriate key arrangement.
The authorised recipient uses the required decryption capability to recover the content.
The recipient address and chosen attachment still need checking.
Transport encryption, message encryption and storage encryption protect different parts of the email lifecycle.
Sensitive content is not automatically protected merely because an email account has a password.
Explain how the message is encrypted and how the recipient uses the appropriate key arrangement to recover it.

A firewall controls traffic entering or leaving a device or network.
It can be implemented in hardware, software or a combination.
It is commonly placed at a boundary between an internal network and an external network.
Configured rules determine which traffic is allowed or blocked.
Rules can consider addresses, ports, protocols or application information.
A personal firewall protects an individual device's network traffic.
A firewall is different from software that scans stored files for virus signatures.

A firewall inspects network traffic against configured rules.
It blocks traffic that does not meet the permitted conditions.
It can restrict access to particular destinations or services.
It can control which applications communicate over a network.
Logs and alerts help an administrator investigate suspicious traffic.
Allow lists and deny lists can support access restrictions.
The quality of protection depends on the rules and correct configuration.
A firewall does not guarantee detection or removal of every malicious file.
Restricting access through filters or allow/deny rules differs from merely observing browsing history.

Authentication checks that a user is who they claim to be.
A knowledge factor is something known, such as a password or PIN.
A possession factor is something held, such as a security token or registered device.
An inherence factor is a characteristic of the user, such as a fingerprint.
Combining different factor types can strengthen authentication.
Two secrets of the same type do not necessarily provide two independent factor types.
A factor category and an example should be distinguished.
Distinguish each factor category from a corresponding example.

Two-factor authentication combines two different types of authentication factor.
For example, a password can be combined with a code from a registered token or phone.
The user completes the initial login and supplies the additional required proof.
The system verifies both before permitting the protected action.
A one-time password is intended for one use and may expire after a short period.
A stolen password alone is less useful when a separate factor is required.
The concept is the additional independent authentication requirement, not merely the sequence of screens.
Codes and tokens still need protection from deceptive requests.
Explain the concept and additional security layer, not only the steps of a particular login procedure.

A user ID identifies the account being accessed.
A password is a secret used to authenticate access to that account.
The system checks the submitted credentials.
The user receives the access rights assigned to the account.
Account identifiers support monitoring of account activity.
Password masking reduces casual observation of the displayed entry.
Repeated failed attempts may cause a lockout or another protective response.
Different users can choose the same password, so password uniqueness should not be assumed.
The user ID identifies the account and the password authenticates access. Do not assume that every password is unique.

A strong password or passphrase is long and difficult to guess.
Avoid personal details, common predictable choices and obvious keyboard sequences.
Character variety can make a chosen password harder to guess, but length and unpredictability are important.
Use a distinct password for each account to limit the effect of one compromise.
A memorable but unpredictable phrase can be easier to manage than a short complicated pattern.
Do not share credentials or expose them to observation.
A strong password does not stop phishing, keylogging or every form of interception.
Extra authentication can reduce dependence on the password alone.
Give distinct strength rules and justify unpredictability rather than choosing a password only because it is memorable.

Keep account credentials secret and use appropriate protection against spyware or keylogging.
Mask password entry when other people can observe the screen.
Entering a new password twice can detect a typing mismatch during setup.
Attempt limits or temporary lockout reduce repeated online guessing.
A reset process verifies the request and provides a controlled way to set a replacement.
Check reset messages independently if they are unexpected.
Change passwords when compromised or when required by an appropriate account-recovery process.
Frequent compulsory changes can lead to predictable variants or forgotten passwords.
Masking, double-entry verification and authentication serve different purposes.
Match the safeguard to the threat: protecting against keylogging differs from preventing observation or reducing password guessing.
Audience age, experience, expectations and knowledge

Consider the target audience's age, experience, expectations and existing knowledge.
Adapt the level of detail and complexity to what the audience can understand.
Choose an approach and examples relevant to the audience's interests.
Use appropriate language, layout and media.
Different audiences may need different versions of the same information.
Age, experience, knowledge and expectations are distinct characteristics.
Use audience research rather than assuming that every person in a group has identical needs.
Give distinct audience characteristics and avoid repeating one already supplied in the question.

Interview a representative cross-section of the intended audience.
Use questionnaires or online surveys to gather information from more people.
Ask about background, interests, prior knowledge and expectations.
Identify accessibility and language needs.
Use clear questions appropriate to the respondents.
Choose a research scale suitable for the size and importance of the ICT solution.
Findings should guide content and design decisions.

Organise the responses collected from audience research.
Look for common characteristics, interests and needs.
Identify differences between important groups within the audience.
Draw conclusions about suitable language, detail, examples and interaction.
Use the findings to decide which features the solution needs.
The depth of analysis should suit the size and complexity of the project.
Research is useful when its results influence the final product.

A sales-team presentation can include technical facts and detailed product information.
Staff may need sales statistics, profitability information and relevant bonus arrangements.
Professional language and a more formal layout can suit staff training.
Charts can help explain sales or financial comparisons.
A customer presentation should emphasise product features, benefits and price.
Customer language should be clear, friendly and no more technical than necessary.
Suitable images, video or demonstrations can make the customer presentation eye-catching and understandable.
The comparison concerns the stated sales team and customers, rather than substituting age groups.
Compare the stated sales team with customers: technical detail and profitability for staff versus clear product features and price for customers.

Use language appropriate to the audience's knowledge and experience.
Explain unfamiliar terms and avoid unnecessary jargon.
Specialist terminology can be appropriate for an audience that understands it.
Keep content accurate, clear and focused on the purpose.
Use a tone that respects the audience.
Avoid offensive or inappropriate language.
Short, simple wording can help younger users or people using a second language.
A professional audience may need a more formal style and greater technical detail.
Relate language, tone and complexity to the audience’s interests and knowledge rather than listing generic factors.

Text, images, sound, video and animation can support the message.
Use media relevant to the topic and audience.
Graphs can clarify statistics or comparisons.
Animation can illustrate a process that is difficult to describe with static text.
Consistent layout and balanced white space make the content easier to follow.
Excessive effects or irrelevant sound can distract from the main point.
Balance media with readable text and suitable headings.
Choose features for their explanatory or engagement value rather than adding them without a purpose.
Link the selected media or design feature to the audience and explain its purpose. A feature name alone lacks development.

Match presentation duration to the purpose and audience.
Keep content focused on the information the audience needs.
A long presentation needs sustained interest and engagement.
Very young audiences may find long sessions difficult to follow.
Remove unnecessary repetition or detail.
Allow time for explanations, questions and any planned activity.
Duration and content depth should be considered together.

Questions can encourage the audience to think and respond.
Demonstrations or short activities can help users explore an idea.
Interactive elements can give users choices or feedback.
Games and activities can engage younger users when relevant to the learning goal.
Participation should support the message rather than distract from it.
Not everyone is comfortable taking part publicly.
Provide a suitable way for the audience to engage without forcing unwanted participation.
Explain how an interactive activity engages the intended audience instead of merely naming interactivity.

Use examples that relate to the audience's interests and experience.
Choose a level of difficulty appropriate to their existing knowledge.
Examples should help explain the point rather than introduce unrelated detail.
Respect cultural, personal and dietary preferences where relevant.
Avoid examples or language likely to offend or exclude the audience.
Keep the example accurate and connected to the intended message.
Connect examples and content to the audience’s experience and interests; avoid repeating an age-only explanation.

Identify the age range of the intended website users.
Consider the audience's income or purchasing context when advertising products.
Identify interests that affect the content users want.
Consider disabilities, impairments and accessibility needs.
Consider language and technical experience.
These characteristics influence content, layout, navigation and interaction.
A website should be designed for its intended users rather than one assumed generic audience.

Age can influence suitable language, content complexity and text-image balance.
Young children may benefit from simple wording, larger text and relevant images or activities.
Older children and adults may need more detailed content appropriate to their knowledge.
Use an uncluttered layout and navigation that users can understand.
Readable text, contrast and consistency can support users across age groups.
Do not assume age alone determines someone's interests or technical ability.
Use audience evidence to select the actual design.

Match advertised products and prices to the intended purchasing audience.
A product range should be relevant to the customers the site aims to reach.
Select articles, offers and examples that reflect the users' interests.
For a music site, content can focus on the genres the target group follows.
Keep information on topic so users can find what attracted them to the site.
Income and interests affect content choices rather than replacing accessibility or usability requirements.

Use clear fonts and text large enough to read.
Provide sufficient contrast between text and background.
Make important controls large enough to identify and operate.
Text-to-speech can provide an alternative to reading displayed text.
Voice input can reduce reliance on finding and typing into small controls.
Keep wording and navigation clear.
Do not rely on a red-versus-green distinction alone to communicate meaning.
Accessibility choices should address the users' actual impairment and task.
Give features for the specified visual impairment, such as larger fonts, high contrast or text-to-speech, rather than unrelated technology.

Interview representative users of the proposed website.
Use questionnaires or surveys to gather age, interests, background and access needs.
Ask about the information and tasks users expect.
Identify language, device and accessibility requirements relevant to the site.
Analyse responses to find patterns and important differences.
Use those conclusions to guide content, navigation and presentation.
Testing with intended users can reveal whether the selected design meets their needs.

Use simple short words and sentences appropriate to the children's reading level.
Use readable, sufficiently large text.
Relevant images can reduce dependence on long passages of writing.
Bright colours, animation, video or sound can attract attention when used purposefully.
Games and activities can encourage interaction with the content.
Use white space to separate information and avoid overcrowding.
Provide an interface that is easy for the intended children to use.
Explain how each selected feature supports the young audience.
Develop each feature for younger users. Use precise descriptions such as bright colours rather than vague fun colours.
Needs of adults and older children

Provide interesting content relevant to the audience.
Use an attractive, organised display with balanced white space.
Combine text and images according to the information being communicated.
Use a language level appropriate to the users.
Clear headings and bullet points can make information easier to scan.
Use readable fonts and suitable contrast.
Formal language and layout may be appropriate for a parent or professional audience.
Include technical detail only where the audience and purpose require it.
For a parent newsletter, explain suitable language, clear layout and images; do not treat a printed document as software with video.

Use readable fonts and allow a suitable text size.
Provide sufficient colour contrast.
Keep page layout and navigation consistent.
Use clear controls and an understandable interaction method.
Explain unfamiliar technical terms where necessary.
Avoid unnecessary input or confusing navigation routes.
Older users have varied experience, so assess their actual requirements rather than assuming inability.

Audience appreciation makes the solution more likely to be fit for purpose.
Suitable language helps users understand the information.
Relevant content attracts attention and maintains interest.
Readable displays and accessibility features allow more people to use the solution.
Clear navigation reduces confusion and frustration.
Appropriate interaction avoids unnecessary typing or difficult control sequences.
Respectful content helps meet users' expectations.
Each design feature should be linked to a need and its effect on the user.
Explain why the selected content or language suits the audience instead of giving an undeveloped feature list.
Applying audience appreciation to other ICT products

Audience appreciation applies to presentations, websites, games, databases and other ICT solutions.
Identify who will use the product and what they need to do.
Match content and complexity to their knowledge and experience.
Choose suitable language, media and examples.
Provide usable controls and appropriate accessibility support.
Collect and analyse audience information before committing to a design.
The same principle can produce different design choices for different products and users.
Apply age-related design choices to the actual ICT product and explain their relevance.

Copyright protects intellectual work and gives the rights holder control over specified uses such as copying.
The owner can grant permission through a licence.
Unauthorised copying, distribution or reuse of protected software can infringe those rights.
Permission may be required before copying code or including protected material in another product.
Acknowledge sources where required, but a credit alone does not automatically replace permission.
Copyright helps recognise creators, protect their work and discourage plagiarism.
Copyright concerns intellectual work; data protection concerns appropriate handling of personal data.
The permitted uses depend on the licence and applicable rules.
Explain rights over intellectual work and permission to copy. Copyright is not data protection and does not prohibit every authorised copy.

Software piracy is the unauthorised or illegal copying of software.
It can include distributing or selling copies without the required permission.
Installing software beyond the acquired licence permissions can also breach the allowed use.
An authorised copy or installation allowed by a licence is different from piracy.
Technical controls and licence terms can be used to discourage unauthorised use.
Piracy concerns software rights rather than virus infection or personal-data protection.

A licence defines the permitted use of software.
A single-computer or single-user licence does not automatically permit unrestricted use across a network.
A suitable multiple-computer or network licence allows use within its stated conditions.
Conditions can limit installations, users or simultaneous access.
Organisations need permission covering the way the software is deployed.
The licence must be checked rather than assuming that possession of one copy permits every installation.
Explain software-use restrictions such as network permission rather than repeating only permission and source-credit actions.

A product key is a supplied code used to support authorised installation or activation.
It may contain letters and numbers.
The user enters the code when the software requires it.
The program or an online service checks whether the key is valid.
Activation rules can limit unauthorised installations or use.
Online account checks can also enforce permitted access or concurrent-use limits.
A product key is different from an ordinary account password or an anti-virus tool.
Name the product key and explain the supplied code and its use; merely expanding the method’s name is insufficient.

A licence agreement sets out conditions between the software provider and user.
It states what use, copying, installation or distribution is permitted.
The user may need to accept the agreement before installation or use continues.
The terms can define user numbers, installation limits and restrictions.
Accepting an agreement does not grant rights beyond those stated.
Licence conditions are a rights-management measure rather than a method of scanning for malware.
Describe the agreement between vendor and user about permitted software use, not a malware-protection process.

Packaging can carry a notice warning against unauthorised copying.
A hologram or similar security mark can help identify genuine packaging.
The visible mark provides an authenticity indication for purchasers.
It discourages distribution of obviously counterfeit copies.
A packaging label does not technically stop a file being copied.
Physical marks can be used alongside licence, key or activation checks.
Explain how the notice or hologram supports identification of genuine software rather than only naming it.

Some software checks that its required original CD, DVD or memory device is present.
The program refuses to run if the required medium is absent.
This links operation to possession of the supplied medium.
It can discourage unauthorised use of copied program files.
It is a software-protection approach, not simply supplying the program on a disc.
The exact check depends on the software and its licensing design.
Explain that operation depends on the required original medium being present, rather than only saying the software is on a disc.

A software-protection dongle is a hardware device connected to the computer, often through USB.
It supplies required authorisation information or functionality.
The program checks for the dongle.
Without the required valid dongle, the software will not run or unlock its protected functions.
It discourages use of copied software without the authorised hardware.
The word dongle can also describe devices such as wireless adapters; that is a different use of the term.
Describe the connected hardware and the software refusing to run without it. Anti-virus is not a software-piracy control.

Software-industry and intellectual-property organisations can support efforts against unauthorised software distribution.
The textbook gives FAST, IIPA and JIPA as examples in its historical discussion.
Their activities can include awareness, representation or support for rights enforcement, depending on the organisation.
Rights holders can pursue infringements through the applicable legal processes.
Possible consequences can include an order to stop unauthorised use or financial penalties.
A historical case illustrates enforcement but does not establish a universal current penalty.
Organisational roles and legal consequences depend on the place, time and circumstances.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Email laws and consent rules aim to reduce misuse of electronic communication.
The textbook describes obtaining opt-in permission for relevant mailing lists.
Recipients should have an appropriate way to opt out or unsubscribe.
Sender information and subject lines should not be false or misleading.
Organisations should explain how subscribers' personal information is used.
Collecting addresses without proper permission can breach applicable rules.
The exact obligations depend on the jurisdiction and type of message.
Mailing-list administrators need to maintain consent and membership records.
For a mailing list, explain opt-in, opt-out and administrator constraints rather than generic recipient behaviour or hacking.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Use language appropriate to the recipients and purpose.
Do not send abusive, threatening, discriminatory or exploitative messages.
Do not distribute obscene images or illegal material.
Respect other people's personal information and confidentiality.
Avoid forwarding content likely to embarrass or harm someone.
These responsibilities apply to email, messages and online forums.
A recipient being able to delete a message does not make inappropriate content acceptable.
Give specific, developed communication rules and respect others’ confidentiality rather than vague warnings.
Communication with other ICT users using email

An employer's policy should explain permitted business and personal email use.
It can specify approved accounts, devices, style and tone.
It should state prohibited content and confidentiality requirements.
Rules can cover retention, filing, delegated access and automatic replies.
Security procedures should address suspicious messages, attachments and filtering.
Monitoring arrangements and staff responsibilities should be clearly communicated.
Training helps employees understand and follow the policy.
The policy should fit the organisation and applicable rules.
Communication with other ICT users using email

An email or attachment can contain copyright-protected or confidential material.
Receiving a message does not automatically give unrestricted permission to copy or redistribute its contents.
Check the relevant permissions, licence terms and organisational policy before forwarding.
Check the intended recipients and any confidentiality instructions.
Share only information the new recipients are authorised to receive.
Protect sensitive attachments appropriately.
A copyright notice and an encryption control serve different purposes.
Absence of a confidentiality notice does not by itself establish unrestricted reuse rights.
Check the exact recipient and intended attachment, remove unnecessary personal information and protect confidential content.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Use strong, unique credentials and appropriate additional authentication.
Protect the account against unauthorised access and avoid sharing passwords.
Email filters can reduce unwanted messages.
Up-to-date anti-virus or anti-malware can check supported threats in messages and attachments.
Check actual sender addresses, links and unexpected requests.
Use suitable encryption for confidential transfers.
A strong password does not itself stop a user opening malware or responding to phishing.
Match each safeguard to the particular threat.
Give threat-specific email precautions. Naming a firewall or spam filter alone did not meet this phishing-prevention question.
Communication with other ICT users using email

A passive attack observes or discloses information without changing the communication being observed.
Unauthorised reading of a message can breach confidentiality.
An active attack changes data or disrupts communication or service.
Examples include modifying a message or overwhelming a service with traffic.
Malicious messages can attempt to infect or deceive the recipient.
Encryption protects confidentiality, while other controls are needed for integrity, access and service availability.
Classify an attack by what it does rather than assuming every attack has the same effect.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Netiquette means acceptable and courteous behaviour when communicating online.
It includes respecting other users' views and privacy.
Clear, considerate messages reduce misunderstandings.
Recipients cannot normally see the sender's facial expressions or body language.
A joke or abrupt wording can therefore be misunderstood.
Netiquette concerns communication conduct rather than being a definition of anti-virus or hacking protection.
Explain courteous email communication, not unrelated security topics such as viruses or hacking.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Do not send abusive or threatening messages.
Do not send unwanted repeated messages or spam.
Keep the message clear, concise and relevant.
Check spelling, grammar and the intended meaning before sending.
Respect privacy and avoid disclosing information that could embarrass another person.
Avoid whole messages in capital letters, which can appear to be shouting.
Use slang, emoticons and text shorthand only where suitable for the audience.
Acknowledge quoted material and do not present others' work as your own.
Be tolerant of minor mistakes and avoid unnecessary hostile replies.
If examples are requested, give a distinct email example for each rule rather than merely rewording the rule.
Communication with other ICT users using email

An email group is a named collection of recipient email addresses.
Selecting the group lets a sender address the same message to multiple people.
Groups can support meetings, team announcements or targeted information.
They reduce repeated manual entry and the risk of omitting an intended member.
Administrators need to keep addresses and membership current.
Opt-in, opt-out and relevant sending limits must be managed.
Large groups can create size, volume or administration constraints.
An address group is different from a collection of email messages.
Define a group as a collection of contact addresses, not a group of email messages.
Communication with other ICT users using email

The To field normally lists the main recipients.
Cc stands for carbon copy and sends a copy to additional interested recipients.
To and Cc addresses are normally visible to the recipients.
Bcc stands for blind carbon copy.
A Bcc recipient's address is not shown to the ordinary recipients as part of the other Bcc list.
Bcc recipients can normally see the sender and visible To and Cc addresses.
Bcc recipients do not normally see the other Bcc addresses.
The sender knows the addresses used; Bcc does not hide the sender's identity.
Write out carbon copy and blind carbon copy and explain which recipient addresses are visible. Bcc does not conceal the sender.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Bcc can reduce disclosure of mailing-list members' addresses.
A sender can put their own address in To and the intended recipient group in Bcc.
Recipients receive the message without the full Bcc address list being displayed.
This helps prevent ordinary recipients copying the whole recipient list.
Visible To and Cc addresses remain visible.
Bcc is not message encryption and does not stop a recipient forwarding the content.
A recipient can reveal their involvement by replying or otherwise sharing the message.
Explain hidden Bcc recipient addresses; do not claim that the sender is unknown.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Forwarding sends a received message to another recipient.
It can include the original text, attachments and address information.
Automatic forwarding can pass on unwanted or malicious messages without review.
Forwarding confidential content can disclose it to unauthorised people.
Repeated forwarding can spread spam and affect reputation or filtering.
Check the content, attachments, permissions and recipient before forwarding.
Use automatic-forwarding rules only where appropriate to the account and organisation.
Communication with other ICT users using email

An attachment is a file sent with an email.
It can contain a document, image, archive or executable program.
Unexpected or untrusted attachments can carry malware.
Check that the sender and reason for the file are credible.
Use up-to-date protection to scan the attachment before opening its contents.
Do not run a suspicious executable or enable unsafe content merely because a message asks.
For outgoing files, check the selected attachment and exact recipient address.
Remove unnecessary personal data and protect confidential content.
Focus on attachment precautions: current virus checking, the correct file and the exact recipient address.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Email providers or organisations can limit message and attachment size.
A large attachment may be rejected or fail to reach the recipient.
Compression can reduce some file sizes, depending on the content.
A suitable file-transfer or cloud-sharing service can provide a download link instead.
Set sharing permissions for the intended recipients.
Check that the recipient can access the file and that any link remains valid as required.
Sending a link does not remove the need to protect confidential information.
Large mailing lists can add further sending or size constraints.
Explain the relevant mailing-list constraint, such as message size or sending limits, rather than unrelated security issues.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Spam consists of unsolicited electronic messages, commonly sent in bulk.
Messages may be sent to large or indiscriminate address lists.
They can advertise products or contain deceptive links and requests.
Some spam is automated and not individually personalised.
Poor spelling or urgent wording can be warning signs, but neither is universal.
Spam can also occur through text messages or other messaging services.
Use appropriate filters, avoid publishing an address unnecessarily and block unwanted senders.
Do not respond to suspicious spam or follow its links.
Give several actual spam characteristics, such as unsolicited bulk delivery, rather than only saying it is unwanted.
Communication with other ICT users using email

Spam takes time to identify and remove.
Bulk unwanted messages use storage, bandwidth and processing resources.
Important messages can be harder to find in a congested inbox.
Some spam carries malware or directs users to fraudulent sites.
Repeated unwanted messages can annoy or distress recipients.
Large volumes can interfere with normal service.
Costs or data use can increase depending on the communication service.
Not every spam message is malicious, but unsolicited bulk delivery creates problems even without malware.

The internet is a worldwide network of interconnected networks.
It provides the infrastructure for communication between connected systems.
The World Wide Web is a collection of linked web pages, sites and resources accessed over that infrastructure.
A browser retrieves and displays web resources using HTTP or HTTPS.
The web is a service using the internet, rather than the internet being part of the web.
Other internet services include email and file transfer.
A direct comparison should distinguish the network infrastructure from the web resources and service.
Compare directly: the internet is the global network infrastructure; the web is a service of pages and resources carried over it.

The internet carries many communication services, including email, messaging and file transfer.
The web uses clients such as browsers and servers that supply resources.
HTML describes the structure of web pages.
Browsers interpret page code and present text, images and other media.
HTTP or HTTPS governs requests and responses for web resources.
URLs identify the locations of resources.
A browser can run client-side scripts to support interactive pages.
The internet and its services are related but are not interchangeable terms.
Keep the network infrastructure distinct from the web service and browser used to access it.

An intranet provides private organisational information and services.
Access is restricted to authorised users.
It uses internet technologies such as web pages and network protocols.
It can hold staff documents, internal announcements or business applications.
Authentication, access permissions and firewall controls protect internal resources.
The organisation manages the relevant content and access.
An intranet is different from the publicly connected internet, although remote access may use the internet.
Do not misread intranet as internet. Compare internal access with authorised external access explicitly.

An intranet can tailor information and tools to the organisation's users.
Access controls can limit exposure of confidential internal information.
Internal communication and shared documents can be managed centrally.
Administrators can restrict external links or access as required.
Controlled access reduces some external exposure but does not eliminate security risks.
Performance depends on the actual network and system, not the word intranet alone.
Unlike an extranet, ordinary intranet access is primarily for internal authorised users.
For intranet-versus-extranet comparisons, explain the internal and external audiences as well as relevant shared features.

An extranet extends selected organisational resources to authorised external users.
Examples include customers, suppliers or other trading partners.
It can provide controlled access to part of an organisation's intranet.
External users authenticate and receive only the access they are permitted.
It supports sharing information and communication between organisations.
Intranets and extranets can both use internet technologies and restricted access.
An intranet mainly serves internal users; an extranet also serves authorised outsiders.
Extranet access is different from making every internal resource public.
Explain authorised outside access and compare it with internal intranet access; do not confuse either with unrestricted public access.

An authorised user can access an intranet remotely through a suitable connection.
The user authenticates to the organisation's access service.
A VPN creates a protected connection or tunnel over another network such as the internet.
Encryption helps protect traffic between the remote device and VPN endpoint.
Permissions control which internal services the user may reach.
A mobile network can provide the underlying connection without itself granting intranet access.
Device security and correct access configuration remain necessary.
A VPN does not by itself make every remote device or website trustworthy.

The internet connects networks worldwide; an intranet is a restricted organisational environment.
Internet services support a wide range of organisations and purposes.
An intranet's content is primarily selected for its organisation's needs.
An intranet is managed by the organisation; the internet has no single overall owner.
Intranet access normally requires organisational authorisation.
Some internet resources are public, while others also require authentication or payment.
Both can use the same underlying web and network technologies.
Security and speed depend on the actual implementation rather than a universal public-versus-private rule.

A blog is an online journal or series of posts on a topic.
Posts are typically written by one author or a controlled publishing team.
Entries are commonly displayed in reverse chronological order, with the newest first.
Posts can include observations, links and multimedia.
Readers may be allowed to comment without being allowed to rewrite the author's posts.
Categories can organise posts.
Authors remain responsible for the content they publish.
A forum instead supports ongoing discussions contributed by many members.
A blog is typically an author’s journal with reader comments; a forum supports discussion by many members. Make the comparison explicit.

A microblog uses short, frequent posts.
Posts can provide brief updates, comments or links.
Microblogging can be part of a social-networking service.
Followers can receive updates according to the service's features.
A business blog publishes material to promote or explain an organisation and its activities.
A full blog normally supports longer entries than a microblog.
Length limits and features depend on the particular service.

A wiki is a web application for creating and maintaining shared pages.
Authorised members of a group can create, edit or remove content according to permissions.
Many authors can contribute.
Pages can be linked and organised around topics.
Editing can take place through a browser.
Revision history records changes and can help restore earlier content.
Access rules vary; a wiki does not necessarily allow every internet user to edit it.
A wiki is a type of collaborative system, not merely the name of one well-known site.
Describe a wiki generally, not one named site. Editing depends on authorised group membership; not every internet user can necessarily edit it.

A blog typically publishes posts controlled by an author or publishing team.
Readers can comment where allowed, but do not normally edit the original posts.
A wiki allows authorised contributors to revise shared pages.
Blog posts are commonly arranged newest first.
Wiki organisation is usually topic-based through pages and links.
Both can publish text, images and links through a browser.
A wiki's revision history supports tracking collaborative changes.
The main difference is how content is created, edited and organised.

Social-networking services connect people or groups through profiles and shared activities.
Users can post text, images, video or other content.
Features can include messages, comments, calls, groups and event pages.
Users can follow or invite contacts and control aspects of profile visibility.
Groups can share announcements, ideas and learning resources quickly.
Organisations can use them to communicate with a community or advertise events.
Risks include disclosure of personal data, abuse and unwanted contact.
Privacy settings, respectful behaviour and blocking or reporting tools support safer use.
Explain the benefit to the specified organisation, such as easier communication or access to resources, rather than merely listing group features.

A forum organises discussions into topics, threads or sub-forums.
Members can start discussions and post replies according to permissions.
A moderated forum has a person or team enforcing its rules.
Posts may be checked before publication or reviewed and removed afterwards, depending on the arrangement.
Moderators can restrict spam, abusive language, personal-data disclosure and off-topic material.
An unmoderated forum lacks that routine content review.
A blog typically centres on an author's posts, while a forum's direction is developed by many members.
Membership does not automatically permit editing other people's posts.
Explain moderation through monitoring and removing inappropriate material and preserving confidentiality, rather than generic social-media drawbacks.

An Internet Service Provider supplies users with internet connectivity.
It operates or arranges the network links and equipment needed for access.
A customer normally has an account or service arrangement.
Connections can use technologies such as fibre, cable or mobile networks.
The service may include account details, addressing or access equipment.
Charges and connection terms depend on the provider and plan.
An ISP provides connectivity rather than being the web browser or a search engine.

A web browser retrieves web resources from servers.
It interprets HTML and other page resources to render the page.
It can display text, images, audio or video and run supported client-side scripts.
Links and back or forward controls support navigation.
Bookmarks store page addresses for later access.
History records previously visited locations according to the browser's settings.
A home page can provide a starting page.
A search engine is a service used through a browser, not the browser's definition.
Explain retrieval and interpretation of page resources. Do not replace the browser’s technical role with a search-engine description.

A hyperlink is a selectable connection to another resource or location.
It can be attached to text, an image, an icon or another suitable object.
Following the link can open another page, a file or a location within a page.
Its destination is specified by a URL or reference.
An anchor or fragment target identifies a particular position within a document.
A link can point to that target.
Appearance can vary; a hyperlink need not always be blue underlined text.
A moved or deleted destination can leave the link broken.
Explain a clickable link to a resource or location, and distinguish it from an anchor target.

URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator.
It identifies a resource's location or how it can be accessed.
The scheme identifies the protocol, such as https.
The host or domain identifies the server location by name.
A path identifies a route or resource within that location.
A resource name can identify a file such as index.html.
Some URLs include a query or fragment in addition to the main location.
A domain, filename and complete URL are related but different items.
Distinguish the domain from the filename and complete URL, and place each item correctly.

A mistyped path or resource name can point to a missing page.
A server can return HTTP 404 when the requested resource is not found.
A page that has moved can leave an old hyperlink pointing to the wrong location.
Check the address and use the site's navigation or search where appropriate.
A misspelled domain can cause a different error or reach an unintended site.
Not every incorrect URL produces a 404 response.
A missing resource is different from having no internet connection.
Explain that a moved resource can leave the old hyperlink pointing to a location that no longer works.

If a resource's address is known, enter its URL in the browser.
Site navigation can lead from a home page to a particular resource.
A bookmark stores the URL for quick return visits.
A search engine helps find a resource when its address is unknown.
Search terms describe the information being sought.
Direct access avoids a new search, but the address can become outdated.
Neither a known address nor a search result alone proves the information is reliable.
A bookmark stores the page’s URL for quick access, not the whole page or a position marker.

A search engine matches a query against an index of web resources.
The returned results are often called hits.
Keywords or other search criteria help identify relevant pages.
The user can find sources without already knowing their URLs.
Ranking determines the order in which results are presented.
Sponsored results may appear prominently.
AI-assisted search can interpret natural-language queries and personalise or summarise results.
AI results can still omit sources or contain incorrect or outdated information.
The service is distinct from the browser used to access it.
Develop benefits and drawbacks of searching. Relevant results are not automatically accurate or reliable.

Use specific, relevant keywords rather than a broad or ambiguous phrase.
Add context such as subject, organisation or date when it helps.
Use supported phrase or advanced-search controls to narrow the results.
Remove unnecessary terms if the search becomes too restrictive.
Review the returned results and revise the query.
Narrower criteria can reduce irrelevant hits and information overload.
A standard-search refinement concerns the query rather than simply replacing the task with an AI search.
Search operators and interfaces vary between services.
For standard-search improvement, explain narrower criteria and relevant keywords rather than continuing to discuss AI.

A bookmark saves a page's URL for quick access later.
It does not normally save a complete copy of the web page.
A document can contain a hyperlink to the source.
Screenshots or saved copies can record information for later reference where permitted.
Content can be quoted or incorporated subject to the relevant permissions.
Record and acknowledge sources to avoid plagiarism.
Check whether an updated source changes the information before reusing it.
A bookmark is different from an anchor marking a location within a document.
A browser bookmark stores an address for quick return access; do not confuse it with an anchor inside a document.

Search tools can find relevant information quickly using suitable criteria.
A known source's URL need not be memorised.
Online sources cover a wide range of topics and media.
Pages can be updated more quickly than a new printed edition.
Research can be carried out remotely without travelling to a library.
Many sources are available without a separate content fee, although access costs and subscriptions may apply.
Multimedia can explain ideas in more than one form.
Relevance, freshness and accuracy still need checking.
Explain finding relevant information quickly, without claiming that all search results are reliable.

Web information may be inaccurate, biased, incomplete or outdated.
Anyone able to publish a site can present unsupported claims.
Large result sets create information overload.
Advertising and ranking can make relevant independent information harder to find.
Searching can be time-consuming when the query is unclear.
Inappropriate content or unrelated links can distract users.
Copying without understanding or attribution can lead to plagiarism.
AI-generated results can include false information or miss useful sources.
Include limitations such as information overload and difficulty locating the exact source, with reasons.

Broad or ambiguous searches can return many irrelevant results.
Important sources can be buried among advertisements or less relevant hits.
The first result is not necessarily the best source.
Users may need to compare several sources and assess their credibility.
Unclear wording can make the intended topic difficult to identify.
Use more precise keywords or narrower criteria to improve relevance.
Refining the query and evaluating results are both parts of an effective search.
Explain how unclear criteria and irrelevant or sponsored hits delay searching, then how narrowing the query helps.

Identify the author or organisation responsible for the information.
Consider relevant expertise and the purpose of the publication.
Check whether claims cite evidence or reputable supporting sources.
Compare important facts with independent reliable sources.
Spelling and presentation can raise questions but do not prove accuracy or inaccuracy.
Endorsements and reviews should be assessed for authenticity.
A domain ending or professional-looking design alone does not establish reliability.
Evaluate the source rather than unrelated product features or price.
Evaluate the reliability of the internet source itself, not a product’s specification or price.

Check when the information was published and last reviewed.
Consider whether it is current enough for the question being researched.
Identify commercial, political or other interests that may influence the account.
Separate evidence from opinion, advertising and unsupported claims.
Check whether competing arguments and relevant limitations are included.
Look for references supporting important statements.
Repeated identical or uniformly positive reviews can be a warning sign.
A source can be useful while still needing corroboration.
Develop reliability checks such as review dates, independent comparisons and potentially fake reviews.

Check that the site represents the organisation it claims to represent.
Review its authorship, contact information, evidence and relevant external references.
Working links and maintained pages can indicate active upkeep.
Broken links or abandoned pages can suggest outdated material.
A convincing layout is not proof that the publisher is genuine.
HTTPS protects the connection but does not establish the truth of the content.
Compare important claims with reputable independent sources.
Assess several signals together rather than relying on one appearance feature.
Assess source reliability through evidence and corroboration; do not substitute the advertised product’s features.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules for communication between systems.
HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
A client sends a request for a web resource.
A server returns a response, such as page data or an error status.
Browsers use the supplied resources to display web content.
HTTP without transport encryption does not protect the content against network eavesdropping.
HTTPS uses HTTP over a protected TLS connection.

HTTPS is HTTP over an encrypted and authenticated TLS connection.
The textbook's SSL terminology refers to the predecessor of modern TLS.
Encryption protects data in transit between the browser and server.
Integrity checks help detect tampering.
A server certificate supports verification of the requested site's identity.
The address uses https, while browser connection indicators depend on the browser.
An encrypted connection does not guarantee that the website's claims or requests are honest.
Do not assume every browser defaults to unencrypted HTTP when a scheme is omitted.
Explain the encrypted browser-to-server link and its protection. Expanding SSL or saying extra security alone is insufficient.

FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol.
It is used to transfer files between a client and server.
It supports uploading and downloading according to access permissions.
A suitable client connects to the server and provides any required credentials.
Ordinary FTP does not itself encrypt the transferred data or credentials.
FTPS adds TLS to FTP.
SFTP is a different secure file-transfer protocol operating over SSH.
Use a compatible transfer client rather than assuming every web browser supports FTP addresses.
Name actual secure-transfer protocols rather than devices or general security procedures.

Protected connections support online banking, shopping and other confidential transactions.
Suitable encrypted protocols protect email transport and file transfer.
Cloud, intranet and extranet services can use protected access.
Calls and messaging can also use appropriate encryption.
The purpose is to reduce disclosure or undetected modification during transmission.
Authentication helps establish the party or endpoint being contacted.
Stored copies and the devices at each endpoint need their own protection.
Using cloud storage or sending a password does not automatically make every transfer secure.
Explain how encryption protects transferred information rather than merely naming another security measure.

Supporters of internet controls argue that they can reduce access to illegal or harmful material.
Controls can help protect children and other vulnerable users.
Moderation can reduce abuse and the distribution of inappropriate content.
Intervention can limit some fraudulent or misleading information.
Clear rules and enforcement can support accountability.
Effectiveness depends on the scope, implementation and reliability of the controls.
Control does not guarantee that every harmful item will be prevented.

Monitoring and enforcement across many sites can be expensive.
Different jurisdictions and global distribution make rules difficult to apply consistently.
Overbroad restrictions can limit legitimate expression or access to information.
Judgements about offensive content can be subjective.
Some harmful activity is already covered by existing rules.
Material may remain available through other routes.
Decision-making and appeal arrangements matter when legitimate content can be blocked.
Arguments should weigh protection against cost, practicality and rights.

Content filters can restrict access to selected sites or categories.
Allow lists and deny lists can be configured on suitable services, routers or devices.
Parental controls can set access times and other restrictions.
Providers may offer filtering services for home or mobile connections.
Monitoring history observes use; blocking or time limits control it.
Filters can miss harmful content or block useful material.
Education helps users recognise risks, verify sources and respond appropriately.
Trusted adult or teacher guidance complements technical controls.
Restrictions should be suitable for the intended users and purpose.
Distinguish monitoring activity from restricting access through blocked sites, filters or time limits.

Local files are stored on a device such as an HDD or SSD connected to the computer.

A file manager displays and organises accessible drives, folders and files.

A lost connection can prevent access to files on a network drive.

Opening loads an existing file into an application that supports its format.
A default application may be associated with a particular file type.
Another compatible application may also be able to open the same file.
Importing brings external data or content into the application or current project.
Imported content may be converted into the application's internal structure.
Opening and importing depend on format support, not merely the filename.

A hierarchical structure organises folders and subfolders within parent folders.
A folder can contain files and further subfolders.
Group related files by a meaningful purpose, project or section.
Separate source material, working files and previous versions where useful.
A planned structure reduces clutter and makes files easier to locate.
The path shows the sequence of locations leading to a file.
Consistent organisation helps users save and retrieve the intended version.

A meaningful filename gives a useful indication of its contents.
Consistent naming makes related files easier to identify and retrieve.
Version numbers or other clear labels distinguish stages of development.
Keeping earlier versions allows previous work to be inspected or recovered.
An archive folder can separate old copies from current work.
Modification dates provide additional information but do not replace clear naming.
Version control is different from keeping an independent backup against storage loss.

Changing format can affect which features are retained.
Check which file is current after saving under a different name.
Renaming an extension alone does not convert the file's contents.

Saving retains work in a supported file format for later use.
A native project format can preserve application-specific editing features.
Exporting creates an output in another supported format for a particular use.
Export may flatten or omit features the destination format cannot represent.
Printing produces output on paper or another supported print destination.
Choose the output method according to whether editing, distribution or hard copy is required.
A file should be saved as well as printed if an editable copy is needed later.

A generic format supports exchange between different suitable applications or platforms.
It reduces dependence on the application used to create the original file.
The receiving software must still support the chosen format.
A native format is designed for a particular application or family of applications.

Interoperability means compatible exchange, not a guarantee that every program opens every file.

When asked for generic interchange formats, do not automatically substitute native Office extensions.

Suitable spreadsheet and database software can import or export CSV.
CSV is useful for exchanging data between packages.

CSV is different from CSS, which describes web presentation.
Expand CSV as Comma-Separated Values and describe a comma-delimited text file. Do not confuse it with CSS.

TXT stores plain text.

Suitable text editors and many other applications can open it.

Meaning depends on the content and text encoding.
A .txt extension identifies the file type rather than specifying a particular software brand.
Describe unformatted plain text; text alone or a software brand is less precise.

RTF stands for Rich Text Format.
It stores text with supported formatting such as emphasis and paragraph settings.
It preserves more presentation information than plain TXT.
Compatible word-processing applications can exchange RTF documents.
Not every advanced feature of a native document is necessarily retained.
A plain text editor may show the RTF control codes instead of rendering its formatting.
RTF means Format, not File.
Expand RTF as Rich Text Format and explain retained text formatting. File does not replace Format.

GIF stands for Graphics Interchange Format.
It is suitable for simple graphics, icons and areas of solid colour.
A palette can contain up to 256 colours.
It supports simple transparency.
A GIF can contain frames for animation.
GIF compression is lossless for the encoded image data.
Converting a high-colour photograph to a limited palette can still lose colour detail.
JPEG is usually more suitable for photographic colour gradients, while GIF supports simple animation.
When comparing GIF and JPEG, explain features of both formats rather than describing only GIF animation.

JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group.
Common extensions are .jpg and .jpeg.
It is widely used for still photographs and images with complex colours or gradients.
Ordinary JPEG uses lossy compression to reduce file size.
Higher compression can reduce detail and introduce visible artefacts.
Re-encoding after editing can introduce further loss.
Ordinary JPEG does not provide GIF-style animation or transparent backgrounds.
File size and visual quality depend on the chosen settings and image content.
Develop the JPEG side of the comparison, including colours and lossy re-encoding, rather than relying only on GIF features.

PDF stands for Portable Document Format.
It preserves page layout for viewing or printing with compatible software.
It can contain text, vector graphics and raster images; it is not necessarily a flat image of each page.
A PDF can include links, form fields and other supported interactive content.
It is useful for distributing a document with a stable appearance.
Suitable software can edit PDFs, although editing may be less convenient than using the original document.
Security settings can restrict some operations but do not make all PDFs impossible to change.
Export settings and content determine the file size; PDF is not always smaller than the source file.
Expand Portable Document Format accurately. PDF can be edited with suitable software; do not say editing is impossible.

Decompression preserves the image data encoded in the PNG.
It supports transparency, including partially transparent areas.
It is useful for web graphics, screenshots and images needing sharp detail.

MP4 is a multimedia container format defined by MPEG-4 Part 14.

MP4 is different from MP3, which is primarily an audio format.
Check that the extension matches the requested category and do not repeat formats excluded in the question.

MP3 is an audio format using MPEG Audio Layer III compression.
It uses lossy compression to reduce audio file size.
It is suitable for distributing music or speech where the quality-size trade-off is acceptable.
The bit rate and duration affect the file size.
Stronger compression can reduce sound quality.
Its main media content is audio, rather than moving video.
Embedded metadata or cover artwork does not turn it into an MP4-style video container.
Use the requested generic format accurately rather than substituting a native Office format or repeating an excluded example.

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.
A stylesheet defines the presentation of web content.
It can control colours, fonts, spacing and layout.
One stylesheet can be linked to several HTML pages.
Shared styles support consistent presentation and simpler updates.
CSS describes styling rules; it is not itself HTML markup.
CSS is different from CSV, a text format for tabular data.
Distinguish CSS from CSV and explain the stylesheet’s role in web-page presentation.

HTML stands for Hypertext Markup Language.
It uses markup to describe the structure and content of a web page.
Common extensions are .htm and .html.
A browser interprets the markup and displays the page.
Elements can define headings, paragraphs, links and references to media.
CSS can supply presentation rules for the HTML content.
HTML source is text-based, although the rendered page can include many kinds of media.
Give a generic website-authoring extension such as htm or html rather than an application name.

RAR stands for Roshal Archive.
It is an archive container that can hold one or more files and folders.
It supports lossless compression to reduce the stored size of suitable content.
It can group related files for transfer or storage.
Compatible software is needed to create or extract the archive.
Already compressed content may shrink little when archived.
RAR is an archive format, rather than an ordinary image, audio or text-document format.
Explain RAR as a compression archive containing other files, not merely an unfamiliar extension.

ZIP is an archive format that can group files and folders into one container.
It commonly uses lossless compression.
Extraction restores the archived files' contents.
Grouping files can simplify transfer and preserve their organisation.
Compression can reduce storage needs and transmission time where the content permits.
Already compressed media may not become much smaller.
A ZIP archive is not automatically encrypted or safe from malware.
ZIP and RAR are archive-format examples.
For an archive-format question, ZIP and RAR are appropriate; an image or document format is a different category.

Choose a format supported by the software and platform that will receive it.
Match the format to the content: for example, CSV for tabular interchange or MP3 for audio.
Consider whether page layout or editable application features must be retained.
For graphics, consider colour range, transparency, animation and compression.
Distinguish a container such as MP4 from an individual image or audio format.
Choose a suitable quality-size balance.
Use the requested generic extension rather than a brand name.
A filename extension should match the actual encoded format.
Match the format to the requested category, avoid brands and do not repeat supplied examples.
Reduce file sizes for storage or transmission

Smaller files use less storage capacity.
At the same connection speed, fewer bytes generally take less time to transfer.
Smaller web media can reduce page loading time.
Compression can help meet message or attachment size limits.
It can reduce network traffic and the data that must be downloaded.
Compression reduces the amount transmitted; it does not itself increase the connection's bandwidth.
The benefit depends on how much the particular content can be reduced.
State that the file size and storage requirement are reduced. Smaller or less space alone needs the file or storage identified.
Reduce file sizes for storage or transmission

The amount and type of content affect file size.
Video size depends on duration, frame data and encoding settings.
For raster images, pixel dimensions, colour depth and compression influence size.
Documents with many high-resolution images can be large.
Large databases can contain extensive records even without video.
Complex formatting or additional project data can add to a native document's size.
A file's extension alone does not specify its exact size.
Address stored file size and the relevant data settings rather than assuming smaller display dimensions alone answer the question.
Reduce file sizes for storage or transmission

Higher pixel detail can support clearer display at the intended size.
Large image files can take longer to load or transmit.
Reducing data can make a web page more efficient.
Too much reduction can remove detail or produce visible pixelation or compression artefacts.
Choose sufficient quality for the intended display or print use.
Check the resulting image rather than judging only the file size.
Smaller storage requirements and smaller displayed dimensions are different properties.
For the requested size reduction, explain resolution, quality, colour depth or compression; simply cropping or changing height and width missed the intended answer.
Reduce file sizes for storage or transmission

Resizing changes the intended dimensions at which an image is displayed or output.
Resampling changes the pixel dimensions by removing or adding samples.
Reducing pixel dimensions can reduce stored image data.
Changing only display dimensions may leave the original pixel data and file size unchanged.
Increasing pixel dimensions does not recreate detail absent from the source.
Quality also depends on compression and colour depth.
Choose changes according to the required output and assess the result.
Distinguish changes to the stored image data from changing its displayed dimensions. Apply the reduction to the exact task asked.
Reduce file sizes for storage or transmission

Compression re-encodes data so it requires fewer bits or bytes.
Lossless compression allows exact recovery of the original data.
A method can find repeated patterns and replace them with shorter identifiers or references.
The decoder uses the encoded information to reconstruct the original content.
Lossy compression discards some information to achieve a size reduction.
ZIP and RAR are archive formats commonly using lossless compression; PNG uses lossless image compression.
A compressed image format is not the same category as an archive holding arbitrary files.
The amount saved depends on the data, and already compressed files may shrink little.
For the compression process, explain repeated patterns being replaced with shorter identifiers. Repeating reduces file size is only a definition.

Choose images that relate to the subject and support the intended message.
Match the style and complexity to the audience.
Use images to explain or illustrate information rather than merely fill space.

A parent newsletter may suit relevant photographs and a formal layout.
Balance images with readable text and white space.
Explain how the choice helps the particular audience.
Relate each image or design choice to the specific audience and explain why it helps; avoid vague audience claims.

Image composition concerns which elements are included and how they are arranged.
Cropping can remove unwanted areas and focus attention on the main subject.
Removing part of an image can also remove context or evidence of scale.
Choose the crop according to the message the image should communicate.
A crop can change a portrait frame into a landscape frame without stretching the objects.
Keep details needed to understand the image.
Different crops of the same photograph can create different impressions.

Aspect ratio is the relationship between image width and height.
It can be written as a ratio such as 4:3 or 16:9.
Maintaining the ratio preserves the image's proportions.
Both dimensions must change by the same scale factor for proportional resizing.
Changing width and height independently can stretch or squash objects.
Cropping can change the frame's aspect ratio while preserving the shape of the retained objects.

Images can be protected by copyright.
Check the applicable licence or obtain permission from the rights holder before the intended reuse.
Permission needs to cover the proposed use, such as publication on a website.
Acknowledge the source and rights information where required.
Giving credit does not automatically replace the need for permission.
Use material whose licence or other applicable permission allows the intended use.
Copyright concerns rights over the work rather than only ownership of a downloaded copy.
Check permission and any required attribution for the intended reuse. Copyright does not simply prohibit every act of copying.

Proportional resizing changes width and height by the same factor.
It preserves the original aspect ratio and object shapes.
Non-proportional resizing changes the dimensions by different factors.
It can make a subject look unnaturally wide, narrow, tall or short.
Use cropping when a different frame shape is needed without stretching the contents.
Check that the image still communicates the intended message after resizing.
Image dimensions, file size and pixelation

A raster image consists of pixels arranged across its width and height.
Reducing its stored pixel dimensions can reduce the amount of image data.
Changing only the displayed size may leave the stored pixel dimensions and file size unchanged.
A lower-detail image may load faster but be unsuitable for large output.
Enlarging a small raster image can expose pixels or make it appear blurred.
File size also depends on colour depth, content, format and compression.
Choose enough stored detail for the intended display or print use.
Distinguish stored file size from displayed image dimensions; identify compression or resolution settings when the question asks for file-size reduction.

A raster graphics editor works with pixel-based images.
It supports changes such as cropping, resizing, colour adjustment and compositing.
Separate layers can help edit parts of a composition independently.
GIMP is an example of a free, open-source raster graphics editor.
A native project file can retain editing information.
Export produces an image in a supported distribution format.
The software category is distinct from a vector drawing package or a file format.

Ordinary JPEG uses lossy compression.
A lower export-quality setting generally creates a smaller file with more information discarded.
High quality generally retains more detail but uses more storage and transfer data.
Strong compression can introduce visible artefacts or reduce fine detail.
Changing JPEG quality does not necessarily change pixel dimensions.
Repeated lossy re-encoding can introduce further deterioration.
Check the exported appearance and file size for the intended purpose.
Explain compression or quality settings in relation to stored file size rather than only changing the displayed height and width.

Resampling changes the number of pixels representing an image.
Downsampling reduces pixel dimensions and usually reduces the amount of image data.
Upsampling adds pixels using an interpolation method.
Extra pixels do not recreate detail that was never captured.
Removing pixels can reduce fine detail.
JPEG quality controls compression and is different from changing pixel dimensions.
A display-size change without resampling can leave the underlying pixels unchanged.
Assess image clarity as well as file size after changing the sampling.
Address the stored image data and the exact reduction requested; changing only display dimensions does not explain reduced file size.

An in-line image is treated like a character within a line of text.
It occupies a position in the text flow.
It moves with surrounding text when text is inserted or deleted before it.
Its size can affect the line or paragraph layout.
It is useful when the picture should remain part of a particular text sequence.
It differs from a floating image with text wrapping around its sides.

Text wrapping controls how text flows around a placed image.
Square wrapping follows a rectangular boundary around the picture.
Tight wrapping follows a closer wrapping outline around the subject or shape.
Through wrapping can allow text through suitable open areas within the wrapping boundary.
The actual flow depends on the image, wrap outline and application settings.
Allow suitable space between text and image to maintain readability.
Wrapping affects surrounding text, while cropping changes the visible image area.

Top and Bottom wrapping keeps text above and below the image.
Text does not flow alongside the image's left or right side.
The picture occupies a separate horizontal area in the layout.
This can keep a wide image clear of adjacent body text.
The surrounding paragraphs continue before and after that area.
It differs from Square or Tight wrapping around the sides.
Behind Text versus In Front of Text

Behind Text places an image beneath the text in the stacking order.
It can be used for a background or watermark effect.
The image must not make the text difficult to read.
In Front of Text places the image above the text.
An opaque foreground image can obscure words beneath it.
Position, transparency, brightness and contrast affect the resulting readability.
Stacking an image over text is different from wrapping the text around it.

Rotation turns an image around a point through a specified angle.
It changes the orientation of the image.
A 90-degree turn can change a portrait orientation to landscape or vice versa.
A 180-degree turn reverses an upside-down orientation.
Rotation preserves the relative arrangement of objects within the picture.
It is different from reflection, which creates a mirror orientation.
Check whether turning the picture is appropriate for its subject and intended use.

Cropping selects the visible region and excludes material outside it.
It can remove unwanted borders or focus on a subject.
It can change the frame's aspect ratio.
Resizing changes the dimensions at which the image is represented or displayed.
Proportional resizing preserves the original width-to-height ratio.
Cropping does not stretch the retained objects.

Reflection flips the image to create a mirror orientation.
A horizontal flip exchanges left and right.
A vertical flip exchanges top and bottom.
Rotation turns the image through an angle instead of mirroring it.
Reflection can reverse text or change the apparent direction of a subject.
Choose the transformation that produces the intended orientation.
Two transformations can produce different results even when they fit the same frame.
Brightness and contrast for background images

Brightness adjusts the overall lightness or darkness of an image.
Contrast adjusts differences between light and dark tones.
Both can be changed to make important features more visible.
A background image should support readable foreground text.
Reducing distracting contrast or adjusting brightness can help the foreground stand out.
The appropriate adjustment depends on the image and text colours.
Excessive adjustment can remove detail or make the image unclear.
There is no single slider value suitable for every background.

Layers hold separate parts of an image composition.

A higher opaque layer can cover content on a lower layer.
The lowest visible layer commonly acts as a background.
Transparent areas reveal content from lower visible layers.
Separate layers allow parts of the composition to be edited independently.
Changing layer order can change the final appearance without changing each source image.

Transparency lets underlying content show through an image area.

Partially transparent areas blend with underlying content.

A transparent area differs from a white area when placed over a coloured background.

Grouping or linking related layers lets them be manipulated together.
It can keep components aligned when they are moved or transformed.
The related items can retain their individual editing information.
Groups help organise a complex composition.
The exact operations applied together depend on the editor and grouping method.
Grouping is different from merging or flattening the items into one image.
A native project format is needed to preserve the relevant group or link structure.

GIMP's XCF format preserves project structures such as layers and layer groups.
A conventional JPEG or PNG export produces a composited raster image without the project's separately editable layers.
The visible pixels can still be edited, but the original layer structure is not recovered from that export alone.
PNG can retain transparency in the resulting image.
Ordinary JPEG requires opaque output rather than an alpha channel.
Keep the native project as well as an exported copy when further editing is needed.
Flattening the composition does not inherently mean every exported format must lose transparency.

The appropriate document form depends on its purpose and intended audience.

Identify the purpose of the document before creating it.
Identify the target audience and its information needs.
Decide how the content and presentation can suit that audience.
Choose an appropriate delivery medium, such as print or electronic distribution.
Choose an application package suitable for the document and its features.
Plan a balance of text, images and white space.
Consider readable fonts, contrasting colours and accessibility requirements.
Explain how each planned feature supports the particular audience and purpose.
Relate the design features to the specified audience and explain their purpose; vague features without reasons are insufficient.

Clear readable fonts and suitable font sizes help users read the content.
Contrasting colours and balanced white space improve readability.
Younger audiences may benefit from simple wording, relevant pictures and bright colours.

Check entered text and numbers for typing errors.
