Check spelling, grammar and punctuation.
Check letter case, including accidental capitals.
Check character spacing and paragraph spacing for consistency.
Check that all intended information is present and readable.
Correct errors before distributing the document.
Use proofreading for checking a document for errors; do not confuse the term with verification.
Cut versus copy and the clipboard

Copy places a duplicate of selected content on the clipboard while retaining the original.
Paste inserts clipboard content at the chosen destination.
Cut and paste moves content; copy and paste duplicates it.
Clipboard content can include text, numbers and objects.
The pasted appearance may depend on the destination and chosen paste format.

Objects such as shapes and arrows should communicate the intended information clearly.
An arrow can show a direction, sequence or relationship.
Position an arrow so its intended source and destination are clear.
Keep labels and essential information visible.
Avoid objects overlapping or obscuring text unintentionally.
Use a consistent, readable arrangement suited to the document's purpose.

Grouping combines selected objects so they can be handled as one unit.

Grouping helps keep related shapes, arrows and labels together.

Text wrapping controls how body text flows around a document object.

Check that the object and nearby text remain readable.

Treat a column-heading row as a heading rather than a data record.

Cell alignment positions content inside an individual cell.
A centred table can contain left-aligned text.
Changing cell alignment does not necessarily move the whole table.
Distinguish the position of the table from the position of its contents.
Wrapping around a table versus within a cell

Wrapping around a table controls the flow of surrounding body text.
Within-cell wrapping breaks a cell's text over multiple lines.
These are separate layout behaviours.
A narrower column generally causes cell text to wrap onto more lines.
The row height must allow the wrapped content to remain visible.
Changing within-cell wrapping does not by itself determine whether body text flows beside the table.

Horizontal alignment positions cell contents from side to side.
Common horizontal alignments are left, centre and right.
Vertical alignment positions contents within the cell's height.
Common vertical alignments are top, middle and bottom.
Horizontal and vertical alignment can be combined independently.
For example, a heading can be centred horizontally and vertically.
A table can contain different text alignments in different cells.

Borders are formatting applied to the edges of a table or its cells.
Borders can appear in printed or exported output.
Non-printing table gridlines are editing guides that help show cell boundaries.
Removing borders does not necessarily remove the on-screen guides.
Visible guides do not prove that borders will print.
Check the intended output to distinguish printable borders from editing aids.

Column width affects how much text fits on each line within a cell.
Automatic wrapping moves text onto another line when the available width is filled.
A wider column may reduce the number of wrapped lines.
A narrower column may require a taller row to display all the text.
A soft return introduces a line break within the same paragraph.
A paragraph break starts a new paragraph.
A manual line break can control where cell text continues without creating a separate paragraph.

A header is an area at the top of a document page, normally within the top margin area.
A footer is an area at the bottom of a document page, normally within the bottom margin area.
Both can contain text and graphics.
They hold information separately from the main body text.
They help place repeated information consistently across pages.
They are document layout features rather than database fields or data-entry controls.
Describe layout features and their effect rather than listing document contents, database fields or data-entry controls.

A header or footer can contain an author's name.
It can contain a document, chapter or section title.
It can contain a company logo or other identifying graphic.
Page numbers help identify the current page.
A filename or file path can help identify the document.
Date and time information may also be included.
Choose content appropriate to the document's purpose and audience.
Consistency and efficiency of repeated elements

Headers and footers repeat information consistently across pages.
Repeated information normally needs to be entered only once for the relevant section.
This saves time compared with adding it manually on every page.
Page numbers and identifying information help readers navigate the document.
Consistent elements can support an organisation's identity or house style.
Different first-page or facing-page arrangements can be used where appropriate.
A change to a shared header or footer can update its repeated occurrences.
Explain how consistent repeated elements support the organisation’s identity; professional-looking alone is insufficient.

A left tab stop fixes the left edge of tabbed text or numbers at a chosen position.
Text extends to the right from that position.
Different entries can share the same starting point.
A left tab stop aligns an item within a line rather than changing the alignment of the entire paragraph.
It can be used to position a left-hand item in a header or footer.

A centre tab stop fixes the centre point of tabbed text or numbers at a chosen position.
Text extends on both sides of that point as its length changes.
Entries of different lengths can retain the same centre position.
The tab stop must be placed at the intended centre, such as halfway between the text margins.
It can position a central title independently of left-hand and right-hand items.

A right tab stop fixes the right edge of tabbed text or numbers at a chosen position.
Text extends to the left as more characters are entered.
Entries of different lengths can share the same right boundary.
It can align a header or footer item with the right text margin.
It differs from a left tab stop, which fixes the starting edge.

A decimal tab stop aligns numbers at their decimal points.
Digits before the decimal point extend to the left of the alignment position.
Digits after the decimal point extend to the right.
Numbers with different lengths can be compared more easily.
Decimal alignment differs from simply fixing the right edge of every number.
It is useful for presenting columns of decimal values consistently.

Date and time information can be placed in a header or footer.
An automated field supplies a value rather than merely displaying a manually typed label.
Typed words such as Saved on are labels, not automated date fields.
The displayed value depends on the selected field and its update behaviour.
A current-date field is different from a field recording a creation or last-saved date.
Choose an appropriate date and time format for the document.
A typed date remains fixed unless someone edits it.

An automated page-number field displays the relevant page number.
The total-page field represents the document's page count.
Page X of Y combines the current page and total number of pages.
Fields avoid typing each page number separately.
Page-number fields can reflect changes in pagination when the fields are updated.
A typed number is ordinary fixed text rather than an automated page-number field.
Page numbering helps readers identify and navigate pages.

A filename identifies the saved document.
A file path identifies its location in the folder structure.
A full file-path field may include both the folder path and the filename.
Automated document fields use document information rather than a manually typed copy.
Filename and path information can help identify which document was produced.
A long path can occupy considerable header or footer space.
The displayed field value must correspond to the saved document and its current location after updating.

A corporate house style is a set of rules for the writing and presentation of an organisation's documents and materials.
It gives a consistent look and feel across the organisation.
It can specify fonts, colours, logos and layout.
It supports and strengthens the organisation's brand.
Consistent presentation helps customers recognise the organisation.
The term concerns organisational presentation rather than the design of buildings.
Explain house style as organisational presentation rules and develop its purpose; it does not concern buildings.

A house style can specify the font face, font size and text enhancements.
It can define corporate colours and background colours.
It can specify the logo's size and position.
It can define paragraph styles, alignment and spacing.
It can specify page layout, margins and header or footer arrangements.
It can define the placement of text and contact details.
It can specify bullet symbols, numbering and indentation.
Use precise properties rather than merely naming font, colour or logo.
Specify properties such as font type and size, corporate colours, and logo size or position; font, colour or logo alone is too vague.

House style is used across an organisation's documents and communications.
Examples include letterheads, business cards and customer correspondence.
It can also appear on products, advertising and company vehicles.
Websites and presentations can use the same recognisable visual conventions.
Consistent colours, fonts and logo placement connect different materials to the same organisation.
A standard presentation helps customers identify the brand across different media.
Connect the consistent presentation of company materials to recognition of the brand rather than giving an unexplained list of benefits.

House style provides a standard method of presentation.
Materials from the same organisation have a consistent look and feel.
The same fonts, colours and layout conventions are used for equivalent elements.
Repeated header and footer information can remain consistent.
Consistency helps readers recognise related documents and web pages.
A consistent appearance supports the organisation's identity and brand.
Explain how consistent documents or pages are recognisably part of the same organisation; professional-looking alone is insufficient.

Predefined conventions save time planning and setting up new documents.
Reusable styles avoid repeatedly choosing individual formatting settings.
Templates and repeated elements reduce the need to recreate the same layout.
Consistent styles make parts of a document easier to edit.
Shared formatting can reduce the time and cost of producing new materials.
The saving comes from reusing agreed settings rather than designing every item from the beginning.
Explain the practical reason for the house style, such as easier editing or reuse, rather than merely listing a benefit.

Consistent visual features help an audience identify an organisation.
Recognisable colours, fonts and logos connect materials to the brand.
Customers can recognise related correspondence more quickly.
A consistent layout supports and strengthens the organisation's identity.
The same brand can remain recognisable across print and electronic materials.
Explain the link between the visual consistency and recognition of the organisation.
Explain how consistent layout helps customers quickly recognise the organisation’s brand.

Reusable house-style elements reduce repeated manual entry.
A stored address or telephone number is less likely to be retyped incorrectly on each document.
A template can help ensure that required elements such as the logo are included.
Agreed formatting reduces accidental inconsistencies between documents.
The reusable original must be accurate and kept up to date.
A house style reduces risk but does not replace proofreading or checking the content.

Different applications use different mechanisms to maintain consistent presentation.
Web pages can use Cascading Style Sheets, or CSS, to define their appearance.
CSS belongs to the presentation or style layer of a website.
An external stylesheet can be linked to multiple pages and reused.
Inline CSS is written on the relevant HTML element rather than in a separate stylesheet file.
Presentations use master slides and themes for repeated design features.
Word-processed documents use named styles and templates.
These mechanisms help equivalent elements use the same formatting.
Expand CSS accurately and explain its role in web-page presentation; do not confuse CSS with CSV.

Serif fonts have small strokes at the ends of letter strokes.
Sans-serif fonts do not have these serifs.
Serif and sans-serif are generic categories rather than individual font-face names.
Times New Roman is an example of a serif font.
Arial is an example of a sans-serif font.
A requirement for a font category must be met by a font from that category.
The category alone does not determine suitability for every audience or output medium.

Choose a clear, readable font appropriate to the audience and purpose.
Use a consistent font face for equivalent elements.
Limit unnecessary changes between font faces to support visual consistency.
Headings and body text can have different roles while following the same house style.
A formal document may require a more formal presentation than material for young children.
Check that the chosen font and size keep all information fully visible.
Consider contrasting colours, balanced white space and the surrounding layout.
Explain how the font choice helps the intended readers rather than naming a font alone.
Describe the font and layout choices and explain how they improve readability; bare feature names are insufficient.

Text enhancements make selected text stand out.
Examples include bold, italics, underlining, highlighting and font colour.
Bold can emphasise headings or key terms.
Italics can distinguish selected words or titles.
Highlighting changes the background behind selected text.
Font colour changes the text itself.
Use enhancements consistently and keep the text readable.
When a specific enhancement is required, extra enhancements can change the intended style.

Font size is measured in points.
There are 72 points in one inch.
A larger point size generally produces larger text within the same font face.
Point size is a nominal font measurement rather than the exact visible height of every letter.
It is different from the number of characters or the page width.
Fonts at the same point size can appear different in size.

Choose a font size large enough for the intended audience to read.
Larger text can help young readers or people with visual impairments.
Headings and body text need an appropriate size relationship.
The viewing distance and output medium affect a suitable size.
High colour contrast and clear font design also support readability.
Ensure that the selected size leaves all information visible within the layout.
Explain why the chosen size suits the audience.
A particular numerical size is guidance for a task, not a universal rule for every document.
Link font size and other design choices to the intended audience’s age or needs rather than giving generic factors.

A font face determines the design of letters and other characters.
Different faces have different shapes, proportions and spacing.
Two fonts with the same nominal point size can have different apparent heights.
They can also occupy different widths.
Changing the face can alter line wrapping and the overall layout.
Check the actual appearance rather than assuming equal point sizes look identical.

A new document begins with default layout and formatting settings.
A template provides a reusable starting structure for documents.
It can contain page orientation and margin settings.
It can include headers, footers and named styles.
It can hold repeated organisational information and design elements.
Using an appropriate template saves repeated setup work.
A template is a starting structure; a style is a reusable set of formatting properties for document elements.

A named style stores a set of formatting properties.
It can be applied repeatedly to equivalent document elements.
Separate styles can be used for headings, subheadings, body text and lists.
Applying the same style supports consistent presentation.
A style avoids manually selecting each property every time.
Styles can be modified to change the presentation of text using them.
The style's name identifies the formatting definition rather than the document's text content.

A paragraph style can specify a font face and font size.
It can include enhancements such as bold or italics.
It can define paragraph alignment.
It can define line spacing within a paragraph.
It can define spacing before and after the paragraph.
List styles can include indentation, bullets or numbering.
Different document roles can have different defined properties.
Consistent properties give equivalent paragraphs a consistent appearance.

Modifying a shared style can update text that uses that style.
This avoids reformatting each occurrence manually.
A heading style can be changed once rather than editing every heading separately.
Consistency is easier to maintain across a long document.
Changing one selected paragraph's direct formatting is not necessarily the same as changing its shared style.
Check which properties were stored and which text uses the style.
In the textbook example, highlighting was not retained in the saved-style update and needed separate treatment.

Format Painter copies formatting from one area to another.
It can transfer font properties such as colour and bold formatting.
It can also transfer paragraph formatting or an applied style.
It helps make another area match the source's appearance.
It is used in word processing, spreadsheets and presentations.
Copying formatting is different from copying the source text or data.
The destination's content remains while its formatting changes.
Font and paragraph formatting copied together

Format Painter can copy paragraph formatting as well as font formatting.
The copied result may include alignment, spacing and list formatting.
Text can become part of a bulleted list when formatting is copied from a list paragraph.
The result depends on the source and what has been selected.
Check the destination for unintended paragraph or list changes.
Matching the font appearance alone does not prove that only font properties were transferred.
Bulleted versus numbered or lettered lists

A bulleted list uses a symbol to mark each item.
A numbered list uses numeric markers.
A lettered list uses alphabetic markers.
Bullets suit a collection of related points where sequence is not the main meaning.
Numbering or lettering can identify a sequence or provide item references.
Lists can make short points easier to absorb than a continuous paragraph.
Use a consistent marker and layout for equivalent items.
Explain how a list or other design choice helps the intended audience absorb the information; do not give unexplained feature names.

A multilevel list represents levels of information.
Main items form one level; related sub-items form a lower level.
Additional indentation distinguishes a sub-list from its parent level.
Different levels may use different bullet symbols or numbering formats.
Consistent indentation helps readers recognise the hierarchy.
A sub-item should belong logically to its parent item.
The list's hierarchy is distinct from simply adding more space before unrelated text.

A list style stores formatting for repeated list items.
It can specify the font face, font size and text alignment.
It can define the bullet symbol or numbering type.
It can define indentation for a particular list level.
It can set line spacing and paragraph spacing.
Separate styles can be defined for first-level and second-level items.
Applying the appropriate level style gives repeated lists a consistent hierarchy and appearance.

A spell checker scans the document and compares words with a stored dictionary.
A recognised word is accepted and the checker moves on.
An unrecognised word is highlighted as a possible spelling error.
The checker may offer suggested replacements.
The user must judge the intended word and context.
A dictionary match does not prove that the correct word has been used.
Explain comparison with a stored dictionary, not grammar checking or automatic replacement. The user judges the correction.

A correctly spelled word may be absent from the dictionary.
Examples include people's names, place names and specialist or scientific terms.
Latin terms may be unrecognised by an English dictionary.
Different regional dictionaries recognise different spellings, such as UK and US English.
A flagged word is therefore not necessarily incorrect.
A confirmed correct word can be ignored or added to an appropriate dictionary.
A correctly spelled name or specialist term may be absent from the dictionary; explain this rather than assuming every flagged word is wrong.

A suggested replacement is not automatically the word the writer intended.
Read the word in its sentence before accepting a suggestion.
Check whether the original is a correct name or specialist term.
Choose a suitable replacement when the original is misspelled.
Ignore a correct word or add it to the dictionary when appropriate.
A spelling checker does not reliably understand the intended meaning of every phrase.
Human checking remains necessary even after software checks.
For a confirmed correct word absent from the dictionary, ignore it or add it to an appropriate dictionary.

A proofing tool may flag repeated words as well as unrecognised spellings.
An accidental repetition such as the the may need removal.
Both repeated words can be individually present in the dictionary.
The warning concerns repetition rather than the spelling of either word.
Read the surrounding sentence before deleting a repeated word.
Some repetitions can be intentional or grammatically appropriate.

A grammar checker examines text using grammatical rules.
It flags possible problems in language structure.
It may identify punctuation or sentence-construction problems.
It can offer suggestions for revising the text.
Grammar checking differs from comparing individual spellings with a dictionary.
The user must assess whether a suggestion preserves the intended meaning.

Grammar suggestions are possible corrections rather than guarantees.
A checker may identify a problem but suggest an unsuitable replacement.
It may misunderstand the context or intended meaning.
A grammatically acceptable sentence can still contain factual errors.
Read the whole sentence before accepting a change.
Human proofreading is still needed after automated checking.

Validation is an automatic computer check on entered data.
It checks that the data is sensible or reasonable.
It checks whether data meets specified criteria.
Data that fails the rule can be rejected or flagged.
Validation does not prove that a value is factually correct.
An incorrect value may pass if it satisfies the rule.
Testing validation checks helps ensure that unreasonable data is trapped.
Validation checks reasonableness and set criteria; it does not guarantee factual accuracy.

Choose a recognised validation check that suits the field and its permitted values.
Explain how the check applies to the specific data.
Different fields can require different checks.
More than one check may be needed to reject different error types.
A presence check is suitable only when the field must contain data.
A legitimately unknown or inapplicable value may need to remain blank.
Use precise check names such as range, length, type or format.
A check's limitations must be considered as well as the errors it detects.
Name a recognised check and explain why it suits the particular field; field contents or vague check labels are insufficient.

A range check tests whether a value lies between stated lower and upper boundaries.
A limit check tests a single upper or lower boundary.
The permitted endpoints may be included or excluded according to the rule.
A numeric month should be an integer from 1 to 12 inclusive.
A lower limit alone would not reject a month of 13.
An upper limit alone would not reject a month of 0.
The rule must reflect the actual permitted values for the field.
Give the check and its field-specific restriction, such as the permitted range, rather than data alone or an unexplained check name.

A length check tests the number of characters entered.
It can require an exact count or a permitted length interval.
Exactly six characters differs from up to six characters.
A two-character month such as 13 can pass a length check but still be invalid.
Transposed digits can retain the correct length.
A length check does not prove that the characters, value or meaning are correct.
Additional checks may be needed for the same field.
Use the exact required character count and distinguish a length check from range or type checks.

A type check tests whether data has the required data type.
A character check restricts permitted characters.
A numeric-only rule can reject letters where numbers are required.
A numeric value can still be outside the permitted range.
For example, 13 is numeric but is not a valid month number.
An integer restriction is needed when fractions are not permitted.
Explain the actual restriction rather than giving an unexplained example.
Explain that the check restricts the data type or characters; examples alone do not explain what is tested.

A presence check tests whether data has been entered.
It rejects an empty or null value when the field is required.
It does not establish that the entered value is reasonable or correct.
An inappropriate non-empty value can pass.
It is unsuitable when a blank value is legitimately allowed.
For example, a book without a barcode may need an empty barcode field.
Combine it with other checks where non-empty content also has restrictions.
A presence check is inappropriate when the scenario permits the field to be empty; explain that allowance in context.

A format check tests whether data matches a specified pattern.
A reference could require two letters followed by three digits.
A consistency check compares related data for agreement.
A single unrelated field does not provide a comparison for a consistency check.
A check digit is calculated from the other digits in an identifier.
Recalculating and comparing the check digit can detect some transcription errors.
A check digit does not detect every possible error or prove factual accuracy.
Choose the check according to the field rather than applying every check indiscriminately.
Name the appropriate check and describe its precise rule for the field; do not substitute sample data for the check.

Validation feedback tells the user that an entry fails the rule.
A useful message explains what data is acceptable.
For a month field, it can state that a whole number from 1 to 12 is required.
The message should be clear and specific to the field.
It should help the user correct the entry.
Abnormal testing can check whether the intended error message appears.
When testing abnormal data, explain that the rule should trap the error and produce the intended error message.

List validation restricts an entry to a specified set of permitted values.
It is suitable for a finite set of accepted categories.
The values need not form a numeric interval.
An entry outside the permitted list can be rejected or flagged.
A drop-down list can help users choose an allowed value.
Membership in the list does not prove that the correct category was chosen.
Test the permitted entries and values that should not be accepted.
Normal, abnormal and extreme test data

Normal test data is reasonable data within the acceptable limits.
Abnormal test data is data the system should not accept.
Extreme test data lies at the boundaries of acceptability.
For integer months from 1 to 12, 6 is normal and 1 and 12 are extreme.
Values such as 0, 13 or a letter are abnormal for that month rule.
Extreme does not mean a value far beyond the allowed range.
Test that acceptable data passes and unacceptable data is rejected.
An unordered list has no numerical highest or lowest boundary.
When asked for test values, give actual values suited to the stated rule.
Extreme data is at an acceptable boundary, not far outside the range. When values are requested, give actual values.

Proofing checks the accuracy and presentation of completed work.
It includes spelling, punctuation and grammar.
It includes checking page layout and formatting.
It can identify errors not detected by automated tools.
It extends beyond validation rules on individual fields.
The completed output should be checked as a whole.
Proofreading is not the same as verification against an original source.
Use proofreading for checking the document itself; do not confuse it with verification.

Check that the specified styles and margins have been applied.
Check image positions, proportions and text wrapping.
Ensure objects fit within page, column or slide boundaries.
Check for unintended overlaps or hidden content.
Remove unintended blank pages, columns or slides.
Check for widows and orphans.
Appropriate page or column breaks can help correct unwanted splitting.
Review the final layout after changes because content may move.
Explain the effect of a hard break on the column layout, including reducing widows or orphans.

Keep related list items together where the layout requires it.
Avoid inappropriate splitting of tables, graphs and embedded extracts.
Check both page and column boundaries.
A split object can make information harder to follow.
Appropriate breaks can move related content together.
Check that moving an object has not created unintended empty areas.
The aim is a readable final layout rather than an arbitrary break at every object.

A widow is the last line of a paragraph appearing alone at the top of a new page or column.
It is separated from the preceding lines of its paragraph.
It is a layout issue rather than a spelling error.
Appropriate page or column layout can keep the paragraph's lines together.
A hard break can help remove a widow when placed appropriately.
Check the final output even when automatic widow control is available.
Connect an appropriate hard break with removing unwanted isolated lines in the column layout.

An orphan is the first line of a paragraph left alone at the bottom of a page or column.
A heading stranded at the bottom without its following text is also an unwanted layout separation.
The following material appears on the next page or column.
Appropriate layout or breaks can keep related content together.
A hard break can help avoid an orphan when placed appropriately.
Check the final arrangement rather than relying only on automatic control.
Explain how the break changes the layout and helps avoid an isolated line or heading.

Incorrect data can produce incorrect information and decisions.
A wrong contact number can prevent communication.
An incorrect financial amount can cause an incorrect charge or financial loss.
Wrong numeric inputs can lead to incorrect calculations.
Errors in operational data can have serious consequences.
Personal information needs careful checking because people may be affected.
Validation and verification reduce errors but do not guarantee that all data is correct.
Explain why accurate data matters in the scenario and why validation and verification together still cannot detect every error.

Spelling errors are a common data-entry mistake.
Capital letters can be inserted incorrectly or omitted where required.
Transposed digits reverse the intended order, such as 21 instead of 12.
Spaces can be missing or repeated.
Extra line or paragraph breaks can affect presentation.
Data can also contain factual errors even when its spelling and format are correct.
Check the entered content as well as its presentation.

Verification checks that data has been accurately copied or transferred from its source.
It compares entered data with the source or another independent entry.
It helps reduce transcription errors.
Recognised methods include visual verification and double data entry.
It does not prove that the source data is factually correct.
A source error can be copied accurately and pass verification.
Data verification is different from verifying a person's identity.
Verification checks accurate copying from the source, not personal identity or every kind of error.

Visual verification is a person's comparison of entered data with the original source.
The person checks for differences caused during copying.
It can involve comparing each character or value with the source document.
A second person can help notice errors the original operator missed.
Identified differences are checked and corrected.
It checks accurate transfer rather than whether every source fact is correct.
It differs from proofreading a document without comparison to the source.
Describe comparison with the original source to check accurate copying; correct data or proofreading alone is insufficient.

Visual verification can accept an error already present in the source.
If the entered value matches the incorrect original, there is no transcription difference to flag.
A matching telephone number may still be the wrong number.
The check establishes agreement with the source rather than factual correctness.
Other checking may be required to establish the true value.
Verification reduces copying errors but does not eliminate all data errors.
Matching the original source does not prove it is correct; the source itself may contain an error.

Double data entry involves entering the same source data twice.
The entries are made separately, often by two different people.
The computer compares the two sets of entered data.
Differences are flagged for checking against the source and correction.
Re-entering a newly chosen password is an example of comparing two entries.
It differs from visual verification, where a person performs the comparison.
Entering data twice without comparing the entries does not complete the check.
Go beyond entered twice: describe separate entries and computer comparison.

Double data entry checks agreement between the two entries.
The same mistake in both entries produces no difference.
An error in the original source may be entered identically twice.
Matching entries therefore do not prove factual correctness.
A repeated mistyped password can match even when it is not what the user intended.
Independent entries reduce some copying errors but cannot guarantee error-free data.

Validation checks whether entered data is reasonable and meets set criteria.
Verification checks whether data has been copied accurately from the source.
A sensible value can still be copied incorrectly.
An accurately copied value can still be unreasonable.
Validation normally applies automatic rules.
Visual verification uses a person to compare with the source; double entry uses computer comparison of entries.
Neither process alone guarantees that all data is correct.
Define both processes: reasonableness for validation and accurate source transfer for verification.

Validation and verification detect different types of error.
Using both helps reduce the number of data-entry errors.
Verification can detect a sensible value copied incorrectly.
Validation can reject an unreasonable value even when it was copied accurately.
A plausible error already in the source may pass both processes.
For example, a wrong telephone number can have the required length and be copied exactly.
Together the checks improve reliability but do not eliminate every error.
Explain the different errors caught by each process and acknowledge that using both still does not eliminate all errors.

Proofreading is careful reading and rereading to detect errors.
It includes spelling, grammar, punctuation and layout.
It can identify errors that were already present in the original document.
Verification checks the transcription against its source.
Accurately copied source errors may pass verification.
Proofreading and visual verification therefore have different purposes.
Use proofreading when the task is checking the document itself for errors.
The term for checking a document for errors is proofreading; it is distinct from verification.

Choose a chart according to the purpose and relationship in the data.
A pie chart shows parts of one whole.
A bar chart compares values between categories.
A line graph shows trends across an ordered variable such as time.
Consider what the reader needs to compare or identify.
A software recommendation does not replace judging suitability for the task.

A pie chart compares parts or fractions of a whole.
Each sector represents a category's share of the total.
The sector proportions can be expressed as percentages.
The complete circle represents the whole, or 100%.
It can show the proportions of a group choosing different options.
The categories must represent parts of the same total rather than unrelated quantities.

A bar chart compares values for different categories.
The length or height of each bar represents its value.
Category labels identify what each bar represents.
A common value scale allows comparisons between bars.
It can compare the numbers of items sold by different people in the same period.
It is suitable when differences between categories are the main focus.

Bars can be plotted vertically or horizontally.
In a vertical bar chart, bar height represents the value.
In a horizontal bar chart, bar length represents the value.
Excel calls the vertical form a column chart.
Excel calls the horizontal form a bar chart.
Both forms compare values between categories.
The category and value axes change orientation with the bars.

A line graph shows a trend between two variables.
It is often used to show changes over time.
Plotted observations are connected in their meaningful order.
For example, it can show water temperature as heating time increases.
A value between observations may be estimated from the connecting line.
Such an interpolated value is an estimate rather than a directly measured observation.
The choice should reflect an ordered relationship rather than unrelated categories.

Contiguous source data occupies adjacent cells, rows or columns.
Non-contiguous source data is in separated ranges.
A chart may use category labels from one range and values from another.
The selected ranges must contain the intended corresponding categories and values.
Unrelated rows, columns or totals should not be included accidentally.
The location of the source ranges does not by itself determine the appropriate chart type.

Headings in the source data can supply chart labels and series names.
Category entries can supply labels for individual categories.
Including the correct headings helps identify the plotted data.
Automatically generated labels may still be incomplete or unsuitable.
Check that each series and category is correctly identified.
Complete the meaningful chart title and any required axis titles and units.

Automatic chart selection uses software rules to recommend a chart.
The recommendation may not match the purpose of the task.
Inspect whether the data represents parts of a whole, category comparisons or trends.
Choose the type that communicates the intended relationship.
Check that the correct categories and data series have been used.
A chart created successfully by software is not necessarily the most appropriate chart.

A simple chart is often easier to interpret.
Include features needed to explain the data.
Avoid unnecessary decoration that distracts from the values.
Unnecessary 3-D effects can make comparisons harder.
Use clear titles, labels and an appropriate scale.
Keep the design focused on the task and intended audience.

A comparative chart displays more than one data series.
A comparative line graph can show two series over the same period.
A common time axis allows trends to be compared at corresponding dates.
For example, cumulative rainfall for two towns can be plotted over the same months.
Each series must be identifiable by its label, key or appearance.
Use compatible scales and units when the series share a value axis.
Distinguish the source values of each series rather than combining them unintentionally.

A chart title explains what the chart shows.
It should identify the subject and any relevant group, location or period.
Axis titles identify the variables represented by the axes.
Include relevant measurement units such as millimetres or degrees Celsius.
Axis titles differ from the individual category labels or numeric scale values.
Clear labelling lets the reader interpret the chart without guessing.
Where exact wording is specified, preserve the required meaning and wording.

In a vertical bar chart, the horizontal axis is normally the category axis.
It identifies the categories represented by the bars.
The vertical axis is the value axis.
It displays the numeric scale used to read bar heights.
Category labels identify items, while scale labels show numerical values.
Axis titles explain what the categories and values represent.
A horizontal bar chart reverses these orientations.

A legend or key identifies the plotted data series.
It links a series name to a colour, pattern or line style.
It is useful when several series would otherwise be difficult to distinguish.
A single clearly identified series may not need a legend.
Direct labels can sometimes identify the data without a separate key.
Remove a redundant legend only when the chart remains unambiguous.
A legend is different from the chart title or a value label on one data point.

Data labels identify individual plotted data points.
They can show values, category names or percentages as appropriate.
Pie-sector labels can identify each category directly.
Percentage labels show each sector's share of the whole.
Direct labels can make a separate legend unnecessary.
Check that the labels match the correct sector or point.
Position labels so they are readable and do not overlap unnecessarily.

Choose colours that allow the chart and its labels to be read clearly.
Text needs sufficient contrast against the background or sector beneath it.
Different colours can distinguish categories or series.
A changed colour can emphasise a particular data item.
Keep the meaning of colours consistent where a key is used.
Check label placement and readability after changing colours.
The final output medium affects whether colour differences remain visible.

Colours that look different on screen may look similar when printed in black and white.
A colour-only key may therefore become difficult to use.
Distinct patterns or textures can help distinguish bars or sectors.
Different grey tones or gradient fills may help when they remain visibly distinct.
Keep labels readable against the chosen fills.
Check the intended monochrome output rather than relying on the colour screen view.
The reader must still be able to identify each category or series.
Purpose of a secondary value axis

A secondary value axis gives a series its own numeric scale.
It can help display series with different units or very different value ranges.
For example, rainfall and temperature require clearly identified scales.
A small-valued series may be hard to read on a scale chosen for a much larger series.
Separate axes allow each series to be read on a suitable scale.
Label each axis with its variable and units.
Read a series against its assigned axis rather than the other scale.

A combination chart displays multiple series using selected chart types.
It can combine bars and lines, or use suitable types for the separate series.
Choose each series' type according to its data and the intended comparison.
A common category axis can link the series to the same dates or categories.
A secondary value axis may be useful where units or ranges differ.
A combination chart does not automatically require a secondary axis.
Identify all series and scales clearly.

Axis bounds specify the minimum and maximum values displayed.
Choose bounds that accommodate the data being shown.
Major intervals determine the spacing of the main scale divisions.
Convenient regular increments make values easier to read.
A temperature scale may need to include negative values.
When two value axes are used, each needs an appropriate scale.
Check the actual data range rather than accepting automatic bounds without review.
The scale should support an accurate interpretation of the data.

Each value axis must identify the variable it represents.
Include the appropriate measurement units.
For example, one axis can represent cumulative rainfall in millimetres and the other temperature in degrees Celsius.
The reader must know which series uses each axis.
The category axis should identify the shared categories or dates.
A meaningful chart title explains the overall comparison.
Separate axes without clear labels can lead to values being read from the wrong scale.
Numeric and currency formats for axis labels

Numeric formatting controls how axis values are displayed.
A specified number of decimal places gives consistent displayed precision.
Currency formatting adds an appropriate currency symbol.
The format helps identify the nature of the values.
For example, sales income can be shown as currency with two decimal places.
Formatting the labels does not itself change the underlying source values.
The displayed format should match the task and the units of the data.

A plain-text file contains unformatted text data.
Its text is displayed using the word processor's default formatting and layout settings.
RTF means Rich Text Format.
RTF retains text formatting that plain text does not store.
Word-processing document formats can retain saved formatting and layout information.
Check an opened document's actual settings rather than assuming they already meet the requirements.
Formatting support can differ between file formats and applications.
Expand RTF as Rich Text Format and explain retained formatting; use plain text precisely when describing TXT.

Page size determines the dimensions of the paper or document page.
Portrait orientation is taller than it is wide.
Landscape orientation is wider than it is tall.
The orientation changes the space available across and down the page.
A smaller page size provides less space for the same content.
Page size and orientation are distinct layout settings.
Check how text and objects fit after either setting changes.

Margins define space around the main body content.
A page normally has top, bottom, left and right margins.
Larger margins reduce the usable body area.
Changing margins can alter line wrapping and pagination.
Margins help keep content clear of the page edges.
Check that the resulting layout still fits the intended content.

A gutter is an extra margin reserved for binding.
It adds space so fastening or glue does not obscure the text.
It is used for bound books or booklets.
Its position depends on the binding edge.
It may be on the inside edge for side binding or at the top for top binding.
The gutter is additional binding space rather than merely an ordinary margin.
Keep important content clear of the binding area.
Describe an extra margin, state its binding-edge location and explain that it prevents the binding from obscuring text.
Header and footer layout after page changes

Changing page size or margins changes the space available for the layout.
Existing header and footer tab positions may no longer align correctly.
Check left, centre and right alignment against the new usable width.
Long header or footer content may wrap or become crowded.
A gutter can require content to move away from the binding area.
Check the vertical position as well as the horizontal alignment.
The completed header and footer must remain readable and unobscured.

Breaks control where text continues and can separate areas of a document.
A suitable break can help remove a widow or orphan.
It can help keep a related list or object together.
Page, column and section breaks serve different purposes.
Automatic layout controls do not remove the need to check the output.
An inappropriate break can create unwanted empty space.
Review the final arrangement after inserting or removing breaks.
Explain how the hard break changes the column layout and can remove widows or orphans.

A page break forces following text to the start of a new page.
It can be used when a new part must begin on a separate page.
It may leave white space at the end of the preceding page.
It can help prevent unwanted separation of related content.
It does not by itself create a separately formatted section.
A page break differs from a paragraph break or a column break.

A column break forces following text to the top of the next available column.
The next column may be on the same page.
If no further column is available there, the text continues on the next page.
It controls flow within a multicolumn layout.
It can help avoid a widow or orphan.
It differs from a page break, which specifically starts a new page.
Relate the hard break to where text continues in the column layout and its effect on widows or orphans.

A section break separates areas of a document into sections.
Different formatting or layout can be applied to each section.
For example, one section can be portrait and another landscape.
Sections can also use different column arrangements.
A section break helps structure a document.
It differs from an ordinary paragraph break.
A page break alone does not provide the same section-formatting boundary.
Distinguish a section break from a paragraph break and explain that sections can have different formatting.

A next-page section break starts the new section on a new page.
It separates sections and also moves following content to a new page.
A continuous section break starts a new section without necessarily starting a new page.
It can support different column layouts within the same page.
Use the type that matches the intended separation and layout.
The two examples are not an exhaustive list of all section-break types available in word processors.

A section's header or footer may be linked to the previous section.
Linked sections can share repeated header or footer content.
An independent header or footer may require that link to be removed.
Different section layouts should be checked for suitable repeated content and alignment.
Creating a section break does not necessarily make every header and footer independent.
Check the resulting sections rather than assuming their settings are separate.

Columns divide the body area into vertical text regions.
They can provide a newspaper-like layout.
Text normally flows through the available columns.
Different document sections can use different column settings.
A title or table can occupy a full-width section while body text uses multiple columns.
Section breaks define the areas that need different layouts.
Check the reading order and any unwanted splits at column boundaries.

Column layout includes the number of columns.
Columns can have specified widths.
Spacing separates adjacent columns.
An optional vertical line can make the division more visible.
The columns and gaps must fit within the available page width.
Column width affects line length and text wrapping.
Choose an arrangement that keeps the content readable.

Left alignment gives text a common left edge.
Right alignment gives text a common right edge.
Centre alignment places text around the centre of the available width.
Full justification aligns text to both edges, normally by adjusting word spacing.
Alignment is part of the text's presentation.
Different roles such as headings and body paragraphs can use different alignments.
Defined styles help apply the chosen alignment consistently.

Line spacing controls the space between lines within a paragraph.
Common examples are single, 1.5-line and double spacing.
Spacing before a paragraph controls separation from preceding content.
Spacing after a paragraph controls separation from following content.
Paragraph spacing differs from spacing between individual lines.
A heading can need different paragraph spacing from body text.
Consistent settings help create a readable layout.

Editing can introduce inconsistent line and paragraph spacing.
Pasted text may retain formatting from another source.
Inserted or deleted paragraph breaks can alter the visible gaps.
Check the surrounding paragraphs after moving or copying text.
Check both line spacing and spacing before and after paragraphs.
Use the intended styles consistently.
Review the final layout after editing rather than only checking the changed words.

A first-line indent moves the first line relative to the remaining paragraph lines.
A whole-paragraph indent moves all lines in from a margin.
A hanging indent leaves the first line farther left than the following lines.
Left and right indents affect the paragraph's available width.
Indentation is distinct from changing the page margins for the whole document.
Use the appropriate indent for the intended paragraph structure.
Check that related paragraphs use consistent indentation.

Tab stops align text at defined positions without requiring a table.
A left tab aligns the left edge of an entry.
A centre tab aligns the centre of an entry.
A right tab aligns the right edge of an entry.
A decimal tab aligns numbers at their decimal points.
A tab character advances text to the next tab stop.
Default tab stops are used where custom stops have not been defined.
Choose the tab alignment suited to the values or labels being arranged.

Text enhancement makes selected text stand out.
Examples include bold, italics, underline and highlighting.
Font colour can distinguish selected text.
Capitalisation can emphasise a word or phrase.
Enhancement should remain readable and appropriate to the document.
Use the required enhancements consistently.
Extra unrequested enhancements can change the intended appearance.

Superscript uses smaller characters positioned above the normal baseline.
It is used for mathematical powers or indices.
For example, x² uses a superscript 2.
Square and cubic units can use superscripts, such as m² and cm³.
Superscript changes vertical position as well as character size.
It differs from subscript, which places characters below the baseline.

Subscript uses smaller characters positioned below the normal baseline.
It is used in notation such as chemical formulae.
Examples include the 2 in H₂O and CO₂.
The lowered character can carry a specific scientific meaning.
Subscript changes vertical position as well as character size.
It differs from superscript, which places characters above the baseline.

Find locates specified text within a document.
Replace substitutes different text for a matching occurrence.
It is useful for repeated changes such as a company or product name.
The replacement text must be entered accurately.
Search options determine which occurrences count as matches.
Check the result to avoid unintended changes.
Find and replace changes text content rather than merely its formatting in this example.

Match case distinguishes upper-case and lower-case letters.
It can restrict a search to the specified capitalisation.
Whole-word matching restricts matches at word boundaries.
It helps avoid changing a matching sequence inside a longer word.
The two options address different kinds of unintended match.
Choose the settings according to the intended text change.
Review results rather than assuming every occurrence is appropriate.

Replace All changes every matching occurrence within the chosen search scope.
It is efficient when the same change is valid throughout that scope.
Individual replacement lets the user inspect each occurrence.
Context may make some occurrences unsuitable for replacement.
An incorrect search or replacement can spread the same error widely.
Check case, whole-word behaviour and scope before bulk replacement.
Review the edited document for unintended results.

A bookmark names a location or selected area within a document.
It supports direct navigation to a particular part of a long document.
Meaningful names help identify the destination.
Bookmarks can provide targets for internal hyperlinks.
A linked contents entry can lead to a bookmarked section.
The bookmark marks the destination; the hyperlink provides the navigation action.
A bookmark is different from merely typing a heading's name in a contents list.

A hyperlink directs the user to a resource or location.
It can lead to another part of the same document.
It can lead to another document or a web page.
An email link can start a message to a specified address.
Linked contents entries can lead directly to the appropriate bookmarked sections.
A link can be attached to text or an object such as an image.
The visible link text and its actual destination need not be identical.
An internal bookmark identifies a target, while the hyperlink leads the user to it.
Explain that the hyperlink leads to a resource or location rather than merely describing its URL or code position.

A database is an organised collection of data.
Database software stores, retrieves and manages data in a structured way.
It organises data using fields, records and tables.
It can store links between related data.
Queries help find selected records quickly.
Records can be added, edited or deleted.
Reports present selected information.
A database is the data collection; database software is the program that manages it.
Describe database software and structured storage or retrieval; a brand name or comparison with spreadsheets does not answer that definition.

A field represents one item or attribute of data, such as a surname or date of birth.
Each field has a name identifying it.
A field has a specified data type.
Within a table, a column represents a field.
Each record provides a value for that field where appropriate.
Field design can include a length or other restrictions.
Use field and record terminology accurately.

A record is a collection of related fields about one person, object or event.
For example, a student record can contain an identifier, name and date of birth.
Fields within the same record may have different data types.
A table row represents a record.
Records in the same table follow the same field structure.
A record is not the entire database or table.

A database file can contain one or more tables.
A table is an organised collection of related records.
Rows represent records.
Columns represent fields.
A field value occurs at the intersection of a row and a column.
One database can contain several related tables.
Distinguish the database file, its tables and the records within each table.

A flat-file database stores data in a single table.
The table can contain many records.
It is a relatively simple database structure.
A primary key can identify each record.
Data may be represented using delimiters such as commas or tabs in a flat-file export.
Related details can be repeated across records, causing redundancy.
Repeated data can increase storage and the risk of inconsistent entries.
Single table does not mean a single record.
Explain a simple single-table database with records, an identifying key and possible redundancy; single file alone is insufficient.

A relational database stores related data in linked tables.
Relationships connect records through key fields.
A primary key uniquely identifies a record in its table.
A foreign key refers to a key in another table.
Separating related entities reduces unnecessary repetition of their details.
Queries and reports can combine data from multiple tables.
Referential integrity can help maintain valid links.
These are relationships between tables, not merely links between separate database files.
Describe linked tables and keys accurately, not relationships between separate databases or files.

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table.
Its value must be unique for every record.
It cannot contain a null value.
A table has one designated primary key, which can consist of one field or a combination of fields.
A suitable identifier is preferable to a value that can repeat, such as a person's name.
A primary key can be referenced by foreign keys in related tables.
Uniqueness concerns the records in that table.
A primary key identifies a record rather than naming the whole database.
Explain uniqueness, record identification and a non-null value rather than giving isolated one-word characteristics.

A foreign key stores a reference to a key in another table.
It provides a link between related records.
In the chapter's examples, it refers to the other table's primary key.
A foreign-key value can repeat where several records refer to the same parent record.
A foreign key may permit nulls if the relationship is optional.
Referential integrity checks that non-null references point to valid related records.
The relationship is between tables within the database design.
A foreign key does not have the same uniqueness requirement as a primary key.
Explain that the foreign key links to a primary key in another table; distinguish tables from databases and files.

A one-to-many relationship links one record to several related records.
The one side has a unique identifying key.
The many side stores a corresponding foreign key.
The same foreign-key value can appear in several records on the many side.
For example, one teacher can be linked to many student records in the chapter's simplified model.
Each linked record on the many side refers to one matching record on the one side for that relationship.
Cardinality describes how records relate, not how many tables exist in the file.

A poorly structured flat file can repeat the same details in many records.
A relational design separates related data into suitable tables.
The related record's key can be stored instead of repeating all its details.
This reduces unnecessary duplication or redundancy.
Less repeated data can reduce storage requirements.
It also reduces repeated typing and the risk of inconsistent copies.
The benefit depends on an appropriate table and relationship design.
Develop the benefit of reduced duplication, such as less repeated storage or entry, rather than only saying there are multiple tables.

Reduced duplication means a shared detail can be updated in one place.
This saves repeated edits across many records.
It reduces the risk that one copy is changed while another is missed.
Linked tables let queries combine related information.
Reports can present fields drawn from several related tables.
Explain the practical benefit rather than merely calling the query or report complex.
The tables must be linked appropriately to obtain the intended results.
Explain how linked tables make combined queries or reports useful; complex alone does not explain the advantage.
Search speed depends on database design

A relational database is not always faster to search than a flat file.
Search performance depends on the database structure.
Indexes can help locate suitable records.
The amount of data and the query's work also affect performance.
A poorly designed relational query can require unnecessary processing.
Compare the actual designs and task rather than assuming that more tables always mean faster searching.

A field's data type determines what kind of values it stores and how they are handled.
Choose the type according to the data's meaning and intended use.
Text, numeric and Boolean are common generic data types.
Numeric sub-types can distinguish whole numbers, fractional values and currency.
A wrong type can reject required values or lose information.
An identifier containing a letter needs text rather than an integer type.
A string of digits does not automatically need numeric storage.
Data type and display formatting are separate choices.
Use generic data-type names and specify the numeric sub-type where required; a displayed value such as Y/N is not a type name.

Text or alphanumeric data stores letters, digits and other permitted characters.
It is suitable for names and titles.
It is suitable for identifiers that are not used in arithmetic.
Telephone numbers commonly need text storage.
Text can preserve leading zeroes and non-numeric characters.
An ISBN containing X cannot be stored as an integer without losing required information.
The generic name may be text, string or alphanumeric.
Short Text and Long Text are application-specific variants of text storage.
Inspect the actual identifier: a value containing X requires text rather than an integer type.

Numeric data stores values that can be used in calculations.
Examples include quantities, heights and prices.
Choose a numeric sub-type suitable for the range and required precision.
Whole-number quantities can use an integer type.
Fractional measurements need a type that supports decimals.
Telephone numbers and codes are usually identifiers rather than arithmetic quantities.
The presence of digits alone is insufficient to justify numeric storage.
Specify the appropriate generic numeric sub-type when requested, rather than omitting numeric from numeric: currency.

An integer stores whole numbers without a fractional part.
A decimal-capable type supports fractional values.
Choose integer storage with enough capacity for the permitted minimum and maximum.
Choose decimal precision appropriate to the values and calculations.
An integer and a long integer have different storage ranges in Access.
The number of digits alone is not a universal rule for choosing a numeric type.
Displayed decimal places are not necessarily the same as stored precision.
Match the generic numeric sub-type to the values, such as decimal for fractional measurements.

Currency data represents monetary amounts used in calculations.
In generic exam terminology, it can be identified as numeric: currency.
Currency formatting can display a symbol such as £ or $.
The displayed symbol is distinct from the numeric amount.
A consistent number of displayed decimal places helps present prices clearly.
Changing the displayed symbol does not convert the amount to another currency.
Select the type and format appropriate to the field's purpose.
Use numeric: currency when the question requests the generic type and sub-type.

Date/time fields represent date or time values rather than ordinary descriptive text.
They support appropriate comparisons, sorting and date calculations.
The display format can differ from the underlying stored representation.
Store a date of birth rather than a person's age when the value must remain useful over time.
Age can be calculated from date of birth and a relevant reference date.
A stored age becomes out of date unless it is updated.
Changing only the displayed date format does not change the underlying date.
Store date of birth and derive age from it; deleting age without a sensible replacement is insufficient.

Boolean or logical data represents two logical states.
Typical displays include Yes/No and True/False.
A checkbox can display the state.
It suits a property such as whether an item is scented.
The internal numeric representation depends on the software.
The displayed letters Y and N are values or labels, not the generic data-type name.
Use Boolean or logical when asked for the generic type.
Use Boolean as the generic type; Y/N describes displayed values rather than the type.

Autonumber automatically generates identifying numbers for records.
It can provide unique values without manual entry.
It can be used as a primary-key field.
Its role is record identification rather than a calculation based on other fields.
The numbers need not form an uninterrupted sequence.
An automatically assigned identifier does not replace validation of the record's other data.

A storage type determines what values can be held.
A display format determines how values appear.
Percentage, currency symbols and displayed decimal places can be formatting choices.
For example, the same fractional value can be displayed as a percentage.
Showing fewer decimal places can round the display without changing the underlying value.
Calculations can still use the stored value.
Changing presentation is different from changing the data type or stored precision.

Field names should be concise and meaningful.
They should identify the data unambiguously.
Names help users and designers understand the structure.
Consistent naming helps queries and other database objects refer to the intended fields.
A short coded field name may need a clearer label on a form.
User-facing labels should describe the required information clearly.
A field name and the data stored in that field are different things.

A data-entry form provides a user-facing way to enter, edit or display data.
Its controls correspond to the intended fields.
Clear labels explain what information is required.
Navigation controls help users move between records.
Suitable controls can support adding or saving a record.
Help or instructions can support accurate completion.
A form is designed for interaction rather than only presenting a printed report.
Design an interactive data-entry form with appropriate fields, control sizes and structures rather than a report layout.
Forms suited to the target audience

Form wording and layout should suit the intended users.
Clear questions may be more understandable than abbreviated field names.
Use simple instructions where users are inexperienced.
Readable fonts and suitable font sizes improve usability.
High contrast and larger controls can help users with visual impairments.
Provide help where the user needs it.
Explain how a feature helps the audience rather than simply naming a control.
Explain how the design features help users complete the form accurately, rather than merely listing controls or contents.

A bound data-entry control is associated with a stored field.
Entered or selected values must go to the intended field.
A visible control label may differ from the value stored.
For example, a radio-button choice can correspond to a coded value.
Check that each choice maps to the correct stored meaning.
An unbound control does not automatically save a value into a table field.
The form's appearance alone does not prove that its data links are correct.

Keep a form simple and organised.
Group related fields together.
Provide enough input space for the expected values.
Use balanced white space without crowding or excessive empty areas.
Use clear labels and readable text.
Include a meaningful title and completion instructions.
Use suitable navigation, help and data-entry controls.
Explain how the layout helps accurate and efficient completion.
A long title or name needs more input space than a short code.
Provide enough space for the expected field values and a suitable form layout; do not substitute a report design.

Closed questions restrict the range of possible responses.
Radio buttons can allow one choice from a group.
Selection lists can restrict users to permitted entries.
These controls reduce typing and can speed up entry.
They reduce spelling variation and some data-entry errors.
Consistent stored choices are easier to search and compare.
Choose a control whose permitted choices fit the field.
The benefit is the suitability of the method, not merely the presence of the field.
Explain why the entry control is suitable, such as faster choice or fewer entry errors, rather than only describing its use.

A selection list suits a field with a manageable set of permitted values.
It can be useful for staff codes, categories or a defined group of names.
Users select rather than retype an entry.
This can improve speed and reduce inconsistent spellings.
The list must include the legitimate choices.
A very large or frequently changing set may need a different search or entry design.
Names are not inherently unsuitable for lists; suitability depends on the set of possible entries.
Explain how selecting from the permitted entries improves speed or reduces errors for that field.

A list box displays entries for selection.
A combo box combines a selection list with a text-entry area.
A combo box can allow typed input where its settings permit it.
It can also be configured to restrict entries to the supplied list.
A list box's permitted selections depend on its properties.
Do not assume that every combo box accepts arbitrary new values.
The control's settings determine the actual restrictions.

A query retrieves selected data from a database.
Criteria can select records meeting particular conditions.
The query can choose which fields to show.
A saved query stores the search definition rather than a permanently fixed result.
Rerunning it uses the current data, including relevant new records.
Changing stored data can therefore change the results.
Queries can also support calculations and sorting.

AND combines conditions that must all be true for a record to be selected.
A record failing any required condition is excluded.
For example, a car must have the required make AND have air conditioning marked Yes.
The conditions can refer to different fields.
AND narrows the result to records meeting the combined requirements.
Check the exact conditions rather than treating AND as a choice between alternatives.

OR selects a record when at least one alternative condition is true.
A record can satisfy either condition or both.
For example, the make can be Ford OR Toyota.
A record satisfying neither alternative is excluded.
OR supports alternative acceptable values.
It differs from AND, which requires all the combined conditions.

NOT excludes records matching a stated condition.
For example, NOT a specified make selects records whose make does not match it.
It expresses a condition's opposite for the values being tested.
It can be combined with other query criteria.
Check the resulting records against the intended exclusion.
Missing or null values may need separate treatment according to the query system.

Wildcards represent unspecified characters in a text search.
In the chapter's Access examples, * represents a variable sequence of characters.
Text* finds entries starting with the specified text.
*Text finds entries ending with the specified text.
*Text* finds entries containing the specified text.
Wildcard notation depends on the software and query mode.
Match the pattern to the required beginning, ending or contained text.

Comparison criteria test a field against a specified value.
Common operators include =, <, >, <= and >=.
Inclusive comparisons allow the boundary value.
Numeric criteria can select values above or below a threshold.
Date and time criteria can select values before, after or within a period.
Text comparisons are also possible where supported, using the system's comparison rules.
Use the appropriate data type and comparison for the field.

A query can retrieve fields from more than one related table.
The relationship determines which records belong together.
A key value can connect a detail record to its related parent record.
This presents related information without storing all of it repeatedly in one table.
For example, a student record can be combined with the relevant teacher details.
Correct joins are needed to avoid missing or unintended combinations.
The benefit is useful combined information rather than merely having many tables.
Develop the value of combining related data in queries rather than merely calling the query complex.

A field can be used in query criteria without appearing in the displayed results.
The hidden field still controls which records qualify.
For example, a Boolean condition can filter results without showing its column.
Hiding an output field is different from removing its criterion.
The stored field and its data are not deleted.
Check both the selection conditions and the displayed columns.

A calculated field derives a value from other data.
A query can calculate the result for each qualifying record when it runs.
For example, profit can be sale price minus purchase price.
Age can be derived from date of birth and a reference date.
A per-record calculation differs from a total over several records.
Using source data for the calculation avoids manually updating a derived value.
The formula and its data types must match the intended meaning.
Use date of birth to calculate age; a formula based only on an unchanged stored age does not solve the problem.

A summary query calculates results across selected records.
Records can be grouped by a shared field value.
Each group can have a total, average or count.
It can show one summary row per group rather than every original record.
An overall summary can also cover the entire selected set.
Filtering determines which records contribute to the summary.
A summary across records differs from a calculation within each record.

Sorting arranges records in a specified order.
Ascending text order normally runs alphabetically.
Ascending numeric order runs from lowest to highest.
Descending order reverses the chosen order.
Dates can be ordered from earliest to latest or the reverse.
Sorting retains the association between values in the same record.
Sorting orders the result; filtering determines which records are included.
Purpose and choice of report output

A report presents selected database information in a readable layout.
It can be based on a table or query.
Reports can be produced quickly from stored data.
A report can show detailed records and summary information.
An Access report can suit structured, repeated output.
Extracted data can also be included in a word-processed document.
Choose the output form according to its purpose and audience.
Explain the report benefit in the task’s context; an undeveloped feature name alone is insufficient.

A report header appears once at the beginning of a report.
It can contain the report title and introductory information.
A report footer appears once at the end.
It can display overall totals, averages or counts.
These sections differ from page headers and footers that repeat on pages.
Their position determines whether information applies to the complete report or an individual page.

A page header repeats at the top of each report page.
It can contain column headings or other repeated identification.
A page footer repeats at the bottom of each page.
It can contain page numbers and other page-level information.
Repeated labels help readers interpret later pages.
Page sections differ from report sections that occur only once.

The detail section displays information for an included record.
It repeats for each record selected for the report.
Its controls display the relevant field values.
Repeated detail rows follow the same layout.
The record source and criteria determine which records appear.
The detail section differs from a footer summarising many records.

Database information can be exported for use in another application.
Exported data can support further manipulation or chart creation.
It can be included in a word-processed document.
The chosen format determines which data and presentation features are retained.
RTF means Rich Text Format and retains text formatting.
Plain text contains unformatted text data.
Check that the receiving application supports the chosen format.
Exporting a result is different from transferring the complete editable database design.
Expand RTF as Rich Text Format and explain retained formatting using generic terminology.

A report can be adapted to show or suppress selected information.
