For example, a delivery note can omit costs shown on an invoice.
Reusing a layout can reduce repeated design work.
Hiding a control changes presentation rather than deleting stored data.
A visual hiding technique does not guarantee that sensitive data has been removed from the file.
Choose the visible fields to suit the report's purpose.
Check the actual output for unwanted information.

Database records can supply information for printed labels.
Address labels can be used for customer mailings.
Product labels can show selected product details.
A query can choose the records whose labels are required.
Each label uses the relevant fields from its record.
Consistent label layout allows repeated output.
Check that the selected records and displayed fields match the purpose.

SUM adds selected numeric values.
AVG calculates their arithmetic mean.
MAX returns the largest value and MIN the smallest.
COUNT counts records or non-null field values according to the expression used.
An overall report footer can show summaries for the selected records.
A group summary applies to its particular group.
An aggregate differs from a formula calculated separately for each record.
Check which records and values contribute to the calculation.

Multiple sort keys are applied in priority order.
The primary sort key determines the main order.
A later key orders records sharing the same earlier-key value.
For example, surname can be followed by forename within matching surnames.
Each key can use its own ascending or descending direction.
Changing key priority can change the final order.
Sorting must keep the field values of each record together.

A presentation is a series of slides giving information to an audience.
It can support teaching or a lecture as a visual aid.
It can advertise products or services.
It can provide information on a continuous display.
The content and delivery should suit the purpose and audience.
A presentation may be speaker-led or run automatically.

Identify the presentation's purpose and target audience before designing it.
Consider the audience's age, knowledge and experience.
Choose language, detail and length suited to those users.
Young children may need brief content, simple words and relevant colourful images.
Customers may need product features, costs and a simple, eye-catching presentation.
Staff may need professional language, technical facts and charts or statistics.
Use relevant media and keep the content focused on the audience's interests.
Explain how each choice helps the specific audience rather than listing unexplained features.
Relate language, length and focus to the intended audience rather than listing factors without explanation.

Design the slides for the actual delivery medium and screen.
Aspect ratio describes the relationship between slide width and height.
Common examples include 4:3 and 16:9.
Choose the ratio specified for the task or suited to the actual display.
A projector is not inherently restricted to 4:3, nor a monitor to 16:9.
Changing the slide dimensions can affect the placement or fit of objects.
Check that text and media remain visible after a size change.

Use consistent colours and styles across related slides.
Use a limited, coherent range of font faces.
Keep equivalent headings and body text consistently formatted.
A consistent layout makes the presentation more organised and easier to follow.
For an organisation, repeated fonts, colours and logos support its house style.
Consistent presentation helps the audience recognise the brand.
Balance text, images and white space.
Consistency should support the content and audience rather than add unnecessary decoration.
Explain how consistent presentation helps the audience recognise the organisation’s brand.
Plain text versus rich text sources

TXT is a plain-text format containing characters without stored text formatting.
RTF means Rich Text Format.
RTF can retain formatting such as font and text size.
Source formatting can influence the appearance of imported content.
A plain-text source does not carry the same formatting information.
Check the resulting slides after importing either type.
The source format does not remove the need to apply the required presentation styles.
Expand RTF as Rich Text Format and describe retained formatting using generic terminology.

A master slide stores shared design and layout information.
It can define colours, fonts, effects and object positions.
Slides using the master and its layouts can share those features.
A master supports consistent presentation across many slides.
Changing a shared master element can update the slides that inherit it.
It reduces repeated formatting work on individual slides.
Individual slide content remains separate from the shared design.

A master can contain repeated graphics such as a logo.
It can define heading and body-text formatting.
It can include footer information and a slide-number placeholder.
Automatic slide numbers can show the relevant number on each slide.
Associated layouts inherit common elements from the master.
A layout can adapt placeholder arrangements for different content.
Check which master or layout a slide uses when a shared element is missing or inconsistent.

A slide layout defines an arrangement of placeholders.
Placeholders provide areas for content such as titles, text, charts or images.
A title slide may contain a title and subtitle.
Another layout may place a chart beside explanatory text.
Choose a layout suited to the slide's content.
A layout supplies structure rather than the actual message.
The master and layout together support consistent positioning and formatting.

Presentation software may resize text to fit a placeholder.
Automatic resizing can create inconsistent font sizes.
Imported content can also retain unsuitable formatting.
Check the result against the intended styles.
Ensure all text remains readable and visible.
Do not assume that content fitting inside a box means it is correctly formatted.
Review consistency across slides after content or layout changes.

Slides can combine text with charts and tables.
They can include still images, animated images, shapes and symbols.
Audio and video can also be included.
Choose media that supports the subject and intended audience.
Use a suitable balance rather than overcrowding the slide.
Check that each item remains clear and readable.
Multimedia content differs from the transition between slides or an animation applied to an object.
Relate the media choices to the intended audience and explain their purpose rather than giving an unexplained list.

Choose a chart according to the data and intended comparison.
Pie charts represent parts of a whole.
Bar charts compare values between categories.
Line graphs show trends across an ordered variable such as time.
Give the chart a meaningful title.
Label categories, values, units and series where needed.
Check that labels remain readable at the slide's displayed size.
A chart on a slide needs the same interpretive clarity as one in a spreadsheet.

Audio or video can begin automatically or after user action.
The start behaviour should suit the delivery method.
Audio may play on one slide or continue across slides.
A media item may play once or repeat in a loop.
Starting automatically is different from looping.
Playing across slides is different from repeating the same clip.
Check that playback supports the presentation rather than interrupting it.
Purpose of audience notes or handouts

Audience notes or handouts provide a copy of slide information.
They let audience members refer back after the presentation.
Several slides can be placed on one printed page.
Some layouts provide space for handwritten notes.
The content should remain readable in the chosen print layout.
Handouts serve the audience rather than act as private speaker prompts.

Presenter notes contain prompts or key facts for the speaker.
They are associated with individual slides.
They can help the presenter remember explanations not written on the slide.
They do not normally appear on the projected slide.
They may be viewed in a presenter interface or printed as notes pages.
They are not normally distributed as the audience's handout.
Keep the distinction between visible slide content and supporting speaker notes.

A hyperlink leads to another resource or location.
Text, shapes and images can act as clickable links.
A link can lead to another slide in the presentation.
It can lead to an external document or website.
An email link can start a message to a specified address.
Links can offer alternative paths through the content.
Check that the linked object has the intended destination.
The visible object and its destination are distinct parts of the link.
Explain that a hyperlink leads to a resource or location; describing a URL alone does not explain its function.

An action button is an object used to trigger an action during a presentation.
It can navigate to the previous or next slide.
It can lead to the first or last slide.
A home or menu button can return users to a chosen navigation slide.
The destination must match the intended presentation structure.
A familiar button appearance helps communicate its function.
Check the behaviour rather than assuming the icon guarantees the correct destination.

A ScreenTip is visible information associated with an object or link.
It appears when the pointer hovers over the relevant object.
It can explain the object's function or destination.
Clear wording helps users understand what an unfamiliar control does.
It is different from text permanently shown on the slide.
It does not replace alternative text intended for screen readers.

Alternative text describes an object's meaning or purpose.
It supports users who cannot see the object.
A screen reader can read the description aloud.
It is particularly important for informative images and other non-text objects.
Describe the relevant information rather than relying only on the filename.
Alternative text is not normally displayed as part of the slide.
It supports accessibility rather than acting as a decorative caption.

Alternative text provides an accessible description of an object.
A screen reader can communicate that description to the user.
A ScreenTip provides visible information when the pointer hovers over an object.
The two features serve different access needs.
A hover message alone does not provide the same function as a screen-reader description.
Use each feature according to its purpose.
Neither should be confused with the main slide text or presenter notes.

A slide transition is an effect used when moving from one slide to another.
It controls how the next slide is introduced.
A simple replacement or a visual effect can be used.
A transition concerns the change between slides.
It is different from animating an object within a slide.
Choose effects that support clear delivery.
Check that the transition is appropriate to the presentation's purpose.

An animation affects an object within a slide.
It can change how text, an image or another object appears or behaves.
A transition affects the move between slides.
A slide can therefore have both a transition and animated objects.
Animating one object does not mean the whole slide uses that effect.
Choose the correct feature for the intended change.
Keep the distinction clear when describing presentation effects.

An entrance animation introduces an object onto the slide.
An emphasis animation draws attention to an object already present.
An exit animation removes an object from view.
The effect type should match the intended behaviour.
For example, bullet points can use entrance effects as they are discussed.
An object's exit does not necessarily remove it from the editable presentation.
These effects operate on objects rather than replacing the slide itself.

Animation order determines the sequence in which objects are animated.
Start settings determine whether an effect begins on a click or relative to another effect.
A delay controls the wait before an effect starts.
Duration controls how long an effect takes.
Bullet points can be revealed individually instead of appearing together.
The sequence can support the order of the speaker's explanation.
Check the complete playback rather than only each effect in isolation.

Use a coherent approach to transitions and animations.
Consistent effects help the presentation feel organised.
They should work alongside consistent fonts, colours and layout.
Unnecessary changes can distract from the content.
Choose effects that suit the purpose and delivery method.
Where the task specifies a shared effect, apply it to the required slides or objects.
Consistency does not replace checking the actual sequence and timing.

A hidden slide remains stored in the presentation.
It is omitted from the normal slide-show sequence.
It can be retained for optional or later use.
Deleting a slide removes it from the presentation.
Hiding is therefore different from deleting.
Check the normal show sequence to confirm which slides appear.
A hidden slide's contents still exist in the file.

A looped carousel repeats the presentation continuously.
Slide timings allow it to advance automatically.
It can run as an information or advertising display without a presenter.
Media may also need suitable automatic playback settings.
A speaker-controlled show normally advances in response to the presenter's actions.
Manual control lets the speaker vary the time spent on each slide.
Looping, slide advancement and media playback are separate behaviours.
Choose the combination suited to the intended delivery.

Full-page slide output prints the slide content.
Notes pages include a slide and its presenter notes.
Handouts place multiple slides on each page.
A handout layout can provide space for the audience's written notes.
Choose the output according to who will use it and why.
Check that the printed content and labels remain readable.
A static printout does not reproduce live animation, transitions or media playback.
Different output choices expose different supporting information.

A spreadsheet model represents a real system using data and mathematical formulae.
Changing inputs explores possible outcomes through what-if analysis.
Models can support financial, mathematical and scientific tasks.
Automatic calculations allow scenarios to be explored quickly.
A model can be changed as information or assumptions change.
Incorrect inputs or formulae can produce unreliable results.
A model may omit important variables or unexpected events.
Setting up and interpreting it takes time and suitable skills.
Its results support judgement rather than guaranteeing what will happen.
Evaluate the model in the given scenario, explaining calculations and what-if benefits alongside incorrect data, omitted variables and setup needs.
Cells, rows, columns and cell addresses

A spreadsheet organises data in a two-dimensional grid of rows and columns.
A cell is the intersection of a row and a column.
Columns are commonly identified by letters and rows by numbers.
A cell address combines its column and row.
C6 identifies column C, row 6.
Spreadsheet software can calculate results using the values in cells.
A software brand name alone does not define a spreadsheet.
Define spreadsheet software through rows, columns and relevant calculations rather than a brand name alone.

A worksheet is an individual spreadsheet sheet.
A workbook is the file containing one or more worksheets.
Separate worksheets can organise related parts of a task.
A cell reference can identify a value within a particular sheet.
A workbook and one of its worksheets are therefore different levels of organisation.

A cell can contain a number, a text label or a formula.
Numbers can be used in calculations.
Labels identify or explain the data.
In Excel, a formula starts with an equals sign.
A formula can contain cell references, operators and functions.
The calculated result is normally displayed in the cell.
Text that looks like a number is not necessarily stored as a numeric value.
Describe a user-defined formula beginning with =; a function is predefined and may form part of it.

A formula calculates a result from its inputs.
It can refer to values stored in other cells.
Changing an input changes dependent results when recalculation occurs.
This avoids manually repeating each dependent calculation.
Linked calculations support spreadsheet modelling.
The result is only reliable if the inputs and formula are appropriate.
Automatic calculation does not prove that the model reflects real life accurately.
Explain how automatic calculations or scenarios help the specific modelling task rather than listing generic features.

The + operator adds and the - operator subtracts.
The * operator multiplies and the / operator divides.
The ^ operator raises a value to a power.
The sum is the result of addition.
The difference is the result of subtraction.
The product is the result of multiplication.
Brackets can group operations within a formula.
The initial equals sign identifies the entry as a formula in Excel.

Evaluate expressions inside brackets first.
Then evaluate powers.
Multiplication and division have equal priority and are evaluated from left to right.
Addition and subtraction have equal priority and are evaluated from left to right.
Brackets can change the order from the default priority.
For example, =(B2-C2)*D2 calculates the difference before multiplying.
Without the brackets, multiplication would take place before the subtraction.
Check the intended calculation rather than relying only on a mnemonic.
Explain which operation is performed first and use brackets to make the intended calculation order explicit.

A relative reference changes when its formula is copied to another location.
The change follows the row or column displacement of the copied formula.
B2 becomes B3 when copied one row down.
B2 becomes C2 when copied one column right.
The reference retains its relative position to the formula cell.
This supports repeating the same calculation for successive records.
A changing reference can be wrong if it was intended to point to one fixed input.
State how the reference adjusts when copied and why that can point to an unintended cell.

An absolute reference remains fixed when the formula is copied.
Dollar signs fix reference components.
$B$2 fixes both column B and row 2.
Copying a formula does not change that reference to another row or column.
It is useful for a shared rate, constant or other fixed input.
B$2 fixes only the row, while $B2 fixes only the column.
These copying rules differ from the effects of inserting or deleting sheet structure.

A formula can combine relative and absolute references.
A changing row value can be multiplied by one fixed rate.
For example, =B2*$E$1 uses the current row's B value and the fixed value in E1.
Copied one row down, it becomes =B3*$E$1.
The relative part adjusts while the absolute part stays fixed.
Choose the reference type according to which inputs should change.
Check the copied formula rather than only the original result.

A mistyped input can affect every calculation that depends on it.
An incorrect formula can produce wrong results even from correct data.
A copied reference error can spread across several rows.
An apparently plausible result may still be wrong.
Check source data, formula logic and reference types.
A model is only as reliable as its assumptions, data and calculations.
Do not treat automatic recalculation as a guarantee of accuracy.
Explain how incorrect formulae or data can undermine the model’s results and the decisions based on them.

Use test inputs with independently calculated expected results.
Run the formula and compare the actual output with the expected output.
Use suitable normal, abnormal and boundary cases for the rule.
Boundary tests check whether comparisons include or exclude the correct values.
Abnormal tests can check that invalid input is trapped and feedback appears.
If the output is wrong, correct the formula or rule and retest.
Examples alone do not explain the complete testing process.
Check copied formulae as well as the first formula.
Describe test data, expected results, comparison, correction and retesting; test examples alone are insufficient.
Purpose of named cells and ranges

A name can identify a cell or range instead of an address.
Meaningful names can make formulae easier to read.
They make frequently used inputs or ranges easier to remember.
For example, a name such as TaxRate communicates the input's purpose.
The name must refer to the intended cell or range.
Naming a range does not by itself validate its contents.
Use short, unambiguous names that the application permits.

A formula is a user-written expression that calculates a result.
In Excel, it begins with =.
It can contain values, references and operators.
A function is a predefined named operation built into the software.
A function performs a specific task, such as SUM or AVERAGE.
A formula can contain one function, several functions or no function.
=A1+B1 is a formula without a function.
=SUM(A1:B1) is a formula containing the SUM function.
Explain that a predefined named function can form part of a user-written formula beginning with =.

Arguments supply inputs to a function.
Depending on the function, they can include numbers, text, references or conditions.
A function can use an individual cell or a range.
A colon identifies a continuous range, such as A1:A10.
Named cells or ranges can be used where appropriate.
Some functions accept several separate arguments or ranges.
Argument order and meaning depend on the particular function.
The complete formula still needs its initial equals sign.
Include the initial equals sign when giving a complete formula example.

SUM adds specified numeric values.
It can total a range without a long chain of individual additions.
=SUM(A1:A10) totals the numeric values in that range.
It can also accept separate numeric inputs or references.
Use the range containing exactly the intended values.
SUM is a function; the complete entry beginning with = is a formula.
Give a valid function or complete formula as requested; a complete formula needs its initial equals sign.

AVERAGE calculates the arithmetic mean.
It adds the included numeric values and divides by their count.
=AVERAGE(A1:A10) finds the mean of the numeric values in that range.
Blank cells and text in a referenced range are normally ignored.
Numeric zeroes are included.
Check that the selected range represents the intended group.
AVERAGE is different from finding a total or the middle value in sorted data.
Give a valid function example when asked for a function, and a complete formula when asked for a formula.

MAX returns the largest numeric value in the specified data.
MIN returns the smallest numeric value.
For example, they can identify the highest and lowest recorded sales.
The result is a value rather than the name of the record containing it.
Choose the intended range.
Neither function calculates an average or a count.

INT rounds a number down to an integer.
For a positive value, =INT(16.8) returns 16.
For a negative value, =INT(-16.8) returns -17.
Rounding down is therefore different from simply deleting decimal digits.
It changes the calculated result, unlike displaying fewer decimal places.
Choose it only when rounding towards the lower integer is intended.

ROUND rounds a number to the specified number of digits.
A positive digit argument specifies decimal places.
Zero digits rounds to a whole number.
A negative digit argument rounds to tens, hundreds or higher place values.
For example, =ROUND(62.55,1) returns 62.6.
=ROUND(62.55,-1) returns 60.
ROUND changes the result rather than merely its displayed format.

COUNT counts numeric entries.
COUNTA counts non-empty entries, including text.
A blank cell is not counted by either function.
A numeric zero is counted by both.
In a range containing only ordinary text, numbers and blanks, COUNTA minus COUNT counts the text entries.
That difference is not a universal text-only count if the range contains other non-numeric values.
Choose the function according to what should be counted.

COUNTIF counts cells that meet a specified criterion.
It uses a range and a criterion.
The criterion can be text, a number or a comparison.
For example, =COUNTIF(A1:A10,">=10") counts values at least 10.
A cell reference can supply the criterion.
COUNTIF counts matching entries rather than adding their values.
Ensure the comparison includes the intended boundary.

IF tests a condition.
It returns one result when the condition is true and another when it is false.
The results can be text, numbers, references or calculations.
For example, =IF(A1>=50,"Pass","Fail") includes 50 in the Pass band.
Text results are enclosed in quotation marks.
The comparison must match the intended rule.
IF selects a result; it does not by itself prove that the input is valid.

A comparison must include or exclude the intended boundary.
>=10 includes 10, while >10 does not.
For whole numbers, >9 can describe the same accepted values as >=10.
For fractional inputs, 9.5 satisfies >9 but not >=10.
Do not replace an inclusive comparison with a nearby integer threshold unless the input domain justifies it.
Test the boundary and nearby values.
Use actual test values when the question requests data.
Use actual boundary test values and explain how they check the formula’s comparisons.

A nested function contains another function as an argument.
Nested IF formulae can classify values into several bands.
The order of the tests must reflect the intended thresholds.
In a descending-threshold structure, test higher bands before lower ones.
An earlier true condition can prevent later alternatives from being reached.
Check exact boundaries so no value falls into an unintended band.
Test representative values from every outcome.
Nesting is different from merely placing separate formulae in adjacent cells.

SUMIF adds values associated with entries meeting a condition.
It tests a criterion range.
It totals corresponding numeric values in the sum range.
For example, it can total hours for records with a particular job title.
The tested entries and the values being added must correspond.
SUMIF adds matching values, whereas COUNTIF counts matching cells.
Choose the criterion and both ranges carefully.

A lookup finds a value in source data and returns associated information.
The lookup value identifies what to search for.
The source range contains the values and related results.
Choose the function according to the source's horizontal or vertical arrangement.
Decide whether an exact or approximate match is required.
Check that the returned field is the one intended.
A lookup returns associated data rather than simply counting matches.

LOOKUP finds a value in a source row or column and returns a corresponding result.
Its vector form uses a lookup vector and a result vector.
It uses approximate-match behaviour.
The lookup vector needs the appropriate ascending order for reliable results.
If no exact match exists, it can use the largest value not exceeding the lookup value.
It is therefore different from an explicitly exact-match lookup.
Choose the lookup method according to the source arrangement and matching requirement.

HLOOKUP searches horizontally across the first row of a table.
It returns the corresponding value from a specified row.
The row index is counted from the top of the lookup table.
An exact-match option is appropriate when an exact code is required.
Approximate matching requires suitably ordered source data.
Fix the table range if it must stay unchanged when the formula is copied.
H refers to the horizontal search direction.

VLOOKUP searches vertically down the first column of a table.
It returns the corresponding value from a specified column.
The column index is counted from the left edge of the lookup table.
The standard function returns from that column or columns to its right.
An exact-match option is appropriate for an exact identifier.
Approximate matching requires suitably ordered source data.
Check the lookup column, return index and copied range references.
V refers to the vertical search direction.

A formula can refer to data in another workbook or file.
An external reference identifies the source file and relevant sheet or range.
This allows related data to be reused without manually retyping it.
The reference must point to the correct source.
Moving or renaming the source can affect the link.
Check that the required source is available and its values are current.
External data can change the results when linked values are refreshed or recalculated.

XLOOKUP uses separate lookup and return arrays.
It can search a horizontal or vertical set of values.
The return array supplies the corresponding results.
It can return a value to the left of a lookup column.
It does not use VLOOKUP's column-index approach.
The arrays must correspond in the search direction.
Its availability depends on the spreadsheet software and version.
Choose its matching and search behaviour to suit the task.

A lookup can specify how missing matches are handled.
XLOOKUP can return supplied fallback text such as Not found.
Exact-match mode requires the intended matching value.
First-to-last search examines entries in that direction.
The search direction matters when duplicate matches exist.
Fallback text indicates a missing match rather than creating the missing source record.
Check the matching rule and search order separately.
The chapter's example uses exact matching and first-to-last search.

Filtering displays records meeting specified criteria.
Records not meeting the criteria are hidden from the filtered view rather than deleted.
Sorting rearranges the order of records.
A filtered result can also be sorted.
Removing a filter can restore the full displayed set.
Filtering chooses which records appear; sorting chooses their order.
Keep related values together in either operation.

Search criteria define which records qualify.
AND requires all combined conditions to be true.
OR requires at least one alternative condition to be true.
Criteria can test text patterns or numeric comparisons.
Inclusive and exclusive operators affect boundary values.
An exclusion must be expressed in the intended condition.
Check representative qualifying and non-qualifying records.
Do not confuse selection conditions with sort order.

In the chapter's spreadsheet wildcard searches, * matches zero or more characters.
A question mark matches one character.
A pattern can combine fixed text and wildcards.
For example, A* matches text beginning with A.
A? requires one character after A in a whole-pattern match.
Wildcard characters have a special meaning in supported search criteria.
The pattern must match the intended text structure.

Begins with searches for the specified text at the start.
Ends with searches for it at the end.
Contains searches for it anywhere within the text.
In wildcard patterns, Text*, *Text and *Text* express these different positions.
Choose the pattern that matches the task's wording.
The same search string can produce different results with different position rules.
Check that unintended longer words or codes have not been included.

Sort all columns belonging to each record together.
Sorting one column alone can detach its values from the correct names or identifiers.
Each row's associated values must retain their relationship.
For example, a score must remain with the student who earned it.
Check the selected range before sorting.
Include all required records and associated fields.
Sorting should change record order, not the meaning of the data.

The primary sort key controls the main order.
A secondary sort key orders records tied on the primary key.
Further keys resolve later ties.
Each level can use ascending or descending order.
For example, department can be followed by surname within departments.
Column headings should be recognised as headings rather than ordinary records.
Here primary key means first sort criterion, not a database record identifier.
Changing key priority can change the resulting order.

Values view displays stored entries and calculated results.
Formula view reveals the formulae behind calculated cells.
It helps inspect functions, references and calculation methods.
A correct-looking value alone may hide a wrong formula.
Formula view supports checking and explanation.
Formula text may need more column width than its result.
Check that required formulae and labels are fully visible in the output.

Wrapping text lets cell content flow onto more than one line.
It can display a long label without requiring a very wide column.
The column width affects where automatic wrapping occurs.
The row must be high enough to show all wrapped lines.
Text can still be hidden if the available cell dimensions are unsuitable.
Check the displayed or printed result.
Wrapping changes the layout of the text rather than the stored words.

Display formatting changes a value's appearance.
It does not normally change the underlying value used in calculations.
Displaying zero decimal places can hide a fractional part without removing it.
INT or ROUND instead changes the calculated result.
A later calculation can therefore differ depending on which method was used.
Choose between presentation changes and value changes according to the task.
Check the stored value or formula when the display is misleading.

Numeric values can be displayed with a chosen number of decimal places.
Currency formatting adds a suitable currency symbol.
Percentage formatting presents a fractional value as a percentage.
Date and time formats present values according to their meaning.
Choose the format suited to the data and audience.
A format name is different from the sample data displayed.
Changing the symbol or display format does not itself convert the underlying quantity.
Consistent formatting helps readers interpret values correctly.
Give the requested display-format name rather than copying the example data into the answer.

Conditional formatting changes appearance according to a rule.
The rule can test a cell's value or another relevant condition.
It can use fill or text colours to distinguish values or categories.
Formatting can update when the relevant data changes.
The underlying data remains unchanged.
Keep foreground and background colours readable.
Check that the correct range and conditions are covered.
A visual rule is different from a validation rule rejecting an entry.
Gridlines, borders and headings in output

Worksheet gridlines are different from explicitly applied cell borders.
Screen gridlines are not automatically proof of printed gridlines.
Printed gridlines depend on the output settings.
Cell borders are formatting applied to selected cell edges.
Row numbers and column letters can be included in output when required.
These headings help identify cell positions.
Check the required print output rather than assuming the screen view will be reproduced exactly.

Print scaling changes how much sheet content fits on each printed page.
Fit-to-page settings can reduce the number of pages.
Excessive shrinking can make text and formulae unreadable.
A single-page output is not useful if its content cannot be read.
Check page width, height and the size of the resulting text.
Use a layout that includes the required information clearly.
Review the output after changing scaling.

A print area restricts output to a specified part of a worksheet.
It avoids printing unrelated or empty areas.
The selected area must include all required data and labels.
Formula output must show the required formulae fully.
The print area is separate from filtering or deleting data.
Check page boundaries, clipping and readability.
An incorrect print area can omit information even when it remains in the worksheet.

Spreadsheet data can be exported for use in other software.
CSV means Comma-Separated Values.
It is a text format using commas to separate field values.
TXT is plain text without spreadsheet formatting.
Plain-text exports do not preserve the complete workbook's styles, charts and editable calculation structure.
Choose the format according to what the receiving application needs.
Check the exported content and required separators.
An extension is a file-format identifier rather than a software brand.
Expand CSV as Comma-Separated Values and distinguish it from CSS; use generic file-format terminology.

A website is a collection of related web pages.
Pages are commonly supplied by a web server and viewed in a browser.
A page can contain text, images, audio and video.
Hyperlinks connect pages and related resources.
Sections and search facilities can help users find information.
Website content can be updated and customised for its audience.
Explain the features in relation to the site's actual purpose.
Explain the website’s features in the specified audience or organisation context rather than giving only general benefits.

The content or structure layer defines the information and organisation of a page.
HTML is used for this layer.
It identifies elements such as text, images, tables and hyperlinks.
Headings and paragraphs give content a structure.
It differs from presentation, which controls appearance.
It differs from behaviour, which controls interactive actions.
Use the layer name when a question asks for a development layer.
Name the content or structure layer and explain what it structures, such as text and images.

HTML means HyperText Markup Language.
It is a text-based markup language used to structure web pages.
HTML files commonly use .html or .htm.
A browser retrieves and interprets the markup and associated resources.
The browser renders the resulting page for the user.
HTML is not the same language as CSS.
A file extension identifies a format rather than an authoring-software brand.
Give the requested generic extension, such as htm or html, rather than a software brand.

The presentation or style layer controls a page's appearance.
CSS means Cascading Style Sheets.
CSS can define fonts, colours, spacing and visual layout.
It can be written within HTML or stored in a separate .css file.
A shared stylesheet can format more than one page.
Presentation is a layer name; CSS is a technology used to implement it.
CSS is distinct from CSV and from HTML markup.
Identify presentation or style as the layer; CSS is the technology rather than the layer name.

The behaviour or scripting layer provides actions and interactivity.
Client-side scripting can respond to user actions.
JavaScript is a commonly used scripting language.
Scripts can control page elements and add functionality.
A browser can run client-side scripts as part of displaying a page.
Behaviour differs from content structure and visual presentation.
Two alternative names for the same layer are not two different layers.
Name behaviour or scripting and explain the actions or interactivity it provides.

HTML tags use angle brackets to identify elements.
Many elements have opening and closing tags.
The browser interprets the markup to build the page.
The tags are not normally displayed as visible page text.
Associated resources such as images may also need to be loaded.
Some HTML elements are void and do not have closing tags.
Rendering the page is different from searching the web for it.
Explain retrieval and interpretation of code and resources; do not confuse the browser with a search engine.

A document-type declaration supplies document-type information to the browser.
In modern HTML, <!DOCTYPE html> identifies an HTML document and supports standards-mode rendering.
It appears before the page's main markup.
It is a declaration rather than an ordinary HTML element.
It does not form part of the visible body content.
It is distinct from the opening html tag.

The head contains document information rather than the main visible page content.
It can contain the page title, metadata, stylesheet links and style information.
The body contains content normally displayed on the page.
Examples include text, images, tables and hyperlinks.
Head and body are the two section names.
Head is not the same term as header or heading.
A body heading differs from the document title in the head.
Use the precise section names head and body; header, heading and footer are different terms.

HTML comments annotate the source code.
They can explain the purpose of a section.
The opening delimiter is <!-- and the closing delimiter is -->.
Comment text does not appear as normal rendered page content.
Comments remain present in the source and are not a place for private information.
HTML comment syntax differs from CSS comment syntax.

The p element defines a paragraph.
Heading elements run from h1 to h6.
The levels express a heading hierarchy.
A heading's structural role differs from a paragraph's role.
Browsers provide default presentation, which CSS can change.
Choose heading levels according to structure rather than simply the desired text size.
A visible heading is different from the title element in the head.

Tables organise information into rows and columns.
The coursebook also uses tables to position page elements.
Cells can hold differently aligned text or other content.
Invisible borders can hide the table lines without removing its structure.
Tables help give elements an organised arrangement.
Table layout does not guarantee identical appearance on every device or browser.
Semantic HTML and CSS provide alternatives for full-page layout.
Use tables appropriately for the purpose and required task.
Explain how the table organises the page’s elements or data rather than merely repeating structure.

The table element contains a table.
tr defines a table row.
th defines a header cell.
td defines a data cell.
caption provides a table caption or title.
Rows contain cells that hold the relevant information.
These elements describe table structure rather than only its visual border style.

thead groups the header section of a table.
tbody groups its main body rows.
tfoot groups footer or summary rows.
The sections distinguish the roles of different rows.
They are parts of a table, not the page's head and body.
CSS can target these sections for different presentation.
Section markup does not by itself calculate totals.

Inline CSS is written in an HTML element's style attribute.
It applies declarations directly to that element.
An example declaration is color: red.
It is different from an internal style block in the head.
It is different from a separately linked external stylesheet.
Repeating inline declarations across many elements makes shared changes more laborious.
Conflicts are resolved through the CSS cascade.
Distinguish CSS in an element’s style attribute from an external file linked in the head.

A pixel value specifies an explicit CSS dimension.
A percentage size is relative to a relevant containing dimension.
A table's percentage width commonly relates to its containing area.
A cell's percentage width relates to the table layout.
Percentage sizing can adapt to available width.
An explicit CSS pixel size is not the same as a percentage of the screen.
Content and other layout rules can also affect the final dimensions.

Table alignment concerns the position of the whole table.
Cell-content alignment concerns where the content sits within each cell.
Horizontal cell alignment can be left, centre or right.
Vertical cell alignment can be top, middle or bottom.
A centred table can contain left-aligned text.
Changing text alignment does not necessarily move the table.
Treat table position and internal content alignment as separate settings.

A border can have a specified style, width and colour.
Table and cell borders can be styled.
With separated borders, neighbouring cells can retain separate boundaries.
With border-collapse: collapse, adjacent table borders share a collapsed boundary.
Border appearance is separate from the cell's content.
Padding and spacing are different from border width.
Check the resulting layout rather than assuming every border rule has the same effect.

colspan makes a cell span more than one column.
rowspan makes a cell span more than one row.
They change how a cell occupies the table's grid.
A heading can span several related columns.
A label can span several related rows.
Column span and row span are not interchangeable.
The surrounding table structure must account for the spanned positions.

Cell padding is the space between the content and its border.
It keeps text or images away from the cell edge.
Padding can be specified separately for the top, right, bottom and left.
It affects the room needed by the cell's content.
It differs from the gap between neighbouring cells.
Suitable padding can improve readability without changing the words themselves.

Border spacing separates adjacent cell borders in a separated-border table.
Padding separates content from its own cell border.
Horizontal and vertical border spacing can differ.
Spacing and padding therefore affect different gaps.
Collapsed borders do not use border spacing in the same way as separated borders.
Choose the property according to the required separation.
Do not describe all table gaps simply as margins.

An image's source reference identifies the resource the browser should load.
The referenced file must exist at an accessible location.
A relative path is resolved from the page's applicable base location.
An incorrect name or path can prevent the image from loading.
Copy the required supporting image files with the site.
Changing the displayed image size does not fix a broken source reference.
Check the page with its supporting files in the intended location.

Alternative text supplies a textual equivalent for an image's relevant meaning.
It helps users who cannot see the image.
A screen reader can announce the alternative text.
It can also help when the image cannot be displayed.
Describe the information or function rather than merely repeating a filename.
A purely decorative image can use empty alternative text.
Alternative text is distinct from a visible caption or hover tooltip.

Changing an image's displayed dimensions does not reduce its original file size.
The browser may still download the full source image.
Physically reducing stored pixel dimensions can reduce image data.
File size also depends on format, content and compression.
Too little detail can make an enlarged raster image blurred or pixelated.
Choose stored dimensions suited to the intended use.
Check image quality as well as download size.

Aspect ratio is the relationship between image width and height.
Proportional resizing changes both dimensions by the same factor.
It preserves the shapes within the image.
Changing width and height by different factors can stretch or squash the image.
Cropping can change the frame shape without stretching retained objects.
Check the displayed image rather than only its numerical dimensions.

The video element provides video content within a page.
Its source identifies the media file.
Alternative source formats can support different browser capabilities.
Playback controls let the user interact with the video.
Control behaviour can include starting, pausing or seeking.
Fallback content can explain that the video element is unsupported.
The referenced media must be available and playable in the intended environment.

The audio element provides sound content within a page.
Source and type information identify the media resource and format.
Playback controls let the user start, pause or otherwise control the clip.
Supported sources can differ between browsers and media formats.
Fallback content can explain unsupported audio elements.
The file must be accessible at the referenced location.
Audio markup is distinct from the actual sound file it references.

CSS colours can be written using supported named colours.
They can also use hexadecimal RGB notation.
Examples of colour names include red, blue and white.
The available named colours are not restricted to just the original 16 basic names.
Hexadecimal notation gives explicit component values.
Choose readable colour combinations appropriate to the content.
A colour value's notation is distinct from whether it is used for text or background.

Six-digit hexadecimal RGB uses the form #RRGGBB.
The first pair represents red, the second green and the third blue.
Each pair ranges from 00 to FF.
00 means zero intensity for that component and FF means full intensity.
Each pair represents a value from 0 to 255.
For example, #FF0000 is full red with no green or blue.
The leading hash identifies the hexadecimal colour notation in CSS.

RGB combines coloured light additively.
Full red, green and blue together produce white: #FFFFFF.
All components at zero produce black: #000000.
Full red and green with no blue produce yellow.
Full green and blue with no red produce cyan.
Full red and blue with no green produce magenta.
These are combinations of light rather than rules for mixing paint.

Foreground text colour and background colour are separate properties.
The color property normally controls text colour.
background-color controls an element's background colour.
The same colour can have different roles depending on the property.
Sufficient contrast helps keep the text readable.
Check the text against the actual background, including any background image.
Changing the background does not automatically choose an accessible text colour.

ol defines an ordered list.
ul defines an unordered list.
li defines a list item.
Ordered lists normally use a sequence of markers such as numbers.
Unordered lists normally use bullet markers.
A list inside another list represents a lower level.
CSS can change marker appearance and indentation.
List structure is distinct from manually typing marker characters into paragraphs.

An element's id can identify a specific location in a page.
IDs must be unique within the document.
A fragment link can lead directly to that identified element.
This can support navigation to a section of a long page.
Meaningful identifiers help organise destinations.
An in-page target is different from a browser bookmark storing a page address.
The target marks the destination; a hyperlink provides the navigation action.
Explain the identified in-page location and the link that jumps to it; distinguish this from a browser bookmark.

The a element can define a hyperlink.
Its href identifies the destination.
A link can lead to another page or website.
A fragment destination can identify a position within the same or another page.
Text or images can provide clickable link content.
A link can help users move directly to relevant information.
The visible source object and the destination are different parts of the link.
A URL alone does not explain the link's purpose.
Explain navigation to another resource or location; a URL description alone is insufficient.

The target attribute determines the browsing context used for a link.
_self normally opens the destination in the current context.
_blank requests a new browsing context, commonly a tab or window.
The browser and user settings affect the exact tab or window behaviour.
A named context can be reused.
The target setting differs from the href destination.
Opening elsewhere does not change the address of the linked resource.

A mailto link identifies an email destination.
Activating it can open the user's configured email application.
It can supply the recipient address.
It may also supply a subject or other message details.
The user normally reviews and sends the message.
The link does not itself guarantee that an email is sent.
It differs from a hyperlink to an ordinary web page.

A relative path locates a resource from the applicable current or base location.
It can identify a file in the same folder or a related subfolder.
It does not need the complete website address for that relative reference.
Keeping the same relative folder structure supports portability.
Pages and supporting media can be moved together without rewriting each relative link.
The referenced files still need to exist in the expected positions.
A relative path is different from a complete absolute URL.
State what the path is relative to and distinguish it from a complete absolute address.

A local absolute path can include a particular drive and full folder location.
Another computer may not have that drive, folder or file.
A reference tied to the old location can therefore stop working after transfer.
The page may lose a linked image, stylesheet or destination page.
Portable relative references can help when the whole folder structure moves together.
A complete web URL is also absolute but has different availability conditions from a local drive path.
Explain the actual broken reference rather than assuming every absolute URL is invalid.
Explain that a reference to an old location can break the hyperlink after files are moved.

The title element supplies the document's page title.
It belongs in the head section.
Browsers use it for the tab or title bar.
It can help identify saved bookmarks and search results.
It is separate from a heading displayed in the body.
Use a meaningful title identifying the page.
A page title does not replace the visible main heading's structural role.
Identify the page title as document information in the head rather than a body heading.

Metadata is information about the document.
It can describe the author, page description or character encoding.
Viewport metadata can guide display on different devices.
Metadata normally belongs in the head.
It is not ordinary visible body content.
A metadata name identifies the category and content supplies its value where that form is used.
Use head rather than heading or header when naming the HTML section.
When asked where metadata belongs, name the head section, not heading or header.

Character encoding determines how stored bytes represent characters.
A charset declaration identifies the document's encoding.
UTF-8 supports Unicode characters from many writing systems.
A suitable declaration helps the browser interpret text correctly.
Modern HTML uses UTF-8.
The meta element is void and does not have a closing meta tag.
Encoding metadata is separate from a visible font choice.
Identify charset accurately as character-encoding metadata.

Author metadata can identify who created the document.
Description metadata provides a short description of the page.
The name attribute identifies the metadata category.
The content attribute supplies its value.
These items normally occur in the head.
They do not automatically create visible author text or a page paragraph.
A description may inform how a search engine presents the page, but the final snippet is not guaranteed.
Distinguish the metadata category named by name from the value supplied by content.

Keyword metadata lists terms describing the document's topics.
It is source metadata rather than visible body text.
The textbook includes it as a metadata example.
Adding more keyword terms does not guarantee a better search ranking.
Google Search does not use the keywords meta tag for indexing or ranking.
Relevant, accurate metadata should not be confused with a guaranteed search-engine outcome.

The viewport is the area in which a browser displays the page.
Viewport metadata helps control layout on mobile devices.
width=device-width uses the device's viewport width for the layout viewport.
initial-scale=1 sets the initial zoom scale.
These settings support layouts intended for smaller displays.
They do not by themselves make every fixed-size page responsive.
Content and CSS must also suit the available space.

A base element can set a page-wide default target for links.
It belongs in the head.
Individual links can override the default with their own target.
This avoids repeating the same target on every link.
The default target concerns where linked content opens.
It is distinct from the base URL that a base element can also specify for resolving relative URLs.

A shared stylesheet defines reusable presentation rules.
Several pages can link to the same CSS file.
Changing a shared rule can update the appearance of the pages using it.
This saves repeated formatting work.
Consistent fonts, colours and layout support a coherent site and corporate identity.
The stylesheet remains separate from each page's content markup.
Its file reference must be correct and accessible.
Explain reuse across pages and the separate stylesheet file rather than relying only on font examples.

Inline CSS is written in an element's style attribute.
Internal CSS is written in a style block, commonly in the head.
External CSS is stored in a separate linked stylesheet.
A shared external file can be used by multiple pages.
An inline declaration directly targets its own element.
Internal rules apply according to their selectors within that document.
All three forms participate in the cascade rather than representing three different languages.
Compare the separate linked file with declarations on the relevant HTML element; do not call an external file embedded CSS.

The cascade resolves competing CSS declarations.
Normal inline author declarations take precedence over normal author stylesheet rules.
Important declarations and other cascade conditions can alter the outcome.
Selector specificity matters among otherwise comparable rules.
When relevant precedence and specificity are equal, the later declaration wins.
A later external stylesheet does not automatically override every earlier or inline declaration.
Apply the rule to the same element and property when reasoning about a conflict.
Avoid treating the chapter's simple examples as universal priority rules.
For the simple conflict described, explain that the inline style takes precedence over the external rule.

A CSS rule contains a selector and a declaration block.
The selector identifies the elements to which the rule applies.
The declaration block is enclosed in braces.
Each declaration pairs a property with a value using a colon.
Semicolons separate declarations.
For example, p { color: blue; } selects paragraphs and sets their text colour.
Correct syntax is needed for the intended declaration to apply.

Several selectors can share one declaration block.
Commas separate the selectors in a group.
For example, h1, h2 can share a colour rule.
Grouping avoids repeating the same declarations.
Each listed selector matches its own set of elements.
A comma-separated group is different from a selector describing a parent-child relationship.
Change the common block when all grouped selections need the same update.

An external stylesheet is saved as a .css file.
HTML links to it using a link element in the head.
The href identifies the stylesheet's location.
rel="stylesheet" identifies the relationship.
A relative path must locate the correct file.
The file must be included with the site's supporting resources.
A broken link can leave the page without its intended external styling.
CSS files contain stylesheet rules rather than a complete HTML document.
Explain that the external stylesheet is a separate file linked from the head.
Purpose and syntax of CSS comments

CSS comments annotate stylesheet source.
They start with /* and end with */.
Comment text does not apply a style declaration.
Comments can explain the purpose of a rule or section.
They differ from HTML's <!-- and --> delimiters.
A comment is not normally visible page content.
The source remains readable to anyone who can access it.

HTML uses markup elements to describe content and structure.
CSS uses selectors and declarations to describe presentation.
A CSS declaration uses property: value syntax.
A CSS rule is not enclosed in an HTML paragraph or heading tag inside a .css file.
The HTML style element can contain CSS within an HTML document.
Invalid syntax can prevent the intended styling from applying.
Keep the two languages' roles and syntax distinct.

A font-family list gives preferred fonts in order.
The browser tries available fonts from that list.
A generic family supplies a fallback when named fonts are unavailable.
For example, Arial, sans-serif provides a named preference and a generic alternative.
Multiword family names can be quoted.
The font actually displayed depends on available fonts and character coverage.
A fallback list improves resilience without guaranteeing identical rendering everywhere.

Serif fonts have small finishing strokes.
Sans-serif fonts do not have those serifs.
Cursive fonts resemble joined or handwritten lettering.
Fantasy refers to decorative font designs.
Monospace fonts use equal advance widths for characters.
Monospace is different from proportional spacing, where widths vary.
These are generic families rather than individual font-face names.
Choose the family to suit the content and audience.

CSS font sizes can use explicit length units or relative values.
Examples of absolute CSS units include px, pt and pc.
For font-size, em is relative to the inherited font size.
ex relates to the font's x-height.
Size keywords provide another way to express the intended scale.
Relative sizing depends on its context.
A CSS pixel is not necessarily one physical hardware pixel.
Check readability at the intended display size.

font-weight controls weight, such as normal or bold.
font-style controls styles such as italic.
text-decoration can apply an underline.
text-align controls horizontal text alignment.
text-indent controls indentation of the first line.
color controls text colour.
Use properties according to the intended effect.
Changing appearance does not replace choosing the correct structural HTML element.

CSS can give a page or element a background colour.
It can also reference a background image using a URL.
The referenced image must be accessible.
A background image is distinct from an img element carrying content.
A background colour can remain visible where the image does not cover the area.
Choose colours and images that keep foreground content readable.
Background styling belongs to presentation.

A background image can repeat to fill an area.
It can repeat in both directions.
repeat-x repeats horizontally and repeat-y vertically.
no-repeat prevents tiling.
The chosen behaviour depends on the image and design.
A repeated pattern differs from stretching one image.
Check that repetition does not interfere with the content.

Background position controls where a background image is placed.
The image may sit behind text or other content.
Busy or high-contrast backgrounds can make text difficult to read.
Suitable text colours and spacing improve clarity.
Content can be kept clear of an important background area.
Check the final layout at the intended sizes.
Positioning a background does not automatically reserve layout space for it.

Reusable CSS rules can define table presentation.
They can specify dimensions, borders and background colours.
Cell rules can define padding and content alignment.
Border spacing and border collapse control different aspects of the table's boundaries.
Shared rules keep related tables consistent.
Specific rules can adapt selected tables or cells.
Separate the table's data structure from its visual formatting.

A class identifies a selected group of elements.
HTML uses a class attribute containing the class name.
A CSS class selector begins with a dot, such as .highlight.
The same class can be reused on several elements.
An element-type selector such as h1 targets that element type.
A class can add or change presentation for only selected elements.
Both class rules and element rules are author-defined CSS rules.
Classes are not restricted to being stored in an external file.
Use the dot-prefixed class selector accurately and distinguish it from an element selector such as h1.

CSS selectors can target different parts of a table.
table targets the table element and tr targets rows.
th targets header cells and td targets data cells.
thead, tbody and tfoot identify table sections.
Class or more specific selectors can target selected cells or tables.
Different parts can have different backgrounds, borders and text alignment.
The chosen selector determines where a rule applies.
Check the final cascade when several rules affect the same cell.
